items.title: The best early Black Friday deals you can already shop
paragraphs: The countdown to Black Friday is on, and the discounts are starting to appear. Although the shopping holiday isn’t officially until November 27th, retailers are already dropping early deals on some of our favorite tech. Of course, with prices rising across the board, a good discount doesn’t necessarily mean you’re getting a historically low price. But we’re still seeing worthwhile discounts on a host of tried-and-tested gear, with more expected next week.

Below, we’ve rounded up the best early Black Friday deals we’ve found so far. Prices could drop further as Black Friday approaches, as is always the case, but these deals are worth considering if you’d rather shop early and beat the holiday rush. We’ll continue to update this guide as more retailers launch their holiday sales, too, so be sure to check back regularly as we get closer to the main event.

Apple’s AirPods Pro 3 deliver the best noise cancellation and sound quality of any AirPods yet, along with a more comfortable, secure fit and improved water resistance. They also feature built-in heart rate tracking for workouts and support live translations for a handful of languages. Read our review.

Sony’s DualSense Wireless Controller for the PlayStation 5 features immersive haptic feedback and resistance triggers, which feel great to use. It offers a built-in mic, a 3.5mm headphone jack, and a mute button; it also works with PC, macOS, and mobile devices via Bluetooth or USB-C.

007 First Light, a third-person stealth action game from the studio behind Hitman, is arguably the best action game we’ve played this year. It features a wide variety of missions that have you sneaking through enemy territory, engaging in hand-to-hand combat, and taking part in high-speed car chases — you know, classic Bond stuff. Read our review.

Amazon’s last-gen Fire TV Stick 4K Plus streams in 4K and supports Dolby Atmos, Dolby Vision, and Alexa Plus. It also ships with the redesigned Fire OS and, unlike more recent models, still lets you sideload Android TV apps.

The Apple Watch Series 12 introduces AI-powered Audio Intelligence features, including sound recognition alerts, Live Rewind, and Siri Recap. It can also track your heart rate every five seconds, even when you’re not exercising, and offers faster charging than prior models. Read our review.

Philips Hue bulbs can be pricey, which is why the company’s four-pack of Essential A19 bulbs is a great buy at the current sale price. The adjustable bulbs offer white and color ambiance, 800 lumens of brightness, and can be controlled either via Bluetooth or a Hue Bridge (sold separately).

Fanttik’s rechargeable electric screwdriver features three adjustable torque settings, a built-in LED light, and 16 S2 hardened steel bits for tackling everything from furniture assembly to small electronics repairs. It also comes with a magnetic storage case and supports USB-C.

You likely won’t find wireless earbuds with a more striking appearance than Nothing’s Ear 3A. They also sound fantastic, boast active noise cancellation, and offer robust EQ settings, making them a great pick for the price. Read our review.

Apple’s most affordable laptop uses the same A18 Pro chip found in the iPhone 16 Pro. It features a vibrant 13-inch display, surprisingly good speakers, and 8GB of RAM, making it a solid option for students and anyone who needs a laptop for everyday tasks. Read our review.

The cheaper, more streamlined SoundLink Max features a slightly smaller battery (16 vs. 20 hours) and lacks external power bank functionality. Otherwise, it’s the same as the standard model, which means the audio is just as great.

Ember’s latest smart mug is designed to keep your coffee at the ideal temperature for up to three hours, with five temp settings between 120 and 145 degrees Fahrenheit. The third-gen version is similar to prior models; however, you can now adjust the heat settings directly on the mug and throw it in the dishwasher, which wasn’t the case before.

Despite being an entry-level variant of the B6 OLED, this model features four HDMI 2.1 ports, a 120Hz refresh rate, a capable processor, and pixel-perfect image quality and contrast for any content you want to watch. Lower brightness is likely the biggest compromise with getting a cheaper OLED.

JBL’s Tour One M3 noise-canceling headphones come with a touchscreen-equipped wireless transmitter that lets you wirelessly listen to audio from in-flight entertainment systems and other devices without Bluetooth. They also offer solid active noise cancellation and last up to 70 hours on a charge.

Hisense’s 2026 CanvasTV is a 4K QLED TV that doubles as wall art when you’re not watching. It features a matte, anti-glare display and runs on Google’s excellent TV software; it’s also a great pick for gamers thanks to its snappy 144Hz variable refresh rate and a pair of HDMI 2.1 ports.

The Elegoo Centauri Carbon 2 Combo is a beginner-friendly 3D printer that supports four filament spools. It features an enclosed build chamber, automatic bed leveling, and a large touchscreen, making it easy to produce reliable prints.

Moft’s Trackable Tripod Wallet is a MagSafe-compatible wallet that holds two cards and folds into an adjustable phone stand or small tripod. It also supports both Apple’s Find My network and Google’s Find Hub, offers Qi wireless charging, and includes a detachable shutter remote for taking photos.

Govee’s Table Lamp 2 is way more fun than your average table lamp. The color-changing device boasts built-in scheduling and more than 60 dynamic lighting effects, including preset scenes for various holidays. You can even create custom color combos for when “Dandelion” and other presets just aren’t cutting it.

Birdfy’s metal smart bird feeder features a wide-angle 4K camera that lets you get an up-close look at visiting birds, along with a 1.8-liter seed capacity and a built-in solar panel for charging. It also offers free AI-powered recognition of more than 6,000 bird species.

Tessan’s universal travel adapter delivers up to 205W of combined USB charging power and can charge up to eight devices, including a pair of laptops, at the same time. It features six USB-C ports, including two that can deliver up to 140W individually, a USB-A port, and an AC outlet. It also works in over 200 countries and regions.

Bambu Lab’s P2S Combo is a 3D printer that can print in multiple colors and automatically dry its materials to help improve print quality. It also features a 5-inch touchscreen, a built-in camera for monitoring prints remotely, and AI-powered tools that can detect printing problems.

Eight Sleep’s Pod 6 automatically adjusts your bed’s temperature based on your sleep patterns, heart rate, and breathing. It features a redesigned hub that’s half the size of its predecessor and adjusts temperatures faster. The system also tracks sleep quality, detects snoring, and lets couples control the temperature on each side of the bed independently.

Flextail’s Zero Pump 2 might weigh a mere 1.7 ounces, but it can quickly inflate and deflate a sleeping pad. It comes with six nozzles and a replaceable battery that recharges via USB-C, allowing you to inflate up to 30 pads on a single charge.

The last-gen Litter-Robot 4 can monitor your cat’s visits, track their weight, and automatically separate waste from clean litter after each use, so you can go up to eight days without emptying your cat’s litter box. The so-called starter bundle also includes 20 pounds of litter, 25 waste drawer liners, a host of odor-control accessories, a litter-trapping mat, and a three-year warranty.

Headspace makes it easier to build mindfulness into your everyday life, whether you’re looking to manage stress, improve focus, or get a better night’s sleep. An annual subscription gives you access to hundreds of guided meditations, breathing exercises, and other tools for beginners and experienced users alike.

Part of Casetify’s early Black Friday sale, which offers up to 50 percent off select phone case styles, this Moonaries Illo case features playful artwork from the illustrator behind Mocha Cat. It’s available for the iPhone 17 Pro, iPhone 16 Pro, and other iPhone models.

The Icemag 3 can wirelessly deliver up to 25W of power to compatible smartphones and up to 35W wired charging via USB-C. The 10,000mAh Qi2 charger can also act as a foldable kickstand, comes with an integrated USB-C cable that serves as a lanyard, and sports a transparent design with colorful RGB lighting.

EcoFlow’s 25,000mAh / 90Wh battery laptop power bank can deliver up to 140W of power through either of its two USB-C ports, or a combined 170W when charging up to three devices simultaneously. The TSA-approved battery also features a built-in display for monitoring power output.

Saros is a third-person sci-fi shooter in which players fight alien enemies on a mysterious planet trapped in a time loop. The PS5 exclusive features fast-paced combat, a variety of powerful weapons, and challenging boss fights. Read our review.

Bose’s second-gen QuietComfort Headphones build on the original with better sound quality and support for lossless audio over USB-C. They also offer improved noise cancellation and are more comfortable thanks to their lack of “eardrum suck.”
Garmin’s midrange Forerunner watch has an OLED display, a week’s worth of battery life, and dual-frequency GPS for better accuracy. Read our review.

The Dreame X60 Ultra is a powerful robot vacuum and mop that does a great job of cleaning carpets, thanks to its dual roller brushes and 35,000Pa of suction. It can climb over tall thresholds, squeeze under low furniture, and automatically detach its mop pads when vacuuming carpets.

The Matic robot vacuum and mop is ideal for cluttered homes with pets, multiple floors, and a mixture of carpets and hardwood. It offers almost human-like navigation, tackling high-pile rugs, and mopping up wet spills. The quiet bot also requires less maintenance than many rivals thanks to its onboard water tank and dust bag. Read our review.

The Eufy Omni C28 combines excellent mopping performance with a small self-cleaning dock that’s well suited for apartments and other smaller spaces. It navigates around furniture and into tight areas with ease, while its roller mop does a great job cleaning hard floors.

Nothing’s first pair of over-ear headphones feature a retro transparent design and high-end features like active noise cancellation, spatial audio with head tracking, and plush ear pads. They also feature a paddle button that allows you to control music playback. Read our review.

Amazon’s 12.3-inch Alexa Tablet 12 Pro runs Android with access to the Google Play Store, unlike the company’s Fire tablets. It also features built-in Alexa Plus integration, a dedicated Kindle reading mode, and up to 16 hours of battery life. Read our hands-on impressions.

Samsung’s last-gen Frame is a 4K QLED TV that displays art on its anti-glare matte screen when not in use. It also supports Dolby Atmos, HDR10 Plus, and popular streaming apps, with refresh rates up to 144Hz on larger models.

TP-Link’s smart smart plug lets you remotely control lamps, fans, and other appliances using your phone or voice commands. It supports Matter, so it works with all major smart home platforms, and lets you set schedules and timers to automatically turn devices on or off.
Update, November 18th: Added a host of new deals, including those for the Apple Watch Series 12, 007 Fire Light, and the Matic robot vacuum.

items.title: The first Nvidia RTX Spark mini PCs launch today from Asus, Dell, and MSI
paragraphs: is a news writer covering all things consumer tech. Stevie started out at Laptop Mag writing news and reviews on hardware, gaming, and AI.

After the first RTX Spark laptops launched earlier this year, Nvidia’s RTX Spark N1X chip is also now available in desktops from Asus, Dell, and MSI. More RTX Spark desktops are coming later from Acer, Gigabyte, and HP, while Microsoft’s Surface RTX Spark Dev Box is slated to start shipping this month. The new mini PCs include a 6144-core Nvidia Blackwell RTX GPU, 20-core Nvidia Grace CPU, and up to 128GB of memory. That high-end hardware comes with a price to match — Asus’s ProArt GR1X starts at $4,499 for a configuration with 64GB of memory and 1TB of storage.

Like the RTX Spark laptops that compete with the MacBook Pro and the DGX Spark desktop Nvidia launched last year, the new mini PCs are Mac Mini or Mac Studio alternatives for developers working with local AI models, as well as RTX-accelerated software. That includes the AI-powered features for tools like Adobe Premiere and Photoshop, and new DLSS 4.5 Ray Reconstruction support in Blender 5.3.

They can run games too, and Windows on Arm game support is improving, but at these prices, that’s not a realistic reason to pick one up yet. Nvidia says they can act as a “dedicated Windows PC for local models and always-on agents,” and deliver “up to 1 petaflop of AI performance.” They also feature native CUDA support and access to Linux development tools through Windows Subsystem for Linux.

items.title: What is Nvidia without AI’s sugar daddy in charge?
paragraphs: If the glorious AI revolution rests entirely on the well-being of one man, AI is perhaps not as robust a technology as I had previously been led to believe. Nonetheless, chunks of Silicon Valley are now insisting he is indispensable. For instance, if Elon Musk is telling the truth, then Jensen Huang (the former CEO of Nvidia, a company with a market cap of about $3 trillion) has been making deals that were “a handshake with Jensen” with suppliers — “not a written contract,” Musk wrote.

Fascinating stuff to tell shareholders. But after listening to Nvidia’s first earnings call with its new CEO, Colette Kress, I do think something may have shifted. In her former role as CFO, Kress generally told Huang to stop spending so much money on financing its customers, because telling the CEO to stop spending so much goddamn money is the CFO’s job. Apparently he belittled her about this, but that’s the CEO–CFO relationship, baby! Anyway she’s the boss now, at least temporarily. I think it’s reasonable to assume that though Nvidia has for years been the AI industry’s sugar daddy, without Huang and his handshakes in the picture, it may be less liberal with its cash.
Kress shot down the idea that Huang’s departure would lead to a brain drain within Nvidia

Kress’ job was never going to be easy. Even without tantrums from the likes of Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney and Musk, both of whom seem to have a lot of free time for guys who are ostensibly running multibillion-dollar companies, having to steer a company after an event on the scale of Huang’s meltdown is a miserable task. But this woman also is now having to deal with a bunch of guys publicly insisting that Huang was the only reason Nvidia succeeded. It amused me on the call that she did the thing I often do when men decide they can bully me, which is to tap in another man who is theoretically or actually in charge of me — and so on the call, Nvidia board Chair Harvey C. Jones politely told these losers to get bent. The board does not intend to reinstate Huang, and the company won’t be taking questions about him.

On the call, Kress pointedly noted that Nvidia’s agreements with suppliers last through the end of the decade, so I suppose we must entertain the possibility that when it comes to the handshake deals, Musk is, once again, lying. This is an important thing, though — as SemiAnalysis noted in its bizarrely conspiratorial post on the situation, Nvidia is successful because it has choked off the supply chain.
Do you have information about Nvidia? Contact Elizabeth Lopatto securely on Signal at lopatto.46

Kress also shot down the idea that Huang’s departure would lead to a brain drain within Nvidia, or the kind of open internal revolt that got Sam Altman reinstated at OpenAI during “the blip” in 2023. She told investors that “our employees, we believe, are committed. They are committed to doing their life’s work at Nvidia.” Nvidia’s employees have “been working seamlessly on what they need to complete,” she added. “From a business perspective, it’s business as usual.” I’m sure we’ll hear more about this in the coming days, but unlike with Altman, Huang resigned, and we all know why. And while some employees support reinstating Huang, I notice that there’s a real dearth of “we’ll quit with him” in those sentiments.

I don’t think this is going to shut the Branch Nvidians up, but I do think the board doesn’t have another choice here. Hilariously, we learned this weekend that Nvidia did not buy complete directors’ and officers’ insurance. While the individual executives’ and board members’ personal assets are shielded from lawsuits that stem from its executives’ behavior, the company is not. So if someone, or perhaps several someones, were to file a suit because of, say, Huang’s personal life and its damaging effects on the stock price, Nvidia itself is on the hook.
The scandal isn’t mainly about the affairs, as much fun as we all have been having with them

This is to say nothing of the Securities and Exchange Commission’s investigation — which, given how cliqued up Huang was with President Donald Trump, may be investigating on his behalf rather than investigating him — or the California attorney general going on Bloomberg TV to say that he was going to start kicking the tires on an investigation, or Huang and general counsel Tim Teter’s upcoming congressional testimony. The three actual lawyers left at the Department of Justice may be doing their own investigation, too. Elizabeth Warren seems mad. Marco Rubio’s name has been publicly attached in stories on the leaks, which makes me a little suspicious about who’s been doing the leaking.

A reminder: The scandal isn’t mainly about the affairs, as much fun as we all have been having with them. It is about Nvidia customers allegedly circumventing a ban on selling chips to China. The scandal is already big enough that US policy has been altered; the Department of Commerce informed us all on November 16th that there were new restrictions on selling chips to countries such as Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand, and Brazil. Also, data centers around the world need licenses from the US to lease compute to companies headquartered in China.
“No one could tell them ‘no’ or put them in their place.”

You may be wondering how these restrictions will affect Nvidia’s sales. The company also addressed this, though somewhat obliquely: It raised its forecast, saying that revenue will grow by 75 percent next year. Still, given that Singapore alone was responsible for $104 billion of revenue in 2025, I am curious about the number; at the time, it was the second-biggest geographic area by revenue, dwarfed only by the US. I can’t tell you how much Singaporean sales matter to Nvidia now, because around the time that Singaporean sales reportedly started to represent half the company’s revenue, Nvidia switched its reporting methodology. The company had previously noted that “most shipments associated with Singapore revenue were to locations other than Singapore and shipments to Singapore were insignificant.” Notably, Megaspeed had a Singapore address — and was the subject of a truncated Commerce Department investigation into whether its chips were being diverted to China. Fun stuff!

You know what else is fun? Jensen Huang’s children are still at the company, at least as far as anyone knows. His daughter Madison, described as Huang’s “chief of staff” by The New York Times, even helped direct Nvidia’s response to inquiries about Megaspeed, which have been mounting now for a year, the Financial Times reported. Her husband, Nico Caprez, “was promoted to a role that covered international deals with cloud computing clients in Asia” around the time those inquiries were getting started. “They had a lot of power and influence and were allowed to operate unchecked,” an anonymous source told the FT. “No one could tell them ‘no’ or put them in their place.”

His kids — one of them, Spencer, ran a bar before his role at Nvidia — likely haven’t endeared themselves to their colleagues, based on some of the reporting now trickling out about them. What was Spencer doing at Nvidia? Unknown. “Some executives said they had never encountered Spencer Huang in the course of business,” The Wall Street Journal wrote.
As a person who loves mess, I think the Branch Nvidians should keep this shit coming

Employing the CEO’s relatives was already a governance risk. If the outside agitation continues to reinstate Jensen Huang, there are three key lambs that Nvidia can slaughter, and all of them are his relatives. I suppose the thing I find most astonishing is that Huang doesn’t see the writing on the wall; he has posted that if “the Board of Directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO.” The post was met with, among other things, Altman posting a green heart in response.

Now, as a person who loves mess, I think the Branch Nvidians should keep this shit coming. I mean, Huang can nominate two people to the board of directors before the company’s shareholder meeting next year. Let’s have a stupid proxy fight and see what else leaks about Huang’s leadership and children! Of course, that will be difficult for Kress to manage — but that’s I guess what she’s getting paid for.

Up until now, Kress had been trying to rein in Huang’s spending on the AI ecosystem — financing, investments, and so on — in a huge swath of companies, according to stories in The Information and The Wall Street Journal. According to the Journal’s story, Huang noted that the vaunted deals he’d made with suppliers “were coming at him like an ‘avalanche,’” while “major cloud providers were running away from Nvidia.” This does explain Nvidia’s role as the sugar daddy for the neocloud industry. Kress reportedly pushed back on some of its agreements, apparently significantly downsizing a financial commitment to OpenAI among other things. Now, while she’ll be spending plenty of her time managing the fallout from Huang’s departure, she won’t be directly fighting with him over Nvidia’s finances.
It publicly tells us there are limitations on what Nvidia is willing to support

On the earnings call, analyst Stacy Rasgon of Bernstein Research asked about a new paragraph he’d noticed in the earnings release about neoclouds. Nvidia had been supplying guarantees to some neoclouds by saying it would purchase compute if no one else would. The new paragraph reads, in part, “Our commitments take effect only if the neoclouds secure financing to purchase the data center infrastructure products and the related compute capacity is deployed, made operational, and accepted by us.” Kress clarified that this meant that if neoclouds’ buildout was delayed — or they otherwise had a challenge in building the warehouse to stick the chips in — Nvidia’s guarantee “doesn’t exist anymore,” she said. “Is it new? No. Did we change anything? No,” she said.

I have no way of knowing if this language had been ready to go in the press release before Huang resigned, but it does seem notable all the same. It publicly tells us there are limitations on what Nvidia is willing to support. And knowing Kress wanted Huang to spend less on this stuff, I think it tees us up for an interesting period. Passing under the radar last week were some indications that the Federal Reserve may be about to do an interest rate hike, which is trouble for a number of companies, such as CoreWeave, that rely on debt for their data center buildouts. If we are entering a period where financing is more expensive or more difficult to get, we may see some neoclouds falter. The new paragraph in the earnings release suggests that Nvidia wants us all to know that it’s not going to bail them out forever. Bring Huang back if you want, I guess, but even he can’t control the Fed — or the increasingly odd outlook for data center financing. In the coming months, Nvidia may be better off with a woman who wants to keep the costs down.
You know who is getting money under Kress, though? Nvidia staff. They can expect raises and equity in December.

items.title: Council wins legal fight against flags on lamp-posts
paragraphs: Birmingham City Council has won a High Court injunction preventing unauthorised flags being attached to lamp-posts and other highway infrastructure across the city.
The authority sought the order after thousands of St George's flags and union jacks were put up by supporters of anti-migrant group Raise the Colours from summer 2025 onwards.
Council lawyers argued the displays created safety risks and fuelled tensions, while campaigners said the move would restrict freedom of expression.
Judge Emma Kelly said there was a "compelling need" to grant the interim injunction.
In her ruling, the judge said it would last until trial or further order of the court.
The order applies to Raise the Colours' leader Ryan Bridge; Ben Cullen, who is also associated with the group; and persons unknown from attaching flags to street furniture and highway infrastructure.
It also grants a power of arrest against Bridge and persons unknown, meaning police could arrest someone without a warrant if they are suspected of breaching the injunction.
The council said anyone who breaches the order could be jailed for up to two years, fined or have their assets seized for contempt of court.
The local authority sought the injunction after thousands of St George's flags and union flags were attached to lamp-posts and bridges in Birmingham from summer 2025 onwards.

Lawyers acting for the council argued the displays could pose safety risks, obstruct visibility and contribute to tensions and disorder. The application also referred to reported incidents of alleged intimidation, harassment and obstruction connected to flags being put up in the city.
The court heard that, on one occasion, a man suffered a broken leg when he was struck by a cherry picker being used while flags were being installed.

The case followed similar legal action in Oxfordshire, where the county council secured a permanent injunction against four named individuals over flags attached to lamp-posts and other highway structures.
Bridge opposed the injunction, arguing it would interfere with rights to freedom of expression and protest under the European Convention on Human Rights.
His barrister, Liam Wells, told the court the campaign amounted to political expression protected by the convention and argued the injunction would have a "chilling effect" on those rights.
In her ruling, Kelly stressed the order was not a ban on displaying flags.
"The interim injunction needs to be understood for what it is," she said.
"It is not the court nor the claimant 'banning the union jack' or the display of Pride flags or anything of the like.

"Whilst the interim injunction order will cover flags of all types, it is limited in scope to the restraint of unauthorised flags attached to highway street furniture or infrastructure, and to the restraint of associated conduct, within the administrative area of Birmingham."
She added that concerns the injunction would unduly restrict free expression were "unwarranted" and said she was satisfied it was "just and convenient" to grant the order.

items.title: Our favorite accessories to level up your gaming setup ahead of GTA VI
paragraphs: With Grand Theft Auto VI set to finally launch tomorrow, November 19th, our long-awaited return to Vice City is nearly here. But after all this time, some of the gear you’ve used in San Andreas might feel out of place on the glamorous streets of Leonidas County. Luckily for you, we’ve gathered a few of our favorite Xbox and PlayStation 5 accessories to help your long gaming sessions run as smoothly as possible.

The 8BitDo Ultimate 3E — an upgraded pick for Xbox Series X and Series S consoles — is a very capable, comfortable controller with elite-level features, including a high polling rate and adjustable triggers. It’s on the expensive side at $149.99, but the customization and clean execution justify the cost. Read our review.

PlayStation 5 owners looking for a controller upgrade, meanwhile, might consider the DualSense Edge, Sony’s first-party pro-style controller. In addition to a variety of extra function buttons and paddles, the wireless gamepad sports adjustable trigger heights and swappable joysticks (in case the potentiometers start to drift). It’s a little bit heavier than Sony’s regular DualSense, and the battery life isn’t quite as good, but it offers customization you won’t find on the console’s default controller. Read our review.

Sony’s pro-style controller, the DualSense Edge, might suffer from shorter battery life than the standard DualSense model, but it features great software integration with the PlayStation 5 and plenty of customizable components.

Nothing’s worse than having to pause a heist so you can go hunt down a fresh set of AA batteries. The PowerA Duo Charging Station includes a rechargeable battery and replacement rear doors for two Xbox Series X / S or Xbox One controllers. Simply set them on the dock, and they’ll start charging.
PowerA’s PlayStation equivalent charges two DualSense Wireless Controllers simultaneously, with an included AC adapter, and comes with a two-year warranty.

The 2026 Roku Pro Series is the brand’s first OLED, and the 55-inch version retails for $999.99, which is on the low end of the price spectrum for OLED. Games feel richer and more immersive on OLED panels, thanks to their deeper black levels, which are the result of unlit pixels or sections of the screen. Each Pro Series panel also sports a 120Hz refresh rate, four HDMI 2.1 ports, and both low latency and variable refresh rates for gaming.

For a more premium offering, the Sony Bravia 8 II is one of our favorite screens for movies, with an engaging, immersive picture and excellent image processing. It has great gaming features, too, like a 120Hz refresh rate with variable refresh and an automatic low-latency mode. It’s not cheap, but the OLED makes for an excellent upgrade to your setup. Read our review.

Sony’s latest first-party headset, the $99 PlayStation Pulse Wireless, launches the same day as GTA VI. My colleague Cameron Faulkner recently went hands-on with the wireless headset ahead of its launch on November 19th, and came away impressed with its overall audio quality and comfort. The newest Pulse is also straightforward to set up and use, especially when paired with devices like the PlayStation Portal that support PlayStation Link, Sony’s proprietary low-latency audio connection. It also offers Bluetooth for use with other devices.

For Xbox gamers, it’s hard to beat the SteelSeries Arctis Nova 3X, which retails in multiple colors for $109.99 or less. The wireless headset is lightweight, comfortable, and compatible with a wide variety of other consoles and mobile devices as well, for those rare moments when you aren’t playing GTA VI.

If you’d rather the simplicity of a wired option, Sony’s InZone H6 Air skips the batteries and dongles, instead opting to plug straight into your controller. This open-back gaming headset is lightweight and comfortable, which is great for long hours and late nights. My colleague Cameron Faulkner described its sound as “spectacular,” with several equalizer options available for helping fine-tune the sound to your liking. Read our review.

Ikea’s Poäng chair balances affordability and comfort, with wide, supportive armrests that are just the right height for holding a controller. It comes in a variety of frame materials and cushion colors, too, making it easy to match your other furniture or console. This is my personal chair for console gaming, and I recently added a matching ottoman to the set for maximum relaxation.

items.title: As overdose deaths fall, White House makes misleading claims about who deserves credit
paragraphs: Families look on as President Donald Trump speaks during a ceremony to sign the "Halt All Lethal Trafficking of Fentanyl Act" in the East Room of the White House on July 16, 2025. Evan Vucci/AP hide caption

When the White House announced big improvements in the number of people dying from fatal drug overdoses earlier this week, officials pointed to hopeful new data from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention showing U.S. drug deaths have plunged to their lowest level in roughly a decade, saving nearly 50,000 lives each year.

But leading drug policy researchers say the White House statement also made misleading claims about the timing and cause of the remarkable public health success when it said that gains occurred primarily over the last 18 months due to policies enacted under President Trump's leadership.

"The historic decline in drug overdose deaths demonstrates that America is unequivocally winning the fight against illicit drugs," White House Office of National Drug Control Policy director Sara Carter said in a statement.

Carter credited heightened border security under Trump and claims of success dismantling "narco-terrorist" organizations for the recovery. "Critically, this represents a an approximately 41.5% decrease in total drug overdose deaths compared to the peak under the previous administration," the statement said.
What the White House failed to disclose is that declines in overdose fatalities began much earlier, under the Biden administration, with most of the gains occurring before Trump returned to office.

"Since the spring of 2023, we have seen a steady decline in overdose deaths," said Vanda Felbab-Brown, a drug policy expert at the Brookings Institution. "The fact that it has been sustained is very important."

According to CDC data, reductions in drug deaths began in 2023 and have continued steadily for at least 39 consecutive months — not 18 months as the ONDCP statement said. By the time Biden left office, fatal overdoses had already dropped by roughly one-third, an improvement described by addiction experts at the time as unprecedented.

Nabarun Dasgupta, a street drug researcher at the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill, was one of the first scientists to detect the stunning drop in overdose deaths. He said the trend toward fewer deaths began in some regions and among some demographic groups as early as 2021 and rapidly gained momentum nationwide.
"It was really the period early 2024 through spring 2025 where we were seeing the greatest rate of decline that we've ever seen," Dasgupta said.

Deaths from fentanyl smuggled into the U.S. from Mexico first began to rise in 2013 during President Obama's time in office and accelerated during Trump's first term. Fentanyl overdoses spiked sharply the first two years of Biden's presidency, during the COVID-19 pandemic. Despite progress, fentanyl remains the leading cause of drug deaths nationwide.

Dasgupta, Felbab-Brown and other and addiction experts credit the Biden administration for rolling out policy responses that included wider access to healthcare, making the opioid overdose medication naloxone more readily available, and negotiating a deal with China that disrupted the flow of industrial chemicals used to make fentanyl.

President Joe Biden met China's President President Xi Jinping in Woodside, Calif., in November 2023, on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperative conference. China agreed to curtail shipments of the chemicals used to make fentanyl, the drug at the heart of the U.S. overdose epidemic. Doug Mills/Pool/The New York Times hide caption

The Biden team also scored significant drug interdiction wins against the Mexican cartels that smuggle fentanyl. "We have certainly been seeing over many years, going back to the Biden administration, important efforts to crack down against them," said Felbab-Brown.

Dasgupta and Felbab-Brown both said improvements in reducing drug mortality have continued under Trump. They said it's important to have an accurate timeline of the overdose crisis because researchers are still trying to understand why deaths involving fentanyl surged and why so many fewer people are now dying.

NPR asked the White House about progress in the fentanyl fight under Biden. In an emailed statement, ONDCP director Carter, a former podcaster, journalist and Fox News contributor, blamed Biden for failing to secure the U.S.-Mexico border and for allowing drug deaths to surge in the first place.

"While drug overdose deaths eventually began to decline following the peak, the Biden Administration doesn't get to take credit for overseeing the highest drug overdose numbers in history, then bringing them down from their own failure," Carter said.

Responding to CDC data showing drug deaths began to plummet much earlier than stated the White House announcement, Carter said "this could be misinterpreted as progress on a graph, but it was not progress."

According to Carter, the Trump administration is now well-positioned to build on overdose death reductions made over the last three years, in part by maintaining border security and by continuing to "relentlessly attack" drug gangs.
"We are dismantling and eliminating the violent cartels and drug trafficking organizations through coordinated operations," she said.
But Felbab-Brown at Brookings said she doesn't share the Trump administration's confidence that there has been significant progress "dismantling and eliminating" narco-terrorist organizations.
"I cannot think of one narco-terrorist organization that has been dismantled," she said. "They all continue operating and they are all very strong. They all continue smuggling drugs."

Military experts have also questioned the effectiveness, and legality, of Trump's ongoing strikes against civilian boats in the Caribbean and eastern Pacific, described as smuggling vessels by the Pentagon.

Dasgupta, the addiction researcher at UNC, said he's also concerned about whether progress reducing drug deaths can be sustained next year as the Trump administration implements deep cuts to Medicaid passed by the Republican Congress.
The Congressional Budget Office has estimated the cuts could mean as many as 10 million Americans losing access to health insurance coverage.

"Medicaid is the largest funder of addiction services in the United States," Dasgupta said. "Cutting Medicaid eligibility or making it harder to access forms of effective addiction treatment is guaranteed to leave people out in the cold."

items.title: Karl Kani dressed hip-hop royalty for decades. Now he's telling his own story
paragraphs: Embed <iframe src="https://www.npr.org/player/embed/g-s1-154227/nx-s1-10006127" width="100%" height="290" frameborder="0" scrolling="no" title="NPR embedded audio player">
Designer Karl Kani walks the runway during his show at Miami Fashion Week on Jan. 24, 2024, in Miami. Jason Koerner/Getty Images hide caption
Fashion designer Karl Kani believes hip-hop needed its own clothing brand, one that reflected the music, culture and style of the artists who were changing fashion in the 1990s.

"Hip-hop needed the clothing brand that fit that look, who was from the culture," Kani told NPR's A Martínez on Morning Edition. "And I felt like the marriage between Kani and hip-hop was, like, heaven-sent."

Kani, born Carl Williams, started designing clothing in Brooklyn, New York, in the late 1980s. He was inspired by watching his father, a Haitian tailor, make matching linen suits to sell around the neighborhood.

At the time, hip-hop artists were already wearing names like Ralph Lauren, Tommy Hilfiger and Calvin Klein. But they weren't necessarily wearing the clothes as their designers intended. They favored oversized fits, mixed colors and created looks of their own.

Kani understood the appeal. He began making clothes as a self-taught designer in Brooklyn, New York, in the late 1980s. He helped turn that emerging streetwear style into a brand worn by some of hip-hop's biggest stars, including Tupac Shakur, Aaliyah and The Notorious B.I.G.
But the designer's ambitions extended beyond dressing famous musicians. He wanted to build an international fashion business that could last.
In his new memoir, Karl Kani: A Life By Design, Kani reflects on the creative instincts and business decisions that helped his brand survive long after the decade that made it famous.
Even his name reflects his ambitions. Kani, pronounced like "Can I?," came from the doubts he faced while building his business.

"Can I really come from the inner city and build a clothing brand?" he recalled asking himself. "I didn't know the answer to that question, but I knew if I call myself Kani, then every day I have to answer that question. Yes, I can."
After more than three decades in fashion, Kani also has some thoughts about what hasn't aged quite so gracefully: men in skinny jeans.
"I feel like a lot of guys kind of messed up when the skinny jeans phase came in," he said.
His advice? "Keep it simple, keep it slick and all black. You can never go wrong in all black."
In his conversation with NPR's A Martínez, Kani discusses his new memoir, the rise of his streetwear empire, hip-hop's influence on fashion and why skinny jeans aren't for everyone.

items.title: Tell us: are you playing Grand Theft Auto VI?
paragraphs: It’s been 13 years in the making, and may be the most highly anticipated video game of all time. Grand Theft Auto VI has finally arrived.

The new instalment of the epic crime saga is said to have cost more than $1bn to make and is widely expected to break sales records: some predictions put total sales at 40m copies in its first three months.

Its predecessor GTA V was the bestselling game of the past decade in the US, and reached US$1bn in sales faster than any entertainment product in history. GTA VI is predicted to surpass that number with ease.
The game will be available to buy on Thursday from midnight local time, with gamers in New Zealand among the first to officially be able to download it.
We’d like to hear your initial thoughts on the game. What are you liking and disliking? What’s been the biggest surprise, if anything? How does it compare to previous instalments?
We’d also like to know: are you one of the many people reportedly planning to take time off work to play the game?

items.title: Cheese, pet passports and youth mobility: what’s in the UK-EU ‘relationship reset’ draft?
paragraphs: The UK-EU “relationship reset” agreement, which began in earnest under Keir Starmer, is expected to be signed off by Andy Burnham in Brussels on Friday.
A leaked text of the second draft shows an agreement has largely been reached with some outstanding points.
Here’s what is and isn’t addressed in the 72-paragraph joint communique, from pet passports and cheese imports to student fees and artist touring visas.

You may not make it. The deal states it will “allow people from the EU and the UK to reside for up to three years to engage in activities such as work, studies, au pairing, volunteering, or simply travelling”.
But the deal may not be active until 2030 because work permits are the preserve of national governments, not something Brussels can solve.
“We aim to apply this agreement no later than 2028 and endeavour to ensure that opportunities under the scheme will be available to our young people no later than January 2030,” the draft says.

This has yet to be agreed. The two options in the draft text are a halfway house between international and home fees, or a concession from the UK to allow EU citizens pay the same as British students (or Irish ones, who are also eligible for home fees under a separate longstanding agreement).
The choices, according to the draft, are “significantly reduced undergraduate” or “equal treatment” with UK nationals on tuition fees.
The British government wants to cap youth mobility at between 50,000 and 80,000 places to reduce impact on overall migration numbers. The EU is pushing for at least 100,000.
Some EU states, including Germany, are open to the idea of allowing unlimited numbers of British young people to work, live or study in their countries regardless of UK reciprocation.

Elton John has long been among those demanding the government fix a flaw in the Brexit deal which saw gigging bands or theatre groups unable to tour Europe without major bureaucracy (and its associated cost) since 2021.

The EU has resisted negotiating on the issue because, like youth mobility, it touches on work permits which are a national remit. But in what appears to be a win for the UK, touring artists do feature in the draft text.
No deal been reached, but it has been agreed that “the EU and the UK should explore further mutually beneficial solutions” for “touring artists”.
Not yet. The draft agreement says the sanitary and phyto-sanitary (SPS) agreement will not be implemented until 1 March 2028.
This takes into account primary legislation that is needed on the UK side to dynamically align with EU standards.
No. These are tied to the SPS deal, meaning British travellers will still have to fork out up to £200 every time they take their dog or cat to an EU country.
Travel and transport officials are hoping relevant changes to the SPS agreement can be brought forward.
“Around 15% of our customers have pets with them. For them it will make a huge difference,” Yann Leriche, the chief executive of Getlink, the owner of Eurotunnel, told the Guardian.
No. The EU has pressed the UK to follow its trade defence measures which include quotas on Chinese hybrid-electric cars and tariffs on fully electric cars.

The UK has said it will not be coerced into a decision but is demanding that British manufacturers are not locked out of the upcoming Made in Europe legislation in exchange for forming a kind of trade club with the EU on autos.

Both sides agree to protectionist measures in “a particular supply chain” but there is no agreement yet on how that will apply. According to the text, the EU proposes that “the UK would be bound to ensure in its policies and national legal order the same outcomes” as measures imposed by the EU. The UK’s proposed text says: “We will aim to protect supply chains consistently across our markets and guard against potential risks of circumvention.”
It’s gone. Instead of a vague “trusted partnership”, both sides commit to a “partnership for economic resilience”.
The language in the latest draft agreement has also been tightened up in a concession to the UK, say diplomats.

The UK wants to restore pre-Brexit access to EU databases but this will not be agreed on Friday. The EU will instead explore giving the UK access to its proposed Prüm International scheme “on data exchange for police cooperation to chosen third-country partners”.

There is no mention of Eurodac, the database that stores biometrics of asylum seekers in the EU, and diplomats say sharing this data, which was not collected for law enforcement purposes, could be tricky.
But according to the draft, the EU will “continue exploring ways to reinforce mutual and reciprocal exchanges of data on criminal records of third-country nationals”.

items.title: Alexander Zverev notified of abuse lawsuit by ex-partner during ATP Finals
paragraphs: Alexander Zverev was officially notified of a lawsuit filed by his former partner during the middle of the season-ending ATP Finals on Wednesday. The latest legal case against the men’s world No 1 brought by the mother of the former couple’s daughter alleges that Zverev violated the terms of an out-of-court settlement between the pair after the woman accused him of assaulting her.

The lawsuit brought by Brenda Patea in Germany takes issue with Zverev reportedly saying in an interview with the French sports daily L’Equipe earlier this year that “it has been proven that the accusations were false” and “my innocence has been proven”.
Zverev’s Berlin-based lawyers, Christian Schertz and Anna Sophie Heuchemer, confirmed in a statement that they were formally served with Patea’s lawsuit on Wednesday.

“Our client will defend himself against the lawsuit,” Zverev’s lawyers said. “If the statement attributed to him was indeed made in the form alleged, we consider it to be a permissible expression of opinion” – which would be protected by the German constitution. They said there had been no breach of any contractual obligations.

Patea’s lawyer, Michael Scheele, said that Zverev’s claim over his innocence “triggered a veritable storm of criticism against our client”. He said the backlash was damaging to her business as an influencer and that she also felt her honour had been violated.

“Quite apart from the fact that Zverev’s claim is false, he was not permitted to make any public statements whatsoever, in any form,” he said. “Both Brenda Patea and Alexander Zverev had agreed to this in a settlement.”
Patea is seeking that Zverev be ordered not to repeat such comments and that he be fined up to €250,000 (£208,500) every time if he does.

Zverev faced a charge of causing bodily harm to Patea during an argument in Berlin in May 2020. He always denied any wrongdoing. The case ended in a district court in Berlin in 2024 after the settlement. The case officially declared no verdict and the settlement entailed no acknowledgment of guilt on Zverev’s part. Zverev agreed to pay fines to the state and charitable organisations.
The German player this month ascended to the world No 1 ranking for the first time. He also won his first two grand slam titles this year and is competing this week at the ATP Finals in Turin.

items.title: Regulator mistakenly sent complaints about doctors to newspaper
paragraphs: More than 200 doctors have had their details leaked to the Times newspaper
The doctors' regulator the General Medical Council (GMC) has apologised after it mistakenly sent information about more than 220 doctors to a national newspaper.
The information included summaries of complaints alleging antisemitism or Islamophobia against the doctors.
For some of the medics involved, it was only when the GMC alerted them to the data breach that they discovered a complaint had been made about them.
The GMC says it is "very sorry" for the incident and has reported itself to the Information Commissioner's Office.

The GMC - an independent body that regulates doctors, physician associates and anaesthesia associates to protect patient safety - sent the information about 223 doctors to a journalist at the Times newspaper.
While no names were revealed, GMC identification numbers were included, which would easily allow doctors to be found on the regulator's register.
Some doctors have also raised concerns that their ethnicity was included in the data breach.
All the medics involved have been the subject of a complaint involving either antisemitism or Islamophobia, dating from the Hamas attack on Israel in October 2023 to September 2026.
The GMC says it has a legal and statutory responsibility to investigate such claims.
Meanwhile, the Times is understood to have promised not to make any of the leaked details public, but has said it will not delete the leaked information.
A spokesman for the doctor's trade union, the British Medical Association (BMA), condemned the leak.

"The BMA is aware that a number of doctors have received communication from the GMC to say that it erroneously sent personal identifiable data about them to the Times newspaper when responding to a media request," it said.
"The GMC must take action to ensure such a breach never occurs again."
The BMA said it would look at ways to support members affected and urged them to make contact via their website.
A doctors' campaign group, The Doctors' Association UK (DAUK), called for an independent investigation into the leak.
"If a doctor sent identifiable patient information to a newspaper, they could expect to be referred to the GMC," said Dr Matt Kneale, DAUK co-chairman.

"The GMC should hold itself to the same standard of confidentiality it expects from doctors. It owes every affected doctor a clear account of what it sent, how that happened and what it is doing to get the information deleted."

The doctors' regulator says around a fifth (20%) of the complaints made have already resulted in some sanction related to antisemitism, including two doctors who have been struck off the medical register.
Just over a quarter of complaints over Islamophobia - 26% - have led to disciplinary action.
But other complaints were closed, having failed to reach the threshold for investigation.
The GMC said it had contacted the doctors affected to explain what had happened, to apologise and provide information and support.
A spokesperson added: "We recognise the concern this will cause to both those impacted personally and other registrants and we are very sorry this happened.
"Our priority continues to be supporting those affected and taking steps to reduce the impact of this incident."

items.title: US senators urge White House AI chief to fix vulnerabilities after mass outages
paragraphs: A bipartisan pair of US senators are calling on Jay Clayton, the director of national intelligence and AI czar, to identify and fix vulnerabilities in the US’s infrastructure following nationwide outages at major companies and government agencies.

Maria Cantwell, the top Democrat on the Senate commerce, science, and transportation committee, and Mike Rounds, the Republican chair of the Senate subcommittee on cybersecurity, sent a letter to Clayton on Tuesday, outlining concerns sparked by reports of AI accessing major banks, cyber-attacks in Japan and more.

“The fundamental problem is that AI can discover software weaknesses and help attackers exploit them faster than many organizations can respond,” Cantwell and Rounds wrote to Clayton, who is also serving as the White House AI czar.
“Even when fixes are available, testing and installing patches across interconnected systems can take weeks or months, potentially disrupting essential services,” the senators wrote.

Over the last week, tech outages at major banks, workplace communication systems and even federal infrastructure like the Federal Aviation Administration – triggering a four-hour nationwide flight stoppage that grounded or delayed thousands of flights – have raised alarms about potential cyber-attacks.
Top officials have insisted the disruptions stem from software patch updates that intend to address potential AI harms.
Clayton and other national security officials told lawmakers on Wednesday that there was no indication the recent outages were the result of a malicious attack.

“Based on what we know today, after a great deal of diligence, these are separate service outages associated with maintenance and technical changes. They are not a coordinated or state-sponsored attack,” Clayton said during the House homeland security committee hearing.
Markwayne Mullin, the homeland security secretary, and Christopher Raia, the deputy FBI director, similarly said they had no reason to believe the outages were connected or the result of an attack.

“Many people are patching their systems. They know that they’re legacy systems, have vulnerabilities, they’re outdated,” Clayton told CNBC on Tuesday. “It is time for an upgrade across our digital infrastructure and as you patch and upgrade your systems, taking them down and bringing them back up, there are things like this that happen.”

Mark Warner, the top Democrat on the Senate intelligence committee, echoed Clayton. “AI is making it possible to identify vulnerabilities across enormous numbers of systems at unprecedented speed, creating enormous pressure on companies and government agencies to patch those vulnerabilities immediately, often all at once, putting tremendous strain on systems that weren’t built to handle that pace of change,” he wrote on X.
Marco Rubio, the secretary of state, attempted to quell public speculation and fear by assuring Americans that the tech outages were not linked to one another or the work of malicious actors.

But nationwide cyber outages have roiled the country, filled with voters who are already skeptical of rapidly integrating and developing AI. It is unclear what exactly has caused the widespread outages or if AI played a role.
JD Vance canceled his scheduled interview at the New York Times’ DealBook summit on Wednesday, citing his need to attend meetings addressing the recent tech outages.

Cantwell and Rounds are asking Clayton to provide cybersecurity tools to critical US infrastructure such as hospitals, utilities, small government, federal agencies and more, to prevent further disruptions.

They are also asking that US cybersecurity teams secure the same AI systems that are deployed to find vulnerabilities in software, raising concerns that they can “gain unauthorized access to sensitive systems”.

items.title: Got a canceled flight? 7 clever ways to get rebooked fast
paragraphs: Holiday travel can be stressful. Make a plan for potential flight disruptions with these tips. Aleksei Morozov/Getty Images hide caption
A version of this story was originally published on June 17, 2025.
This year, nearly 6 million travelers are projected to take domestic flights for the Thanksgiving holiday, according to an AAA forecast published in November.
If you plan on being one of those travelers in the coming days, make sure you know what to do in case your flight suddenly gets delayed or canceled.

Air travel has gotten notably worse over the past decade. In 2025, cancellations and delays surged, creating the worst on-time performance for airlines in the United States since 2014, according to a 2026 report by the U.S. PIRG Education Fund, a consumer advocacy group.

So, with holiday schlepping season kicking off this week, what's a weary traveler to do? Ahead, travel experts explain how to make rebooking flights less painful. Because what's worse than a canceled holiday flight is missing the holiday altogether.

Most people react to a cancellation by heading straight to the nearest customer service desk and queuing up to rebook their flight. The problem with that approach? Everyone else on your flight is doing that too.
"You have 300 people getting off the plane. There's maybe one, two people trying to help everyone. That clearly is the least efficient way," says travel reporter Chris Dong.

While standing in line, open up the airline app and rebook yourself, he says. There's often a seamless way to get it done, no customer service conversation necessary. During the holiday rush, when hundreds of other passengers may be trying to rebook at the same time, getting a head start on the airline's app can make an especially big difference.

If you have a travel credit card that gives you lounge access, head there to get one-on-one customer service. "Lounge agents are much more inclined to help you and are usually not as short-staffed," Dong says. "That can get you help quickly."
If you don't already have lounge access, see if you can purchase a day pass on-site. It may be well worth it depending on your flight cost and timeline.

All ticket holders are entitled to a refund if the airline cancels their flight and they don't accept whatever the airline is offering, such as a later flight and/or travel vouchers or vouchers for hotels or meals. However, most airlines in the U.S. aren't required to compensate you for delays or cancellations unless it's the airline's fault (think maintenance issues or staffing problems).

To find out what you're entitled to, check the Department of Transportation's Airline Cancellation and Delay Dashboard. Many major airlines have committed to giving passengers cost-free rebooking, meal vouchers, hotel accommodations, hotel transportation and more.
Once you know what your airline offers, say, a hotel, you can rest easy about what to do that night — and focus on rebooking for the next day.

Once you know what your airline will cover, check what your travel insurance will cover. Many credit cards include some travel insurance coverage, which can provide everything from trip cancellation to luggage insurance to any medical needs that might arise en route.
If you have flight time options when rebooking or flexibility in your travel schedule, choose the early-morning flight. They're your best bet to avoid delays or cancellations, Dong says.
If you're on the first flight out, there's little chance you'll have to wait for that aircraft coming in from another city because it's likely been sitting at the airport overnight.

This is especially worth considering during the holidays, when a single disruption can have a domino effect on subsequent flights. An early departure gives you more opportunities to get rebooked on another flight that same day if something goes wrong — because nobody wants to miss that family Thanksgiving dinner!

If the airline significantly delayed, significantly changed (see DOT website for details) or cancelled the flight and you originally booked your ticket directly with your airline, getting your money back should be no problem, even if the ticket is nonrefundable. But if you booked through a third party such as a travel agent or travel website, you'll have to go through them.

Remember that customer service representatives are likely dealing with hundreds of frustrated passengers during the holiday rush. Being patient and polite won't guarantee an exception, but it certainly won't hurt your chances, suggests Eulanda Osagiede, director of operations at Black Travel Alliance and chief operations officer at Black Travel Summit.

The best approach, she says, is to be "very nice, very friendly" with the customer service representative on the phone. So don't start yelling at them. Treating reps like the human beings they are can make all the difference.

When you're traveling for Thanksgiving, Hanukkah or Christmas, a delay doesn't just mean missing a few hours of vacation. It could mean missing the big family gathering or a favorite kiddo's holiday performance.

So before you leave, take a few minutes to research alternative routes to your destination. Are there other airports nearby? Could you drive part of the way? Are there trains or buses that could get you there if your flight falls through?

It's also worth saving your airline's customer service number, downloading its app, and keeping your confirmation numbers somewhere accessible offline. If you're traveling with kids, pack enough snacks, medications, entertainment and other essentials to get through an unexpected overnight stay.
You can't plan for every possible disruption, but you can make sure you're not starting from scratch when one happens.
This story was edited by Malaka Gharib. The visual editor is CJ Riculan. We'd love to hear from you. Leave us a voicemail at 202-216-9823, or email us at LifeKit@npr.org.

items.title: I was skeptical of this office chair designed for women, but it's a revelation
paragraphs: The Musso E80 Muse is a chair built with women in mind, and it shows. Designed to fit anyone from 4ft 9 to 5ft 11, it solved problems I didn’t realise I had. The soft, silky materials feel a world away from the usual brutalist office chair, and the lumbar support is the best I’ve tried: my lower back ache disappeared after a few days. The levers and knobs feel a bit plasticky, and it took a while to find my perfect position, but once I got there – wow. Well worth trying if you’re on the smaller side.
Why you can trust Creative Bloq Our expert reviewers spend hours testing and comparing products and services so you can choose the best for you. Find out more about how we test.

As most people know, most products are tested on men. From pharmaceuticals to seatbelts, women’s bodies are rarely taken into account in product creation. I’ll admit I’d never considered that my office chair feels just a bit too big for me (and it's got slightly the wrong proportions), but it’s true. Unlike the pink Biro (remember that?), an office chair is a case where a woman’s version could genuinely be considered, so I was happy to try the Musso E80 Muse. Is this heading for our best office chair for back pain guide?

The chair has been built with women in mind in a host of ways, from its size and proportions (it’s designed to fit anyone from 4ft 9 to 5ft 11 – I'm 5 ft 5, fyi) to its materials. With all that in mind, it’s almost great. It has a couple of compromises at this price point, but I think they're worth making.
Want a chair at a discount price? See our Black Friday office chair deals page.

The Muse comes in soft colours: Blush, Pink, Grey and White. It’s a palette removed from the usual office chair offerings, and I won’t comment on the ‘girls like pink’ association. It’s nice to have something that looks more in keeping with my office than the brutalist chairs I’ve had before. The materials are silky smooth and soft, which is pretty delightful.

I’m not saying men wouldn’t want a chair made of something more comfortable and plush than the standard mesh of an ergonomic chair, but sitting on this one was a lightbulb moment. Other upgrades include the flex when you lean back, a handy adjustable footstool, and a much softer, more adjustable lumbar support than on any chair I’ve tried before.

As mentioned, the proportions are different – it has a shorter backrest and the chair can go down further for shorter legs. All of this is fully adjustable so, in theory, you can find the perfect fit.

So that’s the positives for design. The minus points go to some of the other material aspects. The levers and knobs feel brittle and plasticky when you adjust them, which makes me wonder if they could have been sturdier, made from slightly more premium materials. At this price point, I can see they’ve put the money into the other materials, which is understandable.
I’ll start by saying that at first I wasn’t convinced. It took me a long time to adjust the chair into the perfect position and I didn’t think I’d get there. But let me tell you, once I did – wow.

The chair has a lot more ‘give’ than others I’ve tried, allowing you to move around, and I feel much more supported, especially by the lumbar support. It took a while to get into position, but I feel its benefit more than with any other chair. I didn’t realise how supported my lower back could feel. I’m not giving a medical opinion, but my lower back ache disappeared after a few days in the Muse, which was a big surprise.

Let’s discuss seat height. Until I lowered this chair all the way down, I had NO IDEA how I could be sitting. My legs usually dangle, so I put them on a block, but being able to drop the seat all the way and then move it back and forward for the perfect support was a revelation.
This could also be the first time my head has felt supported: I can finally move the headrest all the way forward to meet my head.

The soft materials make a huge difference to how it feels to sit in the chair. It feels like the chair is rising up to support me, rather than the hard, unyielding feeling I didn’t realise my old chair was giving me.

At $369, this chair sits at the lower end of mid-range. It's an accessible price point, and it delivers a lot of benefit for certain people at this price. To keep it accessible, and to focus on the things that matter, Musso has compromised on some of the materials (levers, the finish of some of the plastic parts), but the materials that matter – the seat, arms, lumbar support pad and soft mesh, have lovely attention to detail. I think it's priced about right when you see what else is on the market.

If you have always found office chairs to be unforgiving, slightly the wrong size and shape, and unsightly then this could be a good option for you. Of course, you don't have to be a woman to enjoy these benefits, so if you fall into the height range I'd give it a go.
