items.title: The best TVs in the UK for every home and screen size, tested
paragraphs: If your TV looks like an off-cut from Stonehenge, isn’t quite as smart as your microwave or, heaven forfend, is boring old HD rather than 4K HDR (high dynamic range), it could be time to invest in something more up to date.

But even a cursory look at the latest TVs available will confirm a bewildering array of options, from super-slim models with unfeasibly large screens to high performers that rival the picture quality at your local cinema.

It’s difficult to know where to begin. But don’t despair. I’ve tested nine models and whittled them down to my six recommendations to help you find the best TV in time for the festive family binge-watching season.

This buyer’s guide takes a clear, no‑nonsense look at the latest models worth considering across brands, budgets and platforms. There’s an entry‑level option from Samsung, a feature‑packed mid‑range Hisense model that surprises for the price, and a high‑end LG OLED for those who want the best possible picture quality. I also highlight other sets that stand out for design, value, performance and smart connectivity.

The aim is simple: help you choose the right TV for your home without undue jargon, hype or guesswork. Whether you’re upgrading your main living room screen or buying a second set for the bedroom, this guide will steer you through the options, so you can buy with confidence.
Best TV overallSony Bravia 7 II True RGB mini LED
Best mini LED TV for gamingHisense U7S ULED mini LED TV
Best gallery-style TVTCL A400 Pro QLED mini LED TV

I’ve been reviewing TVs since the glory days of cathode ray tubes, and over the years have scrutinised every panel technology under the sun. I’ve also talked to engineers behind some of the top brands and sought advice from Hollywood creatives who work on your favourite shows and movies about the best way to enjoy their hard work at home.

All the TVs here were tested straight from the box. I documented installation, ease of use and features before measuring each set’s performance using industry-standard metrics. I then sat back and watched a shedload of TV, from streaming services, Blu-rays and regular Freeview.

I compared the screens in daylight and darkened rooms, and assessed their colour and contrast. I looked for vibrant but natural-looking colours, deep blacks and high brightness, as well as the ability to show shadow detail without reducing darker areas to a black splodge.
I also paid close attention to audio. Today’s thinnest TVs can often struggle to produce rich, engaging sound, which is why so many of us end up adding a soundbar.

Usability was another key factor. Most 32in-plus TVs these days come with some form of smart TV operating system, but they’re not all the same. The better-equipped platforms offer more than just the top streaming services; they’ll often have some form of smart home control. Ease of use is paramount.

I also compared the various panel technologies, as these have a fundamental impact on picture quality. OLED screens produce perfect blacks and look great when you dim the lights. Some QLED models make great entry-level screens, while mini LED TVs generally offer higher brightness, making them a top choice for daytime viewing and, depending on the model, gaming.
All nine TVs were returned to the manufacturers after testing. Three didn’t make the final cut – although there was nothing intrinsically wrong with them.

On the cutting room floor were the Philips 55in OLED761, an extremely well-equipped budget OLED that you can pick up for £1,199; the Samsung 65in S83H, which is a fine entry-level OLED bolstered by a superb Tizen smart TV OS; and the 48in Panasonic Z90B, a great small-screen OLED option.
What we loveBright, detailed picture quality
What we don’t loveBulky screen, so think twice about wall mounting it

The Bravia 7 II is a Christmas cracker of a 4K TV. Image quality is outstanding for its class, sound is great, and it’s a natural partner for a PlayStation 5. If you’re seeking high-impact HDR, strong gaming credentials and Sony’s impressive image processing in a mini LED panel format, this is it.

Why we love it The Sony Bravia 7 II True RGB mini LED TV approaches the luxurious black levels of an OLED TV, long considered the gold standard in picture quality by home cinema fans, combined with the high brightness generally associated with mini LED.

True RGB is the name of Sony’s own mini LED backlight technology. It’s designed to produce greater colour accuracy and contrast than regular mini LED models. While the 55in model reviewed here launched at £1,999, you should expect to pay closer to £1,499 if you find the Bravia 7 II on sale. And while that price might make you wince, it offers outstanding value in the world of TVs.

The downside is that this tech comes with some bulk. It’s a big beast for a 55in screen, and I’d hesitate to wall-mount it. Its design, though, is very cool, thanks to a partly transparent Mirage stand that hides cabling and a textured rear panel.

The set supports 4K gaming up to 120Hz, but only on two of its four HDMI inputs, and one of those has to serve as the eARC connection if you’re hooking up an external sound system. That means owners of both an Xbox and a PlayStation 5 will have to choose which console they want to optimise if they’re also planning to add a soundbar.

The set also has PS Remote Play, which allows you to game on a PlayStation 5 console, even when it’s in another room, over wifi. As for its smart services, Google TV provides access to a wide selection of streaming and catchup channels.

The main reason to buy the Bravia 7 II is image quality. There’s a barrage of proprietary processing at play here, including clever motion control and detail upscaling. HDR performance is superb. Small highlights in dark scenes have gripping intensity, while Sony’s RGB Triluminos Max system produces rich colours without tipping into lurid oversaturation. I thought the set did a fantastic job painting the alien landscapes of Jennifer Lopez’s sci-fi adventure Atlas on Netflix, without sacrificing the deep blacks of outer space.

Sony’s high level of performance extends to audio: 40W of amplification drives two full-range speakers and two tweeters, producing plenty of volume and enough punch to make films and games enjoyable. Dune: Part Two has a dramatic, bass-rich soundtrack that came across well here, while Overwatch on the PS5 offered an enjoyable level of sonic excitement.
Remember that while this Bravia 7 II is more expensive than some 55in rivals, you won’t need to spend more than £300 on a soundbar right out of the gate.

It’s a shame that … the screen only has two HDMI inputs that support 120Hz gaming, especially given that the company is a gaming powerhouse. This restriction limits your options when it comes to system building.
Operating system: Google TV Connections: HDMI, ethernet, wifi, Bluetooth Dimensions (without stand): 122.8 x 5.4 x 70.4cm (WDH) Weight (without stand): 18.4kg
What we loveBright, detailed picture quality
What we don’t loveBulky screen, so think twice about wall mounting it
What we loveHeaps of features at a reasonable price
What we don’t loveNot my first choice for watching films in a darkened room

The Samsung M80H makes perfect sense if you want a feature-packed 55in TV without spending the sort of money you’d need to buy the brand’s leading Neo QLED. It’s perfect for everyday viewing and streaming, and is well equipped for gaming. You get a lot of TV tech for the money.
Why we love it An affordable option in Samsung’s mini LED TV range, the 55in M80H sells for well below the brand’s more ambitious Neo QLED sets, but it doesn’t skimp on features.

There’s 4K 120Hz gaming support across all three HDMI inputs, AI-powered picture processing and Samsung’s excellent Tizen smart TV service, which is home to streaming services, catchup TV players and Samsung TV Plus.

Picture quality is good, albeit not as bright or dynamic as the brand’s more expensive mini LED screens (well, something’s got to give). But it’s perfectly suited to daytime TV and sports – and particularly good for games, as it’s super responsive. I measured input lag at just 10.2ms (with 1080p/60Hz games), which is very good, and it looks great with fast-moving action titles.

Sound comes via a built-in 20W stereo system, which is great for dialogue. The banter in Slow Horses (on Apple TV) really sparkles. It’s worth considering a soundbar, though. In the meantime, take advantage of its Bluetooth connectivity to pair your wireless headphones.
It’s a shame that … the M80H doesn’t quite have the brightness to do full justice to 4K HDR programmes. If you want the best image quality, it’s worth spending a little more.
Smart TV OS: Tizen Connections: HDMI, ethernet, wifi, Bluetooth Dimensions (without stand): 122.5 x 7.7 x 70.8cm (WDH) Weight (without stand): 10kg
What we loveHeaps of features at a reasonable price
What we don’t loveNot my first choice for watching films in a darkened room
What we lovePolished Sky OS with a brilliant selection of channels
What we don’t loveBasic sound quality – a soundbar would improve it

Sky Glass Air is a great way into Sky’s all-streaming ecosystem: it’s a smart-looking television with a simple setup and a large amount of live and on-demand content. Its quantum-dot picture is colourful, and while stereo sound is basic, it’s easy enough to add a soundbar. My 65in model is also available on a four-year contract from £15 a month with a £20 upfront cost, plus your chosen Sky subscription package (starting at £15 a month for new customers, or £18 for existing).

Why we love it The Glass Air is Sky’s second all-streaming TV, after the Sky Glass, which is now in its second generation, and offers the company’s wifi channel experience at a more affordable price than its flagship Glass Gen 2 model. It lacks some bells and whistles, but is lighter and more fashionable by design.
Available in grey, green or white, Sky Glass Air comes in 43in, 55in and 65in screens. My test model was the 65in; it comes with a colour-matched central pedestal stand and remote control.

Sky Glass Air has a QLED panel, but doesn’t match the high brightness or deep blacks of Sony’s Bravia 7 II model. But it’s not directly comparable. That’s because Sky Glass isn’t your typical telly. Sky’s premium TV channels can be streamed straight to the TV: you don’t need a dish, as it gets everything over wifi. The TV is available on contract, much like your smartphone, but can also be bought outright.

Connectivity comprises three HDMI 2.1 inputs, with HDMI 2 supporting eARC for an easy soundbar connection. That’s enough to add a soundbar, alongside a Blu-ray player and games console, although it won’t support 4K/120Hz gaming.

Picture-wise, I found the Sky Glass Air to be bright and colour rich. It uses a 4K quantum-dot LED panel and has an Auto picture mode that adjusts the image according to the type of content you’re watching. This makes it particularly easy to live with.

I loved the way it presented Formula One, with car liveries looking vibrant and glossy, before becoming more cinematic for blockbuster TV shows. The moody science fiction series 3 Body Problem (Netflix) can be tonally quite dark, what with all of its creepy interior shots, but Sky Glass Air made sure there was enough contrast to follow the action.
Sound comes via a 2 x 15W stereo system. It’s punchy enough, but I think a soundbar upgrade is inevitable if you’re a film buff who wants to appreciate the best scores.

The real reason to opt for Sky Glass Air is the Sky OS. Along with all the familiar Sky channels are key streamers such as Netflix, BBC iPlayer, Prime Video and Disney+. The basic Sky Essential TV bundle starts at £15 a month and includes Sky Atlantic, Netflix Standard with Ads, Discovery+ and free-to-air channels including BBC, ITV, Channel 4, Sky News and Sky Arts. You’ll pay extra for UHD, movie channels and sports. If you switch from Sky, the TV can still be used with apps such as Netflix, YouTube and others as long as the TV has been activated with a free Sky iD. The HDMI ports also continue to work, and you can hook up a TV aerial for Freeview channels – although you can expect a disjointed user experience. And cancelling Sky TV does not cancel any finance agreement you have on the set itself.

Where the set falls behind rivals is in its gaming performance. It’s not great if you’re into console shoot-’em-ups. The panel runs at 60Hz, which means it lacks the super-smooth, high-frame-rate gaming support of screens that offer 4K 120Hz, such as the LG C6. It’s fine for casual fun, but serious gamers should play elsewhere.
It’s a shame that … the set doesn’t go out of its way to offer gamers a great user experience. You can still hook up a console, but the input lag is high (I measured 67.5ms) even in its Game mode.
Smart TV OS: Sky OS Connections: HDMI, ethernet, wifi, Bluetooth Dimensions (without stand): 145.3 x 7.7 x 84cm (WDH) Weight (without stand): 18.9kg
For more, read our full Sky Glass Air review
What we lovePolished Sky OS with a brilliant selection of channels
What we don’t loveBasic sound quality – a soundbar would improve it
What we loveNails the essentials, with Freely and HDR for movie fans
What we don’t loveOnly two out of four HDMI inputs support 4K 120Hz gaming

The Hisense U7S makes a persuasive case for stepping up from a standard QLED screen to a feature-packed mid-range mini LED TV. Its picture performance gives films and games real visual punch, and gamers will appreciate the higher-spec HDMI ports. The provision of Freely makes it a lot easier to place about the house, as TV is delivered over wifi and doesn’t need a traditional aerial connection.
Why we love it If you’re looking for a mini LED TV that combines a bright, impressive 4K picture with strong gaming credentials, the Hisense U7S is an easy recommendation.
It’s available in sizes from 50in to 100in. I tested the 50in, and it makes a great first impression.

Colours are rich and well saturated without appearing overcooked, and its HDR performance is extremely strong. Reflections sparkle, lights have convincing intensity, and darker areas retain appealing depth. Black levels are impressively inky, which really helps when watching letterboxed movies – the picture doesn’t look like it’s sandwiched between uneven grey cardboard.
It’s great with games, too. Console play is smooth, with fluid action and outstanding colour. Overwatch is always my go-to when it comes to fast-moving, colour-rich games, and it looked peachy here.

Sound is above average for a thin LED-based TV. The set’s audio system has been developed with French audio specialist Devialet and delivers 40W of amplification, and includes a 20W rear-mounted subwoofer. Speech is nice and clear while action movies pack a punch. When I watched Ride or Die (on Prime Video), the audio had just the right amount of explosive thump, although I did find that if I had the set at full volume, there was some cabinet rattle.

Design is clean and understated. A slim black bezel surrounds the panel, and the central pedestal includes cable management, making the 50in model reasonably easy to position on narrow furniture. The main limitation is connectivity: only two of the four HDMI inputs support 4K at high frame rates, and one doubles as the eARC connection for a soundbar. So if you want to play games on both a PlayStation 5 and Xbox at 120fps and use a soundbar, your options are limited. Of course, you can connect consoles to any of the HDMI inputs if you’re happy to play 4K games at 60Hz.
As mentioned above, the set also has the wireless TV service Freely. You can watch BBC, ITV, Channel 4, Channel 5 and others without connecting a traditional aerial.

It’s a shame that … Vidaa, Hisense’s smart TV system, doesn’t quite have all the same fancy features of rivals, such as Google TV or Samsung’s Tizen. But if you’re just looking for the big-name streaming services, it’ll do the job.
Smart TV OS: Vidaa Connections: HDMI, ethernet, wifi, Bluetooth Dimensions (without stand): 111cm x 5.9 x 64.8cm (WDH) Weight (without stand): 10.6kg
What we loveNails the essentials, with Freely and HDR for movie fans
What we don’t loveOnly two out of four HDMI inputs support 4K 120Hz gaming
For more, read our guide to the best gaming chairs
What we lovePicture frame bezel, with plenty of subscription-free artworks

If you want a TV that can occupy a prominent place on the wall without looking like a black hole when switched off, this is a great buy. The QD mini LED panel delivers high brightness, rich colour and convincing HDR for the money, and Google TV is an easy smart OS to live with.

Why we love it Samsung started this style of TV, but now gallery-style TVs are all the rage – beloved because you can slap on a picture-frame bezel and hang them on the wall, so they look like a work of art (that also happens to show EastEnders).

Now TCL has entered the market, with a twist on the theme. Rather than make the picture frame an accessory, it comes with a walnut-effect one fixed, as standard – one less thing to worry about. To maximise the art effect, TCL supplies free displayable artwork images, many of which are recognisable museum pieces, no subscription required. By contrast, Samsung Frame owners can subscribe to the Samsung Art Store, which offers many thousands of artworks, for a monthly subscription.

My TCL A400 Pro was the 65in, but it’s also available in 55in and 75in sizes. The screen itself has a matte, non-reflective finish designed to reduce distractions from ambient light. This works reasonably well, although it can diffuse black-level performance. I struggled to make out what was happening during a particularly dark scene on the drama Paradise (Disney+).

It features four HDMI inputs, with two supporting high-frame-rate gaming. Streaming and catchup TV come via the Google TV platform, which also offers plenty of lesser-known services available from the Google Play store.

Image quality is very good, with dynamic contrast and high average brightness. The A400 Pro is particularly comfortable for daytime TV, but looks good with movies too. The audio system uses rear-facing speakers, but these still manage to deliver clear dialogue and punchy bass, which really drew me into a binge watch of Clarkson’s Farm on Prime Video – although I still couldn’t understand anything Gerald said.
Bluetooth headphones can be paired. The A400 Pro can also double as a Bluetooth music display, showing artwork and lyrics while music plays, which fits neatly with its lifestyle remit.

Obviously, if you leave the set running in art mode, it’s powered up, and the backlight remains on; energy consumption would be higher than if the set was left in standby (0.5W). But the costs will still be modest; its energy rating is D when running artworks in SDR (standard dynamic range).

It’s a shame that … this stylish gallery TV looks good on the wall and performs better than its price suggests, but the walnut-effect frame is fixed, so you can’t change it if you want to switch up your living room style. Sound quality is solid, but the rear-facing speakers lack the scale and immersion of a dedicated soundbar.
Smart TV OS: Google TV Connections: HDMI, ethernet, wifi, Bluetooth Dimensions (without stand): 145.2 x 4 x 83.3cm (WDH) Weight (without stand): 17.6kg
What we lovePicture frame bezel, with plenty of subscription-free artworks
What we loveExcellent picture quality with deep blacks and good contrast
What we don’t loveVirtual surround sound modes aren’t very convincing

If you want a premium TV with superb image quality and great gaming credentials, the LG C6 doesn’t disappoint. Its Alpha 11 Gen 3 processor brings a tangible increase in HDR brightness over last year’s C-series model, which was well received when first released, while OLED’s inherent black levels and excellent shadow definition remain hugely cinematic. Not cheap, but well worth the investment for serious home cinema fans.

Why we love it In the world of premium TV screens, LG has carved a serious reputation. Its C6 model boasts advanced picture processing and brilliant gaming features. The 65in C6 tested here has an RRP of £2,499.99, but the range spans 42in to 83in, with RRPs running from £1,299.99 to £4,799.99. Prices can be volatile, so be sure to look out for sale discounts.

Build quality is excellent, although the glossy screen lacks an anti-glare, matte-style filter found on gallery TVs and the rival Samsung S90H OLED. This makes the screen quite reflective, so it might be best to avoid placing table lamps in front of the set. You may want to consider the room’s lighting before you install it.

Picture quality is excellent, courtesy of that new processor, and because it’s OLED you can rest assured images are highly dynamic with inky black levels. This is the kind of TV that makes everything look good, from bright, colourful daytime TV fare such as Tipping Point to moody blockbuster TV shows like House of the Dragon.

There’s plenty to watch, too. The webOS 26 operating system has all the key streaming services built in, plus LG’s own free-to-watch channels. It’s all controlled with the latest slim version of LG’s mouse-like Magic Remote, with customisable buttons and voice control.
The screen is ideal for gamers, as all four HDMI inputs support 120Hz gaming from PlayStation 5 and Xbox. Input lag is low, so games play fast and look slick.

The TV’s audio has 40W of total amplification spread across a 2.2 configuration (2 x full-range drivers and 2 x woofers). While LG claims a Virtual 11.1.2 up-mix of stereo courtesy of its Alpha 11 AI Sound Pro processor, I didn’t find the effect very convincing. On the plus side, it plays loud. Consequently, I didn’t feel the immediate need for a soundbar.

It’s a shame that … this polished OLED all-rounder delivers superb pictures, but the glossy screen lacks an anti-glare filter, so reflections can become distracting in bright rooms. And while the C6 represents great value for a premium OLED, it’ll still set you back some serious change.
Smart TV OS: webOS 26 Connections: HDMI, ethernet, wifi, Bluetooth Dimensions (without stand): 144.1 x 4.5 x 82.6cm (WDH) Weight (without stand): 16.6kg
What we loveExcellent picture quality with deep blacks and good contrast
What we don’t loveVirtual surround sound modes aren’t very convincing

Way back when, you only really bought a new TV when the old one gave up the ghost. That’s because tellies were all very much of a muchness. Things are different now: a constant cycle of upgrades, feature improvements and evolving smart platforms serves to constantly tempt us. But how do you know when it’s actually time to make the switch?
As a general rule, when your smart TV stops receiving updates from the manufacturer, and streaming apps stop or disappear entirely, it might be time to consider a new model.

Perhaps you’re investing in a new games console and want a TV that really shows off your system, with advanced motion handling, low input lag and high-frame-rate gaming? A new set could give you a competitive edge.
Perhaps the best reason to buy is the arrival of new panel technologies, such as RGB mini LED, which offer significant leaps in picture brightness and colour depth.

Of course, you can always upgrade your viewing experience without splurging on a new set. If it’s a better smart TV experience you’re after, then adding an HDMI streaming stick is an easy fix. Amazon’s Fire TV Stick 4K Plus is a plug-and-play solution that features all the key streaming and catchup services (Netflix, Apple TV, Disney+, Prime Video and so on) through an easy-to-use interface. It is, however, tightly integrated into Amazon’s shopping portal.

If you’re a Vodafone customer, the new Vodafone TV streaming box could be an alternative solution. Available on a two-year subscription, it comes with Freely streaming channels for a tenner a month, and you can add Netflix and HBO Max with ads for an additional £7 a month. There’s also about 300 cloud games if you run out of shows to watch.
If Sky TV is more your jam, the Sky Stream box with a two-year Ultimate TV package features a slew of Sky channels, plus Netflix, HBO Max, Disney+, Hayu and Discovery+, for £24 a month.

For better audio, simply connecting a soundbar to your TV will almost certainly transform film nights. The Majority Bowfell Halo Atmos sound system is a complete 5.1 home cinema package, and it cost just £115.95 at the time of writing. It includes a compact soundbar, subwoofer and small, semi-wireless rear speakers. It’s great for smaller rooms.

For something more substantial, look at the Samsung HW-Q800B. This mid-price soundbar has dedicated up-firing drivers for height effects, a powerful array of front-facing speakers and a compact subwoofer for room-filling bass.

TVs will typically offer three or four HDMI inputs – but they’re not created equal. While all HDMI inputs look the same and will work with a streaming TV box, Blu-ray player or games console, be sure to check how many HDMI inputs also support 4K 120Hz gameplay.

These faster HDMI ports will maximise the performance of your PlayStation 5 or Xbox. Some TVs, including certain Samsung and LG models, offer this level of connectivity across all HDMI inputs. Others, including models from Sony, Philips and Panasonic, restrict it to just two – and more often than not, one of these will also be the eARC connection you’ll need if you want to add a soundbar.
If you’re not interested in games, none of this matters, but for avid gamers, this subtle detail can be a deal-breaker.

When you upgrade your TV, it makes sense to buy a bigger screen than the one you’re replacing, to better enjoy the resolution available from 4K programmes. A lot of the extra detail in 4K UHD programmes can be difficult to appreciate on smaller displays. The norm is now 55in to 65in, but there’s a move to super-large TVs, 75in and larger.

According to YouGov research, what many would have previously considered a home cinema-sized TV is becoming commonplace. About one in five UK households now owns a TV larger than 50in, while the 43-50in category has emerged as the market’s most common screen size. In my experience, 4K TVs really start to impress at 55in or larger. My preference when buying would actually be a 65in screen, if you can accommodate it, for really immersive viewing.

Remember, thanks to shrinking bezels, you can probably fit a larger screen size in the same space taken by your older set. Improvements in picture quality, including 4K resolution and HDR, also mean you can see more picture details when you watch on a larger screen. Just be sure to measure your space before you buy.

An oft-quoted rule of thumb is that your viewing distance should equate to 1.5 times the screen size of your 4K TV. So for a 55in TV, you’d be sitting about 2m from the TV, and with a 65in you’d be 2.48m away from the screen. At 2.86m, you’re best off with a 75in TV. Of course, take these figures with a pinch of salt. Ultimately, the best screen size is whatever you’re comfortable with.
For more, read our guide to the best 4K wireless TV streamers for more choice, the best gaming chairs and the best TV programmes of 2026 so far

Steve May is a technology and home entertainment specialist, with more than 30 years’ experience writing about TVs, hi-fis and music. From the biggest, thinnest, brightest TVs in existence to sound systems that rival commercial cinemas, Steve has auditioned them all. When not writing about tech, you’ll find him bingeing box sets or cataloguing his Blu-ray collection

items.title: Inside the old gas pipeline where Ukraine is fighting an underground war with Russia
paragraphs: Watch: The BBC's Jonathan Beale joins Ukrainian forces taking the battle below ground and out of sight of Russian drones.

items.title: 'The drones don't fly here' - BBC reports from Ukraine's new front line
paragraphs: Watch: Inside the gas pipeline where Ukraine is fighting an underground war with Russia
There's a new front in the war in Ukraine, and it is underground.
For the past seven months Ukrainian forces have been living and fighting Russian troops in an old Soviet gas pipeline in the north-eastern Kharkiv region.

With a diameter of just over a metre there is enough room only to crawl. But it is relatively safe from the drones that now saturate the skies above the front line – and make it nigh-on impossible for either side to advance.
Going underground is now the "only option", says Zanuda, who has helped plan Ukraine's tunnel operation and calls it a new world of fighting. But, he acknowledges, it is hard.
"On the surface you always have some room to manoeuvre, but here you can only engage the enemy head-on."

The journey to get to this subterranean battleground in the Kharkiv region only reinforced the dangers on the ground: a high-speed move by vehicle across open fields, followed by a long march across muddy ground – accompanied by Ukrainian troops with their weapons loaded, ready to shoot down Russian drones.
Arriving at the tunnel entrance, the first thing to hit you is the lingering smell of gas and fetid air.
Both sides use openings in the pipeline to get to the surface, where most of the fighting takes place. They have made breaches in the ground, and used welding tools to break through the thick steel.

The Russians were the first to exploit the pipe to infiltrate the nearby city of Kupyansk in September 2025. They have used underground pipelines before, during the capture of the city of Avdiivka in 2024, and last year in their bid to recapture areas of Russia's Kursk region.
But Ukrainian forces have slowly turned the tables.
Troops move through the tunnel on special sleds - they call it the Kupyansk metro
A specially designed electric cart transports troops and supplies through the pipeline.

They call it the Kupyansk metro. It occasionally breaks down. We travelled on it for 40 minutes, heads bowed and legs crossed. There is a regular bump as you cross the welded sections of the pipe. It is like an austere fairground ride, without the fun.

Our destination was a break in the pipeline where Ukrainian troops have built dug-outs to store ammunition and equipment, with just enough room to stand. It is where the man they call Musician conducts the movement of troops and supplies. He has been living like a mole, his face engrained with dirt and earth.

Musician tells me he has spent the past three months there, with a few brief visits above ground to clean up or go to the toilet. From time to time we can hear the thuds of artillery rounds above. Musician tells me we are close to the line of contact: "But it's safe underground."
Ukrainian troops like Musician rarely see the sun - but they say they feel safer underground
The cart continues its journey into the bowels of the earth. It returns about half an hour later with more troops covered in dirt. They have been fighting in positions on the surface.
There is a look of relief on their dust-caked faces.
"It's more comfortable in the pipe because drones don't fly here, and neither do artillery shells or glide bombs," says Vovochka, who has been fighting on the ground for the past three weeks.

But there has been fighting in the pipeline, too. Operation Veles, named after a mythical Slavic god of the underworld, began in April. Since then Ukraine has advanced 15km (9.3 miles) along the pipeline.
It has been painstaking, backbreaking work – with the ever-present fear of coming into contact with the enemy.

Back above ground we meet a few of the soldiers, from the 13th Khartiia Brigade of Ukraine's National Guard, who have taken part in the mission. Their first task was to clear the detritus, water and Russian barricades inside the pipeline.
The Ukrainian troops say some of the barriers were boobytrapped or piled with Russian bodies. "When we moved them or climbed over them, we had no idea what was underneath," says Chyzh.
The other danger, he said, was the ricochets from gunfire when they tried to advance. "You never know where a bullet is going to go or how it will bounce."

His comrade Kort says "we were all firing, we were pushing them back". Over the course of the operation Ukraine says it killed more than 100 Russian soldiers and took 30 prisoners. "Yes, there were bodies," says Kort. "I even had to sleep right next to them."
The men live and fight in very tight quarters - but have managed to clear 15km of the pipe
Their commander's former life as a miner helped prepare them for the physical and psychological challenges of operating underground.
From a building on the surface, Biashym keeps in regular contact with his men still in the pipeline. Behind him is a cabinet full of medicine.

Soldiers in the pipeline spend much of their time on their knees and suffer abrasions. Biashym admits some have had panic attacks from living in such a confined space. Others have struggled to breathe.
Hundreds of Colombian volunteers have also been involved in the operation, part of the RUG 23rd Assault Regiment.
Foreign fighters have helped boost Ukraine's depleted ranks. One of the Colombians, whose call sign is Gecko, tells me it took them 30 days to just clear 500m.
"It was difficult, it was hot and I had fear inside the pipe," he said. "But at some point I just thought, OK, just deal with it and let's advance."

Russian forces, like Ukraine's, have built fortified positions inside the pipeline. They still try to infiltrate Ukrainian positions, burrowing their way in and out of the pipe. From a control room above ground we watched Ukrainian drones target another Russian attempt to outflank them.
Ground operations are now nearly impossible... everyone understands, for now, the only way to fight is underground
While some of the fighting taking place underground, there are still battles on the surface and in the air. It has been a combined operation.

But Zanuda, who is chief of the planning section of the 13th Khartiia Brigade, believes it is the best way to fight in the future. "Ground operations are now nearly impossible," he said, adding that "everyone understands, for now, the only way to fight is underground".

There'll be more missions like this, he believes. "Pipelines run everywhere," he said. "You have to remember, back in the Soviet times, oil, gas and ammonia were being transported to Europe, with the entire transit route running through Ukraine."
In reality it has been brutal, gruelling and dangerous work in the harshest of conditions.
It has taken Ukraine seven months to clear 15km of the pipeline.
Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky has hailed it as a success.
It has helped retake lost territory and been a boost for morale, but on its own it has not changed the course of the war.
Additional reporting by Moose Campbell, Volodymyr Lozhko and Rebecca Hartmann

items.title: Police investigate death of boy, 3, after nursery incident
paragraphs: A spokeswoman for Cosy Toes said they were "all heartbroken" by the "wonderful and beautiful" boy's death.
"Our thoughts and prayers are all with his family at this terrible time," she said.
"We will of course give our fullest possible assistance in every way possible to the enquiries that must rightly follow this tragic event."
Anyone with information about the boy's death is being urged to contact police.
Brennan said: "We are in the very early stages of our involvement and are carefully considering events and the evidence available to us.
"For now, we ask that the family's privacy is respected as they begin to navigate the unimaginable loss of their little boy."
Ofsted said it had taken the decision to suspend the nursery's registration in the wake of the incident, meaning the nursery will be closed for six weeks as investigations are carried out.
A spokesperson said: "Our thoughts are with the family of the young boy and everyone affected by this deeply distressing and tragic incident.

"We have worked closely with the police, and we have suspended the nursery's registration. We will continue to support the police and other agencies in their enquiries. We are unable to comment further while the police investigation is ongoing."

items.title: CLB Architects creates ADU in Wyoming with rock-climbing wall
paragraphs: US studio CLB Architects has completed an accessory dwelling unit called Wiley, which features an outdoor climbing wall and compact living quarters for an empty-nester couple.

The small building stands on a one-acre site in Wilson, Wyoming, located just beyond the popular ski town of Jackson. The site is dotted with mature trees and sits along the west bank of the Snake River.
Before the project’s inception, the clients had lived on the property for 25 years – in a modest, 1960s house they had renovated – and had raised their son there.
As their son neared graduation from high school, the couple decided to build an ADU on the property and make it their full-time residence, while renting out the main residence.

“The new house would allow them to remain on the land they had known for decades, while experiencing it in a new way – closer to nature, with stronger connections to light, views and outdoor living,” said Jackson-based CLB Architects.
The house also represents a way to accommodate a growing need for housing while preserving the natural landscape.
“In our region, there’s a clear need for this housing type, which is economical, compact and responsive to place,” said CLB Architects partner Eric Logan.

A primary challenge for the design team was to ensure the house “met the couple’s programmatic and budget constraints” within a very compact footprint. Per country regulations, the new house could not exceed 1,000 square feet (92.9 square metres).
The architects conceived a simple, rectangular volume that rises two levels and is topped with a gabled roof. The house was carefully sited so it would feel separate from the main residence.
“Siting the building toward the back of the parcel and introducing new landscaping and tree plantings created a soft buffer between the two dwellings,” the architect said.

The team carved out portions of the exterior to form inset terraces, along with a climbing wall that is used by the couple’s son while home from college. On the east-facing elevation, a boxy protrusion forms a balcony.

Both inside and out, the team opted for materials that were durable, cost-efficient and complemented the building’s form. Dark corrugated metal clads most of the building, while tight-knot cedar was used for inset areas to provide “warmth and depth”.
The ground level contains a spacious garage for vehicles and outdoor gear. The upper level holds two bedrooms with ensuite bathrooms, all of which are organised around a central living area.

“Locating the main living spaces on the second floor allows the interiors to engage the tree canopy while maximising natural light, offering a more intimate relationship with the landscape,” the team said.

The living area opens onto a west-facing deck, which acts as an “outdoor living room” for much of the year. Large, sliding glass doors diminish the boundary between inside and out and usher in breezes during summer months.

The clients, both of whom have deep experience in design and construction fields, poured themselves into the project. The husband served as the general contractor and engaged local tradespeople to help out.
“A true labor of love, the couple built much of the house themselves, working on the construction every evening and on weekends,” the team said, noting the project was completed in about nine months.
The project offers ideas for how communities in the Mountain West can accommodate growth while preserving the natural landscape.

“With rising land values and the need to accommodate more residents, homes like this – that are compact, efficient, and contextual – can provide more housing while preserving open space,” the team said.
“As local communities grapple with growth, projects like this suggest one path forward.”

Other ADUs in America include a small, cedar-clad dwelling in California’s wine country by Schwartz and Architecture, and a compact, metal-clad building in Austin by North Arrow Studio that resembles a birdhouse.

items.title: Julio Iglesias facing court investigation over alleged sexual offences
paragraphs: Singer Julio Iglesias is facing an investigation by Spain's national court over allegations he sexually abused and assaulted two female former staff members
Two women, who worked for the 83-year-old in the Caribbean, have accused him of abuse which they say took place in the Bahamas and the Dominican Republic in 2021.
The announcement comes after Spanish prosecutors dropped an inquiry into the claims earlier this year after concluding that they lacked jurisdiction because the alleged crimes took place abroad.
Iglesias, who has been a household name in Spain since the 1960s and has sold millions of records worldwide, has previously denied the allegations.

But in a statement published on Wednesday, external (in Spanish), national court Judge Antonio Piña said the account given in the complaint, alongside preliminary evidence provided, justified opening criminal proceedings.
He added that the investigation would cover parts of the complaint relating to potential crimes against sexual freedom, as well as assault and degrading treatment.

But the court will not investigate claims made in the lawsuit of human trafficking or crimes against workers' rights. Piña said these allegations were dismissed after he looked into the hiring of the women and found there was "no deception or artifice involved".
Piña said the former employees had been summoned to testify in person on 3 February.
The announcement comes after Spain's public prosecutor's office shifted its position last month, saying it now believed the court had jurisdiction to investigate the allegations.
In its statement, the national court said Spanish law sets out that courts can hear cases of crimes committed abroad by Spanish citizens provided certain conditions are met.
The allegations against Iglesias first emerged in a joint three-year investigation between Spanish newspaper El Diario, external and television network Univision news, published in January.
In that investigation, the two women were identified as a domestic worker and a physical therapist, who described alleged sexual abuse and degrading working conditions.
The domestic worker, whose name was changed to Rebeca in the reports, said Iglesias would regularly call her to his room at the end of the day and would touch her inappropriately without consent.

Rebeca, a Dominican who was 22 when the alleged events took place, also alleged that Iglesias had forced her to take part in threesomes with another female member of staff. She also described the singer slapping her in the face and grabbing her genitals.

The other woman, a Venezuelan physical therapist named as Laura in the article, said Iglesias had touched her breasts and kissed her on the mouth against her will. She added that he constantly threatened to fire her, controlled how much food she ate and asked her about when her period was due.
Rebeca and Laura filed an initial legal complaint in January against Iglesias for sexual assault and human trafficking.
In a response to the allegations in January, Iglesias said, external: "I deny having abused, coerced, or disrespected any woman. These accusations are absolutely false and deeply sadden me."

On Wednesday, the court said the lawsuit had been accepted based on evidence provided in the complaint. This included a photograph of one of the complainants, showing a bruise on her arm that was "consistent with the possibility of her being grabbed forcefully".

It added that the same photo showed "two marks on one of her thighs that could correspond to a human bite", which the complainant said were "a consequence of her forced participation in acts of a sexual nature".
WhatsApp message exchanges, including New Year's greetings, which suggest an "affectionate" relationship between the women and Iglesias, will also be considered, the court said.

But it added that the seemingly cordial tone, which presents "an apparent discrepancy with certain aspects of the narrative", would be clarified through a "complete and contextualised examination of the communications".

The claim over violations of workers' rights could not be investigated because there is no comparable criminal offence in the Bahamas and the Dominican Republic, where the alleged crimes took place, it said.
Iglesias is one of the most successful Latin artists of all time, having sold more than 300 million records in a career spanning decades.
He is also the father of fellow music superstar Enrique Iglesias.

items.title: Test cricket's sandpaper plot - who was there, who said what?
paragraphs: The Australia playing squad and staff were pictured before the third Test against South Africa in 2018
ByMatthew HenryBBC Sport Journalist and Stephan ShemiltCricket Correspondent
The sandpaper scandal, one of the biggest controversies in the history of Test cricket, continues to engulf Australian sport.

Fresh evidence from Cameron Bancroft - the culprit of the ball-tampering in South Africa in 2018 - has heaped pressure on Australia captain Pat Cummins, former coach Darren Lehmann and Cricket Australia.

In a detailed account of more than 4,000 words published in the West Australian newspaper, Bancroft alleges all the Australia players and coaches present in Cape Town eight years ago knew of the plot.
Bancroft's explosive testimony supports claims made by Usman Khawaja, David Warner and Chadd Sayers.
However, Cummins denied Khawaja's version of events in his own extraordinary news conference in Sydney last week. Cummins spoke to the media for 68 minutes in an address broadcast on live television.
Here, BBC Sport collects the most recent accounts of players and coaches involved in the saga that became widely known as sandpapergate.
Batter Khawaja played all four Tests in South Africa and a total of 88 for Australia before retiring from international cricket earlier this year.
Revelations in his autobiography reignited debate around the sandpaper scandal and made headlines across the globe.
"It was all of us," Khawaja said. "Not the batters, not the bowlers, not the staff. All of us.

"In an ideal world, I don't want to do this. I don't want to be the one who comes out and talks about the truth. The issue is that I genuinely thought after eight years the truth would have been out by now.
"Even in the change rooms when I was talking to them after the game. I said, 'Take this as a team'.
"We did this as a team. We knew what was going on, and we have to take it as a team, and so I was always of that stance."
Warner was Australia's opening batter and vice-captain during the 2018 series. He, along with captain Steve Smith and Bancroft, were the three players punished for the ball-tampering.
The Cricket Australia (CA) investigation in 2018 found Warner developed the plan and that he instructed Bancroft to carry out the cheating.

After serving his ban, Warner returned to play a further 133 times for Australia across formats, including three Ashes series and the 2023 World Cup win. He retired from international cricket in 2024.
In response to Khawaja's book, Warner said: "I thank you for what you've done. It's 100% accurate what you've said. Now everyone knows the truth."
He also accused Cricket Australia of a cover-up, describing the CA investigation as "rushed" and botched".
"As far as l am aware, CA did not interview Josh Hazlewood, Mitchell Starc or Nathan Lyon in their 2018 investigation," Warner said.
"If that's correct, then how can CA push the idea that the bowlers didn't know?"
The Cape Town Test was the 13th of Cummins' Test career. A key bowler, he would go on to be named Australia's Test captain in 2021. It is a position he still holds.
Prior to Khawaja's book, Cummins and the other bowlers from Cape Town - Hazlewood, Starc and Lyon - had always denied knowledge of the plan to use sandpaper.
In an extraordinary news conference last week, Cummins called Khawaja's claims that the whole team knew about the plan "100% wrong" and "utter nonsense".
"I said that consistently for the last eight years," Cummins said. "I did not know that was happening.
"He says that I and others were architects of a scheme to ball-tamper with sandpaper. That's complete and utter nonsense."
Asked if he knew of any plans at any stage to tamper with the ball during the series against South Africa, Cummins said: "No."
Cummins also said he did not remember a meeting where Khawaja had called on the team to take collective responsibility - something his former team-mate claimed.
Opening batter Bancroft was playing his eighth Test in Cape Town, aged 25. He was the player caught using sandpaper on the field.
He played another two Tests after serving his ban and is still playing for Western Australia. He turns 34 this week.

In 2021, Bancroft said it was "self-explanatory" whether the bowlers knew of the plan, and on Wednesday he backed Khawaja's account, saying Cummins' news conference made him "feel angry, betrayed and alone".

Like Khawaja, Bancroft said sandpaper was first used during the second Test against South Africa – the match before he was caught - and also said he had conversations with the Australia seamers about whether the ball was "swinging enough".

He said the entire playing group and staff had "celebrations" about the effect of the sandpaper. He also claimed that coach Lehmann and bowling coach David Saker were present in the initial discussions and that Bancroft's role was also discussed in a team meeting before day three.
In an account published by the West Australian on Wednesday, Bancroft wrote: "All the bowlers gave me feedback if my work on the ball was working. It was helpful.
"Is it going yet? It's not going yet, it needs more. So I would use the sandpaper more on the ball.
"There was even a time I was told to stop out of fear what I was doing was becoming too obvious."
Lehmann was Australia coach at the time of the scandal. He was cleared by the CA investigation and said he had "no prior knowledge" of the plan to ball-tamper.
He resigned after the series and has been Northamptonshire coach since the start of the 2025 English season.
After Khawaja's revelations, Lehmann said: "I don't think everyone would have known [about the use of sandpaper]. You do know ball-tampering is going on because it's been happening for 150 years."
After Cricket Australia said it would hold an open forum, Lehmann said he has "nothing to hide".
Speaking on radio coverage of the third one-day international against England after Bancroft's account was published, Lehmann said: "I need to sit back, process it and work through each allegation.
"That's what I'll be doing over the next few days.
"I need to have a really good read of it. I need to make sure I'm saying what I want to say."
Smith, one of the greatest batters of his generation, was Australia's captain at the time of the scandal.
After serving a 12-month ban, he returned for the World Cup and Ashes the following year and has stood in as captain at times since.
He was found to have been aware of the plan to cheat and to mislead the public and match officials.
Smith, who broke down in tears when apologising at a subsequent news conference, as cameras captured the emotional toll of the moment, has not spoken publicly since Khawaja's book was published.
Speaking about the episode in September this year, he said: "That was a traumatic experience in my life and when I hear the flash of a camera it makes me revisit that in a way.
"I've tried to kind of erase a lot of 2018 and what happened. I can't remember a lot about the series. I've tried to block most of it out of my memory bank."
Marsh was bowling when Bancroft was caught using sandpaper on the ball in Cape Town. As an all-rounder, he was not part of the 2021 bowlers' statement.
Marsh was captain during Australia's recent ODI series against England and refused to answer questions on the topic before the series opener.
"I am not here to share mine [story] today," he said.
"I respect Uzzie [Khawaja] has told his story; my focus is on tomorrow. I am not here to go back on South Africa."
Following the conclusion of the series, Marsh did not take part in his post-match news conference, with 26-year-old bowler Jack Edwards taking his place.
'I've moved on' - Marsh bats away questions over sandpapergate
Paine was Australia's wicketkeeper during the South Africa series and was made captain when Smith was banned.
He served in the role until he stood down in 2021 over a historical investigation into sexually explicit text messages sent to a female colleague.

In his autobiography, Paine said the suggestion everyone in the Australia dressing room must have known about the sandpaper use is "rubbish" and claimed he first found out when images appeared on the big screen in Cape Town.
"Everyone out there was shocked when they looked up on the big screen and saw Cameron Bancroft with a piece of sandpaper in his hand," Paine wrote. "I was stunned. We all were.
"My heart sank, I was thinking, 'What the f***?' A sense of dread came over us all."
Bancroft said he discussed whether the ball was reversing with Paine during the second Test.
Saker was Australia's bowling coach during the South Africa series.
Bancroft alleged Saker was present for discussions about the use of sandpaper and told the batter he needed to do more to the ball.
Saker was also England bowling coach as recently as last month's tri-series in Pakistan. He was an influential part of England's 2010-11 Ashes win.

In 2021, reflecting on the sandpaper saga, Saker said: "Obviously a lot of things went wrong at that time. There was a lot of people to blame. It could have been me to blame, it could have been someone else. It could have been stopped and it wasn't, which is unfortunate.

"Cameron's a very nice guy. He's just doing it to get something off his chest… He's not going to be the last. You could point your finger at me, you could point your finger at Boof [Lehmann]. Could you point it at other people? Of course you could.
"The disappointing thing is it's never going to go away. Regardless of what's said. We all know that we made a monumental mistake. The gravity wasn't as plain until it all came out."
Starc was an integral part of the vaunted Australia attack in Cape Town and remains so in the present day. He is ranked as the number one bowler in Test cricket by the International Cricket Council.

Left-armer Starc repeatedly denied knowledge of the sandpaper plot, including in the statement released with Cummins, Hazlewood and Lyon in 2021, and in a news conference in the days after Khawaja's claims emerged.

Speaking on 10 November, Starc said: "Obviously, there's differing opinions of eight years ago. We were heavily grilled through the process at the time, and since, and I guess I won't speak on behalf of the bowlers, but where I stand, my opinion hasn't changed. My recollection hasn't changed from what we said in 2021.
"I'll stick to what I said five years ago, what I said at the time, eight years ago. Clearly, there's different versions from different people, and I'll leave it where I left it back then."

Along with Cummins and Starc, Hazlewood and Lyon have remained part of Australia's first-choice bowling unit in the eight years since the sandpaper scandal, forming one of the greatest four-man attacks in Test history.

Seamer Hazlewood and off-spinner Lyon joined Cummins and Starc in releasing a statement in 2021, responding to an interview given by Bancroft to the Guardian newspaper when he said the bowlers' involvement in the sandpaper plot was "self-explanatory".
Neither Hazlewood nor Lyon has spoken publicly since the fresh claims from Khawaja, Warner and Bancroft emerged.

Their statement released with Cummins and Starc in 2021 said: "We pride ourselves on our honesty. So it's been disappointing to see that our integrity has been questioned by some journalists and past players in recent days in regard to the Cape Town Test of 2018.
"We did not know a foreign substance was taken onto the field to alter the condition of the ball until we saw the images on the big screen at Newlands.
"We respectfully request an end to the rumour-mongering and innuendo. It has gone on too long and it is time to move on."
A swing bowler, Sayers played his only Test for Australia after the sandpaper controversy erupted – the fourth and final match of the series against South Africa in Johannesburg.
Sayers, who retired from first-class cricket in 2021, spoke to Australian radio station SEN in the aftermath of Khawaja's claims, to corroborate the former batter's account.

Sayers claimed to have removed sandpaper from the field in the second Test against South Africa, the match before Bancroft was caught. He also backed up Khawaja's assertion that the entire Australia squad discussed the sandpaper issue after it was revealed in Cape Town.
Speaking on 15 November, Sayers said: "I am comfortable sitting here that I believe everyone in that side knew what was going on and what was being used.
"It was used in two Test matches and there were discussions in the changing rooms.
"After the occurrence in Cape Town, we all sat in the changing rooms after that day's play and, probably for 60 to 90 minutes, we talked about what had happened and I guess where to next."
Spinner Holland, who retired in 2021, was also a back-up bowler on the trip.
He also said there was a meeting held in the fallout from Cape Town about players taking responsibility.
"Once we got back to the hotel we did sit as a group [to discuss] what had happened and who was going to take the blame," Holland told newspaper The Australian.
"To Davey's [Warner's] credit, from what I remember, he did put his hand up and say he would take some of the responsibility, but not all of it.
"To be sitting there and seeing three blokes hung out to dry when you are supposed to be part of a team was a pretty hard watch."
Batter Handscomb was Australia's 12th man on the day Bancroft was caught, making frequent trips between the field and the dressing room.
Bancroft's account alleges Handscomb was told by Lehmann, via walkie-talkie, to "get the sandpaper off Bangers [Bancroft] now".
Last week, following Khawaja's claims but before Bancroft spoke, Handscomb was asked for his recollections after making a century for Victoria in the Sheffield Shield against Western Australia.

On 11 November, Handscomb said: "I appreciate you have to ask these questions. I've had a nice day today, it's not really something that I want to comment on right now. I'll sort of just let the powers of be do their thing."
Former England batter Hick was part of the Australia backroom team on the South Africa tour of 2018.
Hick was made redundant by Cricket Australia as part of a series of cost-cutting measures in 2020.
Speaking to the Sydney Morning Herald last week, Hick said: "I have seen the various statements around the coaches, and I'm very disappointed with the broad nature of them.
"Khawaja puts it simply: 'It was all of us. Not the batters, not the bowlers, not the staff. All of us'. To me, what Khawaja is implying here is absolutely false.
"In regard to any discussions around the ball-tampering in Port Elizabeth or Cape Town, I will say in true honesty that I did not hear or know anything.
"My first knowledge of all this was, like many, when it appeared on the big screen in Cape Town as I was sat on the outside balcony at the time."
Australian cricket was rocked by the sandpapergate scandal in 2018 and it is back in the headlines in 2026 following fresh allegations by former Australia batter Usman Khawaja.

items.title: The tightest survival scrap for years? Why it's not too early to worry
paragraphs: Is it too early for the Premier League bottom three to worry?
Despite being only 10 games into the season, sitting in the relegation zone even at this early stage is more worrying than you might think.
But with how tight the Premier League table is, this could also be one of the fiercest relegation battles we have seen in a long time.
Two of the current bottom three, Crystal Palace and Manchester United, will resume their campaigns at the weekend with new managers after appointing Thomas Frank and Mauricio Pochettino respectively.
Sunderland, wedged between the pair in 19th, have not pressed the panic button and have kept faith with Regis le Bris.
But is it too early to worry? We look at what the stats tell us about relegation battles in the past and what we can learn for the months ahead.
Looking at every Premier League season since it changed to a 20-team league in 1995-96, the current bottom three have cause to be concerned.
In 19 of the previous 31 seasons (61%), only one of the bottom three sides after 10 games managed to avoid relegation.

For fairness and accuracy, the 'bottom three' are the three sides with the worst record after 10 games, not simply those in the relegation zone after matchweek 10, since in some seasons a team had played nine games by that point.

Only in 10 seasons (32%) have two or more of the bottom three stayed up - and that has not happened in any of the past eight campaigns. The last time more than one team avoided the drop was in 2017-18, when all three survived.
That has only happened twice, although only twice have all three sides been relegated.
Overall, of the 93 previous teams in the bottom three after 10 games, 41 survived and 52 were relegated - a survival rate of 44%.
This is the third time that Palace have been bottom after 10 games. On both previous occasions, they did not just survive but thrived, finishing 11th.

They did so under Tony Pulis in 2013-14 and under Roy Hodgson in 2017-18. Both managers, like Frank, were appointed early in the season following poor starts under Ian Holloway and Frank de Boer respectively.
The 2013-14 season is the only previous time that Sunderland and Palace were the bottom two at this stage. The Black Cats also survived thanks to a great, late escape under Gus Poyet.
This is the first time United have been in the bottom three after 10 games of a Premier League season.
Given the size and resources of the club, it is unlikely they will go down, although the team in 18th place at this stage have been relegated in each of the past six seasons.
Fans of all three clubs will hope for a repeat of 2017-18, when not only Palace but the bottom three improved significantly to finish comfortably mid-table.
While history suggests only one of the bottom three will survive, there is also evidence to suggest that this might not be a standard Premier League season.
Palace have seven points, which is the most the bottom side after 10 games have had for 24 years. The bottom three all had eight points in 2002-03.
Sunderland's eight points is also the most that a side in 19th place have had for 16 years. Wolves had nine points in 2010-11 and survived in 17th.
In fact, only five points separate the bottom half of the Premier League, with Tottenham in 11th on 12 points and Palace bottom with seven – the smallest gap at this stage for 24 years.

The highest that a team in the bottom three after 10 games have finished the season is eighth - Bolton in 2003-04, Tottenham in 2008-09 and Everton in 2017-18 - which suggests it will be Conference League at best for Manchester United next season.
Then again, the table is so tight that only nine points separate Chelsea in fifth and Palace - the smallest gap at this stage for 16 years.
Given that fifth place has been enough to qualify for the Champions League in recent seasons, optimistic United fans may not be ruling it out just yet.
That means even sides who have started well could be involved in the relegation battle.
The most points a team have had after 10 games of a 38-game season and been relegated is 14 - Joe Royle's Manchester City in 2000-01.
The most recent team to start well but be relegated were Eddie Howe's Bournemouth in 2019-20, who were sitting pretty in ninth with 13 points at this stage but went down on the final day.
As mentioned, this season has both the 'best' bottom side in terms of points and the most compact bottom half of the table that we have seen at this stage since 2002-03.
In that season, West Ham were relegated on the final day with 42 points - the most a side have been relegated with in Premier League history.
Given the way this season is shaping up, 40 points might also not be enough to survive.

items.title: Dezeen Events Guide launches digital guide to Miami art week 2026
paragraphs: Dezeen Events Guide has launched its guide to the 2026 edition of Miami art week, which is sponsored by colour specialist Pantone.
The festival, which runs from 30 November to 6 December 2026, takes place across Miami, in neighbourhoods such as the Miami Design District and Miami Beach.
The event includes fairs, exhibitions, installations, open showrooms, talks, launches, pop-up shops and parties throughout the week.
Highlights include the Design Miami and Art Basel Miami Beach fairs, alongside satellite fairs NADA Miami, Art Miami and Fridge Art Fair.
Alongside the guide, Dezeen has created an interactive map for the art week, helping attendees plan their routes around the city.
There’s still time to feature in the Miami art week 2026 guide
Dezeen Events Guide offers a range of listings. Get in touch with the team at eventsguide@dezeen.com to book your listing or to discuss a wider partnership with Dezeen.
Dezeen Events Guide is our guide to the best architecture and design events taking place across the world each year.

The guide is updated weekly and includes virtual events, conferences, trade fairs, major exhibitions and design weeks. For more details on inclusion in the Dezeen Events Guide, including in our guide to Miami art week, email eventsguide@dezeen.com.

items.title: The Zelda 40th Anniversary Switch 2 console gets a tiny discount – here's where to buy it
paragraphs: The limited-edition Switch 2 is still a nightmare to find, but I’ve spotted a small saving on the Zelda console, plus some tempting Ocarina of Time bundles. If the Zelda-themed console has caught your eye, I’ve found two places selling it for less than Nintendo’s asking price.

The Nintendo Switch 2 The Legend of Zelda 40th Anniversary Edition is £429.99 at Argos, undercutting the £434.99 retail price by a small £5. Hardly a king’s ransom, but for limited-edition hardware this in demand, I’ll take it.
The standard Switch 2 is reduced from £419 to £389.

Zelda is having quite a year. Nintendo is celebrating 40 years of the series and has brought back Ocarina of Time in a full Switch 2 remake. Launched on 29 October, the special edition features a black-and-gold Triforce design on the console and dock, with green-and-gold Joy-Con 2 controllers to match. Under the skin, it’s the same as the standard Switch 2, so you’re paying for the looks and the collectability, not extra power.
Check stock before you set off or place an order. Argos lets you check delivery and collection by postcode.

US readers are not so lucky. Restocks are coming but will be limited; the best advice is to visit GameStop in person, as it sells stock only in-store for its retail price of $529.99. I say this because while you can get a console online at places like Best Buy, you'll pay upwards of $739.95. Scaplers in the US are having a field day.
If you don’t care about the special-edition shell and just want to play the remake, the savings are bigger, and both the game and the standard console are in stock.
Very has a standard Switch 2 bundled with Ocarina of Time for £443.99, down from £473.99. That’s £30 off.

There’s also a Switch 2 Sports Resort bundle with Ocarina of Time for £449.99, advertised as £59.99 off the usual combined price. You get a second game thrown in, which is handy if you want more to play on day one.

In the US, you can pick up the Ocarina of Time remake for $54.99 on Amazon, the lowest price yet. That’s $5 off the digital version. Nintendo’s Black Friday bundles include the Switch 2 + Sports Resort for $529 and the Switch 2 + Mario Kart World for $549, both at Amazon.

As I reported before, Woot’s $469 Switch 2 deal remains the lowest price since Nintendo’s May price increases. But the catch is you need a Prime membership to get the deal. Already a member? Then it's a good offer.

It’s a lovely Limited Edition console, especially if you grew up with Link. The Triforce detailing and gold trim set it apart from the standard console, and it’s a neat way to mark four decades of Hyrule. It's the kind of hardware design that makes a perfect gift over a standard Switch 2.
Just don’t forget it doesn’t come with Ocarina of Time. You’ll need to buy the game separately. So the real cost is around $60 / £70 more than the deals I've found.
If playing the remake is the priority, the standard Switch 2 bundle at Very or Woot makes more financial sense. If you’re a Zelda collector, grab the anniversary edition while you can.
