items.title: Democrats formally nominate Hakeem Jeffries for speaker of the House
paragraphs: Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., speaks during a news conference in the U.S. Capitol on Nov. 17, 2026. Anna Moneymaker/Getty Images hide caption
House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries has been nominated by House Democrats to serve as Speaker of the House when the party retakes the majority in the new year.

Wednesday's vote by House Democrats kickstarts the formal selection process for Speaker, which will take place at the start of the new Congress on January 3 with a vote on the floor of the House. If successful, as is widely expected, Jeffries will make history as the first Black lawmaker to serve in the job.

"Our message to the American people who are struggling in this failed economy is a simple one. We hear you, we see you, we feel you, and House Democrats are committed to making life better for you," Jeffries said after the vote.

Jeffries centered his remarks on cost of living issues, saying Democrats would fight to lower the cost of groceries, gas, housing and health care. And in the face of what he described as "unprecedented corruption," Jeffries said Democrats would work to hold officials accountable.
"Not for partisan reasons but for patriotic ones, because the American people deserve better," he said.

The New York Democrat ran uncontested, winning a closed-door vote by a tally of 251 to 11. His victory comes just over a week after House Republicans selected Rep. Jim Jordan of Ohio to be the conference's minority leader; in the Senate, Republicans tapped South Dakota's John Thune for a second term as party leader.

Jeffries, who's led House Democrats since 2023, will need just a simple majority of member votes in a Congress where Democrats are poised to control at least 257 seats, with several remaining races still to be decided.

It's a vastly different reality from what awaited House Republicans four years ago when they regained the House majority. Facing extremely narrow margins, GOP leaders struggled to unite the conference around a speaker and were forced to negotiate with a handful of far-right party holdouts in order to reach consensus. After multiple candidates failed to secure a majority, the party ultimately coalesced around the now outgoing Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La.
While Jeffries will still have to navigate intraparty divides, the size of Democrats' majority affords him room to weather some dissent.

He's faced resistance from some within the party's left-most flank, who argue Democrats should prioritize advancing a more progressive agenda next year, lobbying for votes on Medicare for All and legislation that would stop the transfer of offensive weapons to Israel.

Among those who voted against Jeffries were a number of newly-elected members — some who won with the backing of the Democratic Socialists of America. In a statement after the vote, they said they have engaged in "good-faith conversations" with Jeffries to secure commitments on their policy priorities.

"While we have seen meaningful progress, there is still work to be done to ensure that the direction our party takes this coming Congress reflects what our constituents are demanding of leadership. Those conversations are ongoing. As such, our vote in caucus today was no."

Among those who signed the statement were members-elect Darializa Avila Chevalier and Claire Valdez, both from New York; New Jersey's Adam Hamawy; Frederick Haynes of Texas; Colorado's Melat Kiros; Donavan McKinney of Michigan and Chris Rabb of Pennsylvania.
After the vote, Jeffries told reporters "the results of today's election speak for themselves."

"We're going to work hard throughout every corner of the caucus to deliver for the American people. Our job is to fight MAGA extremism — not each other — to fight MAGA extremism and to get big things done for the American people."

Given that Democrats will hold double digit margins in the chamber — an edge propelled by the success of more moderate candidates in districts President Trump carried in 2024 — it's unclear how much leverage the left wing of the party will have in the speaker's vote.

Divides inside the party may prove more pronounced in the Senate, where some Democrats are more publicly questioning whether current Minority Leader Chuck Schumer of New York is best suited to deliver on voter demands for change.

Schumer faces a challenge from Maryland's Chris Van Hollen, who announced his candidacy last week and is pitching himself as an alternative to the status quo, echoing much of the progressive populist messaging that several successful Senate candidates ran on this cycle. Like Schumer, Van Hollen has also served in Congress for decades.

Schumer, the top Democrat in the Senate for nearly a decade, contends that he still has the needed votes to be elected majority leader. However, Van Hollen's challenge comes as a handful of current and incoming members have declined to back Schumer for the job.
Both sides still have time to shore up votes, with leadership elections set for early December.

items.title: Parents jailed for torture and death of four-year-old girl found along French motorway in 1987
paragraphs: The mother of a four-year-old girl killed in central France and found along a motorway almost 40 years ago has been sentenced to 20 years in prison.
Halima El Bakhti, 72, was found guilty on Tuesday of "torture and acts of barbarity resulting in death without the intent to kill", French media reports.
The girl's father, 74-year-old Ahmed Touloub, was handed a 15-year sentence as an accomplice.

Four-year-old Inass Touloub was found along the A10 road in Suèvres in the Loir-et-Cher department on 11 August 1987. Her body bore multiple marks of abuse, including human bite marks, broken bones and burns with an iron.
She was buried in an unmarked grave near the location where her body was found. Unidentified for three decades, she was known only as the "Little Martyr of the A10".
Then, in 2018, she was identified after the DNA of her brother – tested in an unrelated case – matched with hers, leading to the arrest of their parents.
The trial took place in Loir-et-Cher Assize Court from 2 November, with the verdict delivered on Tuesday after several hours of deliberation.

During the trial, prosecutor Anaïs Allio emphasised that "not a single part of Inass's body was spared", and recalled the "sense of vertigo that overcame us all" upon viewing the "unbearable photographs" from the autopsy, France Info reports.
The jury concluded that the child's mother was suffering from impaired judgement at the time of the girl's death, which reduced the maximum potential sentence.
French media outlet France Info described the two defendants as sitting stoically in chairs before the court with their heads bowed as the reasoning behind the verdict was read out.
El Bakhti and Touloub have 10 days to appeal the verdict.
Inass's death sparked one of France's biggest ever investigations, with the girl's photograph posted in public places and an alert sent to more than 30 countries.

items.title: Anthony Albanese defies critics for Apec summit photo with Vladimir Putin
paragraphs: Anthony Albanese has appeared in a leaders’ photo with Vladimir Putin at the Apec summit in China, despite Australia’s Ukrainian community urging the prime minister to protest against Russia’s war.

After arriving in the Chinese tech capital, Shenzhen, on Wednesday, Albanese said he would respect the wishes of China as the hosts of this week’s Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit and take part in the photo.

He appeared in a group shot that included Putin, the US president, Donald Trump, and China’s Xi Jinping at the summit banquet on Wednesday night. The traditional leaders’ “family photo” is due to be taken on Thursday morning.
“I will bear in mind the wishes of our host,” Albanese said before the event. “China are our host here, I respect that, but we also make our position very clear when it comes to Ukraine.”
Other leaders including Canada’s Mark Carney said they would take part, despite foreign affairs ministers at this month’s G20 talks in the United States refusing to pose with Russia’s Sergei Lavrov.
It is the first time Putin has had a place at the forefront of a grouping of world leaders in nearly a decade.

A professor of international law at Australian National University, Don Rothwell, said posing with Putin risked undermining trust in the international criminal court, where the Russian has been indicted as a war criminal over his invasion of Ukraine and the four-year war.
“For the Australian prime minister to appear in a photograph with Vladimir Putin is not consistent with the international values Australia is seeking to espouse,” Rothwell told Guardian Australia.
The Australian Federation of Ukrainian Organisations chairwoman, Kateryna Argyrou, had urged Albanese to boycott the event.
“Vladimir Putin is not just another world leader attending an international summit,” Argyrou said.
“He is an indicted war criminal and the architect of a brutal war against Ukraine – a war that has brought death, destruction and unimaginable suffering to millions of people.”
China is the latest stop on Albanese’s intense diplomatic tour.
After Quad leaders’ talks in Manila on Tuesday night, the prime minister attended a business event and toured a supermarket selling Australian-made products in Shenzhen.

The city – known as a major hub for electronics, drones and companies including Huawei and electric vehicle brand BYD – is seeing intense security as world leaders gather. Many of the streets have been cleared of local residents, allowing motorcades speedy access to the summit hubs and nearby luxury hotels.
Spruiking investment in Australia, Albanese recalled first visiting Shenzhen in the 1990s and said AI could help bridge economic divides and allow for sustainable growth in the region.
“The economic potential and opportunity of artificial intelligence is enormous,” he said. “Not just for the Asia Pacific, but for the world.”

As well as the main summit, Albanese will take part in bilateral meetings on Thursday, including with Mexico’s president, Claudia Sheinbaum. He will attend a lunch with Carney and the leaders of Singapore and New Zealand.

But the trilateral talks with Trump, Xi and Putin on Thursday are set to dominate conversations in Shenzhen and in capitals around the world. Already likened to the Yalta summit after the second world war, Ukraine’s president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, warned against decisions about his country’s future being made without him.
Albanese will make a diplomatic call on Xi on Friday, before a meeting in Beijing with the Chinese premier, Li Qiang.

On the agenda with both leaders is a push for China to remove 55% tariffs for Australian beef exports, imposed after the country hit an annual quota for sales. Albanese said he would lobby in Australia’s interests.

“Of course we’d rather not have any quotas on Australian goods anywhere in the world, but the fact they’ve hit it is a signal that Chinese consumers want to buy Australian beef because of its quality.”
He said he would raise trade issues as the federal government works to stabilise trade with China after Beijing imposed a major diplomatic freeze on Australia during the former Coalition government.
Albanese praised Xi’s engagement and knowledge of Australia, noting the Chinese leader had visited every state and territory.

items.title: House Democrat warns 13 Trump allies to save their records for upcoming investigations
paragraphs: Rep. Robert Garcia, D-Calif., appears at a news conference outside the U.S. Capitol on Dec. 13, 2023. On Wednesday, he released document preservation letters that lay the groundwork for incoming investigations into the Trump family and its allies. Drew Angerer/Getty Images hide caption

The highest-ranking Democrat on the House Oversight Committee sent document preservation letters to over a dozen of President Trump's allies and family members, laying the groundwork for incoming investigations come January.

"Oversight Democrats are fighting to put an end to this Administration's self-dealing, misconduct, and abuse," said Rep. Robert Garcia, who is poised to become the chair of the committee. "These investigations will lay the groundwork for legislation which helps all Americans. This is just the beginning."
The California Democrat's targets fall into four broad categories: "Trump family corruption, corporate corruption, DHS misconduct, and the White House Epstein cover-up."
"Americans should be secure in the knowledge that their government is focused on their best interests—not on making the President's family richer," many of the letters read.

The Trump administration has previously rejected accusations of misconduct and has warned Garcia that overly zealous investigations could constitute a crime — a claim legal experts have broadly pushed back against, citing Congress' oversight authorities.

In a letter dated Nov. 9, White House Counsel Will Scharf told Garcia the administration was "monitoring" the speech of Democrats in Congress as they mapped out investigative targets into the Trump administration. The letter warned that efforts by Democrats to investigate the administration "may cross the line into blatant criminality."

"As the President has said, he's willing to work with anyone to continue delivering victories for hardworking Americans," White House spokeswoman Lauren Bis said in a statement on Wednesday in response to Garcia's letters. "If Democrats choose to pursue sham investigations and radical left policies, they are choosing to work against the American people."

items.title: Players say goodbye to Grand Theft Auto V with one last drive
paragraphs: The virtual streets of Grand Theft Auto Online’s Los Santos will be spared from their usual explosions and high-speed car chases tonight, as hundreds of players meet for a final journey across the video game’s world before the release of Grand Theft Auto VI at midnight.

Rockstar Games’ multiplayer criminal sandbox normally prompts hostility between its millions of players by giving them ample access to guns, bombs and fighter jets. But fans took it upon themselves to peacefully cruise across the game world together for “one last drive” in virtual California, before the next chapter in the series arrives.

Willy, who goes by zarki_34 online, has played GTA Online for thousands of hours over the last decade. He has organised several of his own final drive events. “[GTA Online] has been part of my life for 13 years … I’m now 26,” he says. “I’ve spent half my life with this game.”
His route took players from the centre of the game’s Los Angeles-inspired city, across rugged coastlines and through so-Cal countryside in one singular trip.

The gamer from southern France livestreams on TikTok and regularly hosts virtual events: from socials where players show off their in-game vehicles to highly choreographed aeroplane stunts. “Some people have been joining for two years,” he said. “Some have become really close friends and I’ve met some amazing people thanks to this game.”
Willy’s social media post about his plans for a final drive in GTA Online quickly went viral. Inspired by the idea, groups across North America and Europe suddenly began to plan their own farewells.

Rockstar is not ending support for GTA Online anytime soon, but as millions of players prepare to move on to GTA VI, Willy wanted to celebrate “an end of era”. “For me, it’s not just about driving cars,” he says. “It’s about bringing people together who share the same passion and creating good memories.”

GTA Online is the multiplayer version of 2013’s Grand Theft Auto V, and was released two weeks after the single-player game. Despite poor performance and lukewarm reviews from critics at the time, years of updates saw the game grow exponentially in popularity and quality while generating billions of dollars in revenue across three generations of video game consoles, starting on the Xbox 360 and PlayStation 3.

Dylan, 34, from north London, remembers playing the game before the kinks were ironed out. “Back then, you’d get kicked out of the server before you could really enjoy it,” he said. After taking years away from the game, the busy dad has recently returned to Los Santos in anticipation of GTA VI. “I love the world building of GTA, their whole atmosphere of the game.”

Dylan has coordinated his own last drive with strangers online, timing it to coincide with the launch of the franchise’s newest entry so that it would “take us exactly to the moment we can press start on GTA VI”.

In GTA Online, players complete missions and activities to grow their criminal empire, working together to plan, prepare and execute high-octane heists. For Jerry, a 20-year-old from Louisiana, this shared experience with up to 30 players at a time is what makes the game special. “People say this community is toxic – it’s not,” he says.
He says he began playing the game alone during Covid, and “started meeting these nice people who would help me along the way”.
Jerry was encouraged to keep playing by a close friend he met on the game, who has since died. “He’s the main reason I’m doing [the last drive], the memory of him,” he said.

While many are preparing to say goodbye to San Andreas after a decade of play tonight, Jerry is holding out a little longer. He has pre-ordered GTA VI, he said, but won’t be leaving Los Santos just yet: “I’m going to stay in GTA Online for at least six months.”

items.title: ‘Zero’ evidence that recent cascade of tech outages are linked, says Rubio
paragraphs: There is “zero evidence” that a wave of IT outages – which have grounded flights, cut off work access, limited bank access, affected Apple and disrupted classified communications – are related to each other or are the work of malign actors, according to the US secretary of state.
Marco Rubio said the US was “not under systemic attack” and a cascade of network problems was “not inter-related”.
In recent days, Microsoft, major US banks, Apple, American air traffic control systems and the National Security Agency have all been affected by technical failures and outages.

“We have zero evidence or any reason to believe that any of these isolated or individual instances have anything to do with nefarious actors, with cyber-hackers, with criminals, with another nation state, with a malign actor of any kind,” Rubio said.

Rubio’s comments came as cybersecurity researchers flagged a vulnerability in Java, a programming language used by 90% of companies in the Fortune 500, a ranking of the largest companies in the US. The researchers at US-based Calif used AI to discover the flaw and recently unearthed glitches in PHP, another computer language.
Calif said the Java flaw could allow hackers to remotely execute code, allowing them to place malicious software on a target’s systems.

The US director of national intelligence, Jay Clayton, said the incidents were caused by security upgrades – such as plugging the flaws in PHP – that took longer than planned or encountered unexpected hiccups.

“Everybody recognises it’s time to upgrade their systems, and as they upgrade them, they’re not coming back as expected in all cases, and in some cases, systems have to hand off to other systems, and those handoffs are not coming back as expected,” he told the Fox Business news channel.

Tal Be’ery, a cybersecurity expert, said he did not believe the incidents were linked directly but had a common underlying theme: AI. IT systems were buckling under the pressure of adding AI or tackling flaws uncovered by AI, he said.

“Our IT infrastructure is brittle, and when AI puts massive extra pressure on it, whether through upgrades to accommodate AI or through the rapid patching that AI-driven vulnerability discovery demands,” Be’ery said.

Since April, when the AI startup Anthropic released its Mythos model, which had a startling ability to flag IT flaws, the amount of vulnerabilities found by leading tech companies has soared eightfold – while OpenAI has also released models capable of finding previously unseen flaws. Researchers at Calif used OpenAI technology to discover the Java flaw.

“[Java] is the beating heart of the modern economy,” Calif wrote in a blogpost. “Banking, aviation, telecommunications, nearly every critical sector runs on Java, including national security systems.”

However, Steven Murdoch, a professor of security engineering at University College London, said the flaw did not apply to every Java user and was specific to a library of code – Base64 – that comes bundled with a version of Java.
“It’s significant but it’s not every Java program that is affected,” he said.
In the UK the National Cyber Security Centre urged organisations to keep their systems up to date, while the US and South Korean authorities also urged Java users to install security updates.

Rubio made the comments as he travelled with Donald Trump for key meetings in the Philippines on Wednesday, before flying to the tech hub of Shenzhen in China for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) summit.

Trump was dismissive when asked whether he was concerned about the outages on Tuesday. “It’s life. When you’re big and powerful and you have all the money, things like that happen. It’s fine,” Trump said in Manila.

The series of outages began on Thursday last week, when Microsoft’s email and other tools went down, affecting millions of workers who rely on them. Microsoft traced the problem to “an earlier network capacity upgrade”.
Flights across the US were grounded the next day in the longest “ground stop” since the September 11 attacks. The US Federal Aviation Administration blamed a router upgrade.

By Monday, banks were in the spotlight, as customers reported difficulty accessing online accounts at several major financial institutions and the money transfer service Zelle after a technical problem at JPMorgan Chase caused ripple effects throughout the financial system. Chase said it was caused by “a software bug” and was “not cyber-related”.
The same day, United Airlines said it had resolved an internal system outage that delayed departing flights.

Then on Tuesday, an internal network that the National Security Agency uses to communicate classified information was offline after what the agency described as “routine maintenance”. Apple also confirmed problems with its iPhone apps, such as Apple Pay and iCloud, on Tuesday but said it had resolved them.
The Democrat Mark Warner, the vice-chair of the Senate intelligence committee, supported the assessment that the outages were not caused by a “coordinated effort” but by attempts to shore up systems.
“The evidence so far points toward legitimate efforts to secure our systems, not malicious activity.”

Cynthia Kaiser, a former deputy director in the FBI’s cyber division, said it was “plausible” that the race to upgrade systems was fuelled by warnings that specific cyber adversaries were planning attacks.

Kaiser, now an executive at cybersecurity firm Halcyon, said she was more concerned about cyber criminals and scammers trying to “capitalise on the confusion to steal money from organisations and everyday people”.

items.title: A TikTok superstar bares all: Siorna Ashby’s best shot
paragraphs: I met Meg at a nude life-drawing class. I was struck by how free she seemed and how powerfully that came through in her modelling. I asked if I could photograph her for my project Body Like Mine. This series explores the difference between how our bodies are perceived externally and how we experience them ourselves. We see a body and we bring our own judgments and assumptions on to it, but the lived experience is very different.

Rather than portraying an idealised body, the project aims to explore what it feels like to inhabit your own body, and to see it as worthy of attention without asking it to become anything else first.

My photography is collaborative. I brought some visual ideas to the shoot, and Meg brought her own ways of moving and expressing herself. The photograph developed between us. I took references from art history: Jenny Saville’s nudes and Lucian Freud’s work have inspired me, along with the sense of flesh and physical presence in Rubens’ paintings.

I lit her in a painterly way and used a canvas backdrop. As I was photographing her, I found myself getting lower down. I wanted the body to have a real presence in the photograph, to become the portrait itself. It was Meg’s idea to scrunch her belly in that way. I asked her to look away so that her face wouldn’t be the first place your eye went. I love how fleshy the image feels. Portraits often rely on the face and eyes to communicate who someone is. Here, I wanted to explore how much of Meg’s presence and personality could come through her body and gesture.

Meg loved it and was delighted when the image was selected to be displayed in the National Portrait Gallery. Her nude modelling is only a small part of what she does – most of her time and energies go into raising awareness about overconsumption and the “tat” that fills our lives and ends up in landfill. She’s a superstar on TikTok!

“Fat women’s femininity is [often] stripped from them and … I am masculinised and called brave for just existing in this body. When I am life modelling, I feel the most feminine and deeply in touch with myself. I am proud to take up space and represent people who often are not,” she says.

My commissioned work specialises in boudoir and nude photography. Coming to this has been a personal journey. I was very critical of my body – I was one of those women who couldn’t look in a mirror. For me, being behind the camera was also a way of avoiding being in photographs. I liked having that control. I started out doing headshots, but when you run your own business, you need to be visible. I became frustrated with all the negative feelings I had about myself, and one day I stripped off and I took my own photographs of my nude body. And when I looked over the images I was shocked to realise that I didn’t hate them. In fact I thought they were beautiful.

And then I noticed a change in myself. I was walking down the street taller. I wasn’t wearing cardigans to hide my arms. And I realised that maybe I can help others. I don’t think a photograph can resolve someone’s relationship with their body, but it can be one part of seeing themselves differently, feeling more connected to their body, or recognising that they are worthy of being seen.

But there is a tension in my work between beauty standards and how women want to be seen. Much of the boudoir photography I do sits in that culture that shapes how women think they should look and what makes a body beautiful or desirable. But who decides what makes a body either of these things? Women’s bodies don’t exist to meet someone else’s expectations of beauty or desirability, which change over time. There is room for wanting to feel sexy, but whose idea of sexy are we working towards?

When I make or look at a nude photograph, I ask what the pose, light, colour and composition are communicating. Whose perspective is shaping the image, and how much say does the person being photographed have in how they are seen?

With Body Like Mine, I want to give more space to people’s own accounts of living in their bodies, particularly where those experiences differ from what others assume when they look at them. The next person I’m photographing lives with endometriosis, and another participant is experiencing memory loss. I want us to explore how those experiences might be expressed in a photograph, guided by what each person wants to share.

Before we photograph, I ask each person to choose a few words that describe what they would like us to express together. Those words give us a starting point for the images. Meg’s were “real”, “joyful” and “free”.
Body Like Mine is part of the Winston Taylor photo portrait prize exhibition at the National Portrait Gallery, London, until 17 January. siornaphotography.com; @siornaphotography

Born: Blackpool, 1983 High point: Having my photograph of Meg Foster, Body Like Mine, selected for the National Portrait Gallery’s Winston Taylor photo portrait prize 2026 exhibition. Top tip: Talk through boundaries before artistic nude or boudoir photoshoots, and keep checking in as you work. Make it easy for someone to change their mind, and be ready to adapt a pose, change direction or put the camera down.

items.title: Young people lose hearing – level 1
paragraphs: Experts say that more than 1 billion young people cannot hear well.
They are between 12 and 34 years old. Young people often hear a loud continuous noise in their ears. Their hearing tests look normal. Later, their hearing test results are worse.
Experts know reasons why this situation happens. Young people listen to their headphones. They go to concerts. The music is too loud. Sometimes, music in restaurants is loud, too.
Decibels tell us how loud something is. The sound of a food mixer is 85 decibels. The sound of a train is 100 decibels. Experts say that it is safe to listen to 85 decibels at work.
Sometimes we can lose hearing when we hear something very loud only once. Loud noise kills the cells in our ears. We cannot fix the situation.
Difficult words: result (the information we get from a test or experiment), headphones (a device which people wear over their ears to listen to music), cell (the smallest part in the human body).
You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

items.title: Young people lose hearing – level 2
paragraphs: British scientists published a study about people 12 to 34 years old; the study said that more than 1 billion of them had hearing problems.

Many young people complain about nonstop ringing in their ears. Hearing tests show no problems, but when doctors repeat the test some years later, the hearing is worse. The main reasons are headphones, concerts, and restaurants where the sounds are too loud for too long. The sound damages the cells in the inner ear, and once this damage happens, you cannot change it.

Scientists say that the safe limit for our ears is 85 decibels over a 40-hour work week. 85 decibels are the sound of a blender, while 100 decibels are the sound of a train. We can also suddenly lose our hearing when we experience a very loud noise just once.
Difficult words: cell (the smallest part in the human body), decibel (the unit which people use to measure loudness), blender (an electric mixing machine).
You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

items.title: Young people lose hearing – level 3
paragraphs: The British Medical Journal published a study which showed that 1 billion young people were at risk of hearing loss.

Researchers shared their analysis of data from 2000 to 2021 on unsafe listening practices. If the volume is too loud for too long, headphones, a concert, or even a restaurant could cause irreversible damage. Young people are complaining about persistent ringing in their ears, although their hearing tests look normal. However, several years later, their hearing reduces.

The loud sounds damage sensory cells in the cochlea, the snail-looking part in the inner ear. Once these cells die, you can’t get them back. 85 decibels sound like a blender, 100 decibels sound like a subway train, and 120 decibels sound like a concert or a siren.

According to experts, 85 decibels during a 40-hour work week is the maximum safe limit. Just 2.5 hours of 92 decibels can damage your ears. However, only one episode of intense noise exposure can lead to lifelong hearing loss.
Difficult words: irreversible (impossible to change or return to a previous condition), persistent (continue over a long period of time), exposure (affected by something).

items.title: Am I Caribbean, or am I a tourist? How art helped me find the answer
paragraphs: When I tell people I’m travelling to the Bahamas to report on Fuze Caribbean art fair, no one believes I’m really going for work. There are smirks and jokes about it being a tough life, about drinking from coconuts on the beach. The tourist gaze pervades global perceptions of the Caribbean. This week, I speak to the region’s artists about how they use images to speak back.

I have Antiguan and Jamaican heritage, so I’m familiar with the fantasies the Caribbean sparks, which Antiguan-American writer Jamaica Kincaid described as so beautiful that its fluffy white clouds, blue spectral waters and “bottomless” black nights seemed “unreal”. Images have done much to flatten the Caribbean in the global imagination – so why shouldn’t Caribbean people use images to speak back?

“Artists from The Bahamas and the wider Caribbean are in constant dialogue with the expectations of outsiders looking at our destinations as spaces of relaxation and service,” says leading Bahamian artist and curator John Cox, who I meet on a gallery tour of the nation’s capital, Nassau. “Those expectations often fetishise exotic notions of paradise, drawing on Hollywood images of an appealing landscape inhabited by people whose lives and cultures are presumed to be less sophisticated.”

Through this process, culture becomes flattened, and local people participate to make a living. Take the capital’s famous straw market, one of the nation’s most popular tourist attractions, where vendors sell bags and other items made from woven silver top and palmetto palms. The market helped local women earn money in the early days of tourism; now many of its goods are imported from China, and you can buy a bag with Minnie Mouse’s face braided onto it. Artist Anina Major, who recently exhibited at TERN gallery in Nassau, has made ceramic sculptures from hand-weaved clay to resemble the baskets. But in her work, they are crumpled and sinking into themselves – a deflated replica of Bahamian identity, performed entirely for the tourist gaze. I encounter this cynicism and resentment towards tourists among many of the Bahamians I meet.

Other artists decentre the tourist, going deeper into cultural traditions, such as Caribbean connection with the sea, the flora and the land. Virtually everywhere you look at the fair, there are fluorescent colours: pinks, yellows and aquas. Antonius Roberts, another of the Bahamas’ foremost and prolific artists, suggests that this palette may be the reason that when he first went to study in the US, he was told to stop “painting Black”. “It was seen as too bright, the paint coming right out of the tube,” he tells me. “I was like: ‘You haven’t been to the Caribbean have you? You haven’t seen our beautiful beaches, right? You haven’t seen our bright tropical sunlight?’”

The 68-year-old now also works with wood, stone, goat skins and other natural and recycled materials, drawing on traditional craft knowledge. Roberts’ works are often towering and awe-inspiring – reflecting the spirit of Caribbean dignity and integrity that he emphasises as we speak. “People want to come here, buy a nice little painting, take it back and say ‘oh I bought this in the Bahamas!’” he says. The cruise industry, which he describes as the “new colonial power” in the region, is complicit in these dynamics, by curating what their customers see – no political art, no climate breakdown.

After the abolition of transatlantic enslavement, perceptions of danger, poverty and uncleanliness plagued the Bahamas, much like other Caribbean countries, well into the 20th century. Economies reliant on exports such as sugar gave way to tourism. Postcards and photography intentionally depicted the Caribbean as a holiday destination, ramping up in the middle of the century. This transformed global – and importantly, American – impressions of the region. The Bahamas was a testing ground for this tourist economy, with external perceptions now deeply shaped by the idea that it is a tropical playground for Americans. Flights from the south of Florida can be as short as 30 minutes, Roberts tells me: “If the Americans sneeze, we get a cold.”

The art fair is hosted at a luxury resort. I feel alienated from the American tourists here on bachelor parties who fill the resort’s casinos, in which it is illegal for Bahamians to play. In a throwaway comment during the gallery tour, I remark that I’m “not like them” – and a Black British curator, who regularly visits her sister in the Bahamas, responds quickly: “You are”.

Kincaid wrote that a tourist is an ugly thing, and as I’m reminded of this, I wonder whether I am looking at the Bahamas from the inside or the outside; whether the love I have suddenly acquired for the fuchsias, turquoises and yellows of the art and the landscape is an act of reclamation or exoticisation; whether going to a half-hour workshop where I poured acrylic paint over a conch shell tokenised Caribbean artists’ tradition of using the land and nature for creativity. I then mentally flog myself for these diasporan thoughts, which feel clichéd. But locals I speak to express a strikingly similar anxiety – that those who go away to study in the US, for example, are told they are not truly Bahamian when they return.

When I’m engaging with the art, I find that there’s a bit more breathing room, and space for complexity. Art doesn’t demand a definitive answer, and doesn’t fix itself or the viewer in place. I wonder if it is uniquely placed to channel the spirit of Caribbeanness, which is so shaped by migration, flux, and expression as collective resistance.

Art can encompass many themes and conflicts at once. Cox is excited about a new crop of Bahamian artists including Cydne Coleby, April Bey and Tavares Strachan. All of them play with composite materials, themes, or images from the past and the future. He says: “[They] retain the beauty and raw, seductive quality of this landscape while bringing forward the complexity of lives filled with diversity, humour, irony and connections to Europe, Africa and the wider West Indies.”

Both Roberts and Cox have become highly respected artists but they have also spent decades incubating others. Roberts helped establish the National Gallery of the Bahamas, and founded several art competitions and galleries, while Cox directed Fuze and has held multiple senior curatorial roles. The fair is significant because it brings together artists from across the Caribbean, even though the Bahamas is often seen as a high-income outlier in the region, which is able to generate more resources and opportunities for its artists.

Cox says: “The Caribbean has been formed through connections with continents across the world. Yet the intelligence, relevance and contribution of the region to global developments are too often underestimated. We encounter that in contemporary art and across the wider cultural sphere.”

“I believe that we have some of the most creative people on earth,” Roberts says. “What is happening in London has a lot to do with Caribbean energy, what is happening in the United States has a lot to do with Caribbean energy. In the art world, in the political world and whatever else, Caribbean people somehow always magically insert themselves into something larger than themselves,” Roberts says.

But they also come back. “My mother told me that my navel string was buried under a silk cotton tree,” he says. She’d hoped that he would stay rooted in his country, and return to help build the nation following independence. Through art, that is what he did – alongside other Caribbean artists who have made space to look inwards, to look at themselves. I look at the art, then I look at myself too. I wonder what I can’t see.

What do you think the role of art is in exploring our cultural identities as Black people? Share your thoughts by replying to this, or emailing us at thelongwave@theguardian.com and we may include your response in a future issue.

items.title: Business Council of Australia more aligned with fossil fuel industry than its members’ values, analysis finds
paragraphs: The Business Council of Australia is lobbying for gas expansion policies that clash with the climate concerns of the majority of its own members, according to new research that raises questions about the sway of a handful of major companies.

The business association also does not publicly disclose who is on its energy and climate committee, prompting transparency concerns among researchers over how its policies are shaped and whose interests they represent.

Analysis by the London-headquartered InfluenceMap found the BCA’s positions aligned more closely with energy companies Woodside, Santos and ConocoPhillips than with the majority of its corporate base, particularly on the energy transition, where it has advocated for new gas supplies over phasing down.
InfluenceMap’s Australia lead, Jack Herring, said major associations such as the BCA are an influential voice in government policymaking.
“These findings suggest the BCA’s climate policy engagement better reflects the narrow interests of members connected to the fossil fuel value chain than its wider membership,” Herring said.

“Advocacy for fossil gas expansion risks undermining Australia’s climate targets and also threatens to create increased health risks and energy affordability and security concerns for everyday households, so this is an issue that affects us all.”

InfluenceMap’s analysis of company positions shows more than two-thirds of the members assessed, including Qantas, Woolworths, Coles, Atlassian, Fortescue and major banks CBA and NAB, advocate for stronger climate policies than the business council itself.
That support typically includes backing faster renewable energy rollout and advocating for more ambitious emission reduction targets.

For the study, the thinktank assessed 58 companies – a representative sample of the BCA’s more than 120 members – drawing on thousands of public statements, government submissions and regulatory filings.
Of those members assessed, 69% backed stronger climate policies than the BCA, a gap that widened to 78% on energy transition issues.
Herring said the BCA does not disclose who sits on its internal climate and energy committees, obscuring how its policy positions are formed.
“We obviously do know who’s on the association board but, beyond that, there’s no transparency around those internal committees,” he said.

A spokesperson for the BCA said the association supported the “national goal of achieving net zero by 2050 and the setting of interim targets, while also delivering reliable and affordable energy and ensuring we don’t undermine our international competitiveness along the way”.
“The BCA has long advocated for gas as an essential part of the net zero transition – ensuring grid stability – while we move to greater reliance on renewable energy,” the spokesperson said.
The BCA declined to comment on the makeup of its climate and energy committee.

The analysis comes as industry groups ramp up lobbying over the “safeguard mechanism”, Australia’s main policy for curbing emissions from its largest industrial facilities, which is under federal review.

While the BCA and most big resources companies publicly support the Paris agreement and Australia’s net zero 2050 carbon emissions target, they interpret what those commitments require in radically different ways to what is widely regarded as climate best practice.

Several oil and gas producer members, including Woodside, argue that increased gas supply is required to support the shift to renewables and enhance energy security in language that has been adopted by the BCA.

This rubs against those BCA members aligned with the findings of the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change, which found greenhouse gas emissions from existing fossil fuel infrastructure were more than enough to push the world beyond its climate goals.

InfluenceMap also found that the business council frequently lobbies for a “technology-neutral” or “technology agnostic” energy transition, which is the same language used by the fossil fuel sector designed to steer renewable energy funding toward gas.

Persephone Fraser, the ethical research and climate policy lead at fund manager Australian Ethical, said misaligned lobbying was a significant risk for companies and their shareholders, and a major risk to the economy.
“Companies must be scrutinising what is being advocated for in their name and actively correcting the record when it is inconsistent with their own positions, and interests,” Fraser said.
“Membership of an industry association cannot mean outsourcing responsibility for climate lobbying.”
Do you know more? Contact jonathan.barrett@theguardian.com

items.title: Seven Anthropic founders who are about to become multi-billionaires
paragraphs: Brother and sister Dario and Daniela Amodei are chief executive and president of Anthropic
ByTom Espiner and Lucy HookerBusiness reporters
In the space of just five years, Anthropic has gone from unknown start-up to tech giant, worth more than a trillion dollars.
The company behind the AI platform Claude was formed by seven people who left rival OpenAI in 2021 and, in a matter of hours, will become multi-billionaires - on paper at least.
Anthropic is floating the business on the US stock exchange and will sell its shares at between $70 - $78 each.
If they go for the highest price, the founders' shareholdings will be worth at least $18.5bn each.
So, who are these people, all in their thirties and forties, who are about to become incredibly wealthy?
In 2020, Dario Amodei was working for OpenAI, the firm that brought generative artificial intelligence to a mainstream audience, when it launched Chat-GPT.
He decided he wanted to do things his own way, and left, taking his sister Daniela, and five colleagues with him.

Amodei grew up in San Francisco, impressing school friends not just with his academic prowess but also his speed on the running track, and his preoccupation with philosophical and technological questions including the potential of machines to gain consciousness and human longevity.
Initially he studied physics at Princeton and Stanford. But following his father's death from hepatitis C, he switched to biology and biomedical sciences.
Amodei did stints at the Chinese tech giant Baidu and Google before joining OpenAI.
But he began to worry that some people within the company were putting profit before safety, prompting the decision to jump ship.
Now 43, he is Anthropic's chief executive, and the person who, in his sister's words, makes the company "ambitious".
Dario and Daniela Amodei, were close growing up and later shared a flat together in San Francisco with other friends. She followed him into OpenAI and joined him when he left to found Anthropic.
She and her brother have always genuinely liked each other, she says, but the only thing she ever did first, was when he followed her in becoming vegetarian.
Amodei studied English Literature at the University of California Santa Cruz, going on to work for Democrat representative Matt Cartwright.
She has also worked at financial services platform Stripe, where she was head of risk operations.
The 39-year-old is president of Anthropic, manages the executive team, and leads the firm's research, engineering, product, governance and commercial work.
Tom Brown, now 39, followed the Amodei siblings when they left to found their new venture.
He led GPT-3 engineering at OpenAI, and prior to that was at Google on its DeepMind project.
Brown established his entrepreneurial credentials co-founding an app called "Grouper" that helps set up drinks between groups of friends.
He has supported US President Donald Trump's stance on datacentres, arguing that they are "an enormous source of prosperity".
Now as chief compute officer at Anthropic he is responsible for how the company secures and uses its computing resources.
Jack Clark, is another arts graduate among the original start-up's founding members and the only one who is not from North America.

Originally from Brighton in the UK, he studied English Literature and Creative Writing at the University of East Anglia and became a technology journalist, writing for publications including ZDNet UK, The Register, and Bloomberg.
He was caught up in the excitement of artificial intelligence and joined OpenAI, where he worked initially in communications, later becoming its policy director.
Now, 37, Clark is head of public benefit at Anthropic. He also leads the Anthropic Institute, an AI think tank.
Jared Kaplan, 42, is chief science officer at Anthropic, and heads its technical research. He is also an associate professor at Johns Hopkins University in Baltimore.
He holds a PhD in physics from Harvard University.

His work on scaling laws - which describe mathematical patterns that show that bigger AI models trained on more data tend to be more consistent - has helped provide AI firms with a framework for predicting AI behaviour, according to Anthropic.
Chris Olah is described as "interpretability research lead" primarily focused on how AI models work with each other.
But according to the New York Times, Olah has spent much of the last year convening meetings with faith leaders from across the religious spectrum.
Described by the newspaper as "boyish" but with "the zeal of an evangelist" the 34-year-old is reportedly exploring the relationship between morality and AI.
He previously led interoperability research at OpenAI, and prior to that was a research scientist at Google Brain.
The Canadian left the University of Toronto early, but later secured a Thiel Fellowship of $100,000, which is a scholarship to help gifted people move into research without a degree.

Sam McCandlish, 36, takes less of a public-facing role than the other founders, but like them will own around 1.6% of the company after its shares go on sale. As a result he too will see his stake crystallise into a hugely valuable asset.
McCandlish is Anthropic's chief architect, and helps shape and implement the company's policy designed to mitigate the risks of AI. Prior to this he worked on safety at OpenAI.
He has a physics PhD from Stanford, and maths and physics degree from Brandeis University outside Boston.

items.title: Hacks, AI or just overdue updates - why have there been so many outages?
paragraphs: As is often the case, many outages were a result of an update or installation going wrong somewhere in a system.
A network upgrade at Microsoft caused servers to become overloaded and shut down.
It was also upgrades to a creaky old network which grounded thousands of planes in the US over the weekend.
Problems with the NSA's internal communication system and, separately, Apple's iCloud and Apple Pay were also blamed on things going wrong during system updates.
Disruption to payments in US banks has been put down to a "software bug" from JP Morgan Chase. The bank says it is not a cyber-security incident.
But some recent problems are in fact related to cyber-security vulnerabilities.
AI was used to discover flaws in Java, the third-most popular programming language in the world.
And researcher Scott Helme also discovered malicious code in Optimizely, a platform which is used by some of the world's largest companies.
Hackers were able to steal about $7,000 (£5,300) in cryptocurrency before they were discovered and kicked out.
Let's address the cyber incidents first - and the role of new AI models.
"I would be very surprised if all of these cyber-attacks and the attackers behind them were not using AI to accelerate themselves," Helme told BBC Radio 4's Today programme.

Since the summer, AI companies such as Anthropic and OpenAI have decided it's too risky to give the general public access to the most advanced models before allowing certain companies and institutions to use them.
In these cases, security professionals can use the same tech to find flaws themselves and alert others before criminals get to them.
This happened in the recent Java incident, as well as the PHP one - where there was a scramble to patch the flaws before they could be exploited.
These are not new - the world stood still in recent years as CrowdStrike and then Amazon Web Services ground many devices and systems to a halt.
Part of this may be down to technical debt - a term used when operators go for quick fixes to software instead of solving an underlying problem.
A build-up of surface-level fixes can eventually end up with more serious problems down the line.
With AI causing many companies to re-evaluate their cyber-security, they may be issuing more updates to patch flaws they have found.
Outages are often also a reminder of the physical tech our online world relies on - such as cables, servers and data centres.
In the US air traffic control incident, for example, the problem came as engineers were replacing outdated copper wires with fibre.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio is adamant the recent incidents are not connected or coming from one attacker.
"We are not under systemic attack," he said. "These events, one has nothing to do with the other, they are not inter-related."
In cases such as PHP and Java, the "good guys" found the flaws, with the help of AI, before the bad guys - allowing them to get together some fixes before the bugs could be widely exploited.
At the same time, Anthropic, among other leading AI firms, has warned of the risks its own products pose.
Outages in particular have an impact on the physical world as they often cause disruption to healthcare, schools and people's ability to do their jobs.
Or, in the case over the weekend, planes' ability to fly.
Watch: Marco Rubio says recent tech outages are 'completely unrelated' to one another
They also shine a light on the world's heavy reliance on a small number of players.
Not just frontier AI companies, but infrastructure providers such as Microsoft and Amazon, which - along with Google - run a huge chunk of the world's computer servers.
In the PHP incident, the world was holding its breath as one programmer - working voluntarily - worked to issue patches in a form that was easily applicable.
And Java, run by another tech giant Oracle, is used by nearly all of the biggest companies on Earth.

"The Oracle Java vulnerability is a stark reminder of how dependent businesses have become on a relatively small number of critical technologies," said Sheila Pancholi, risk assurance lead at consultancy firm RSM UK.
"Organisations need to know where their critical technology dependencies sit, act quickly when vulnerabilities emerge, and test that their response has actually worked."
Meanwhile Xander Van Raemdonck, security engineer at Aikido Security, said the challenge was "knowing whether you're exposed".
"Java is bundled inside a huge amount of business software, so many companies don't have a full list of where it runs," he said.
The AI tools used to help find security flaws are still so new that they will probably continue to find vulnerabilities which have been lingering in code for decades.
"AI is accelerating discovery on both sides and speeding up how much software gets shipped," said Martin Reynolds, field CTO at software delivery company Harness.
"So the volume of what developers need to patch is going up, while the time they have to get the work done it is going down."
Tech debt will need to continue to be dealt with - which means more upgrades to systems and more potential for these to cause disruptions.
Plus there is the constant threat from hackers as they continue to get more sophisticated.
Attackers only need to find one vulnerability to exploit - whereas defenders have to protect against all potential hacks.
"Attackers can move quickly and carefree, and experiment without risk of failure so they can naturally often move a fraction faster," Helme said.
"We're currently observing that small delay between how fast the attackers can move and how fast the defenders can move."
The cat-and-mouse nature of the cyber-security game means it's unlikely to end any time soon - and the impact of AI means the stakes are getting higher.

items.title: Rugby TV pundit says sex assault 'never happened'
paragraphs: A former England rugby league player and TV pundit accused of putting her hand up a woman's skirt in a cricket club toilet has told a jury it "categorically did not happen".
Danika Priim, 42, has been charged with carrying out the alleged sexual assault in the toilets at Horsforth Cricket Club in Leeds on 22 July 2022.
Her accuser, who cannot be named for legal reasons, previously told a trial at Leeds Crown Court how Priim twice reached up her dress and grabbed her underwear.
Keighley-based Priim, who previously represented Bradford Bulls, Leeds Rhinos and England, including at the 2017 World Cup, denies one count of sexual assault. The trial continues.
Two of the complainant's friends told the court they also witnessed what happened in the toilet but, on Wednesday, Priim told the jury she was never in the toilets with the three women.
Prosecutor Chloe Hudson put it to Priim that there were only two alternatives – either she was lying or the complainant and her two friends were lying.
Priim told the jury: "It categorically did not happen."
The defendant agreed she was not suggesting that it was an accident, or the woman had invited her to touch her, or it was a joke.
Priim told the jury she was never in the toilets with the complainant, adding: "I did not touch (her) in the toilets at all."
Hudson said to her: "What you must be saying is that these three got together to make completely false allegations about you."
Priim responded: "It's the biggest question I have – it's the why."
The prosecutor asked the defendant about how the complainant demonstrated to the jury how she was grabbed.
Priim said: "She was lying. I did not do that."
She added: "I'm also a very happy heterosexual woman. I'm with a man. I live with a man."
The prosecutor said: "The truth is that you sexually assaulted (the woman), didn't you?"
Priim said: "The truth is that it never happened."
Hudson asked Priim whether she thought the complainant and her two friends had colluded in a "witch hunt against you".
Stood in the witness box wearing a chunky light brown cardigan and a cream-and-black scarf, Priim replied: "I believe they have."
On Tuesday, the complainant described how Priim "walked straight up to me and put her hand up my skirt and grabbed hold of my pants and my private parts".
The woman said she asked the defendant what she was doing, "then she did it again, grinning at me, and walked off".
One of the complainant's friends told the jury how she witnessed Priim put her hand up the woman's skirt.
She told the court: "I recall seeing her remove her hand, laughed about it and then repeated it.

Giving evidence on Wednesday, Priim said she only went to the toilet once during her time at the cricket club, and produced a photograph she took of her and two friends in there, to help the jury with timings.
She said she drove to the venue and was drinking soft drinks until later when she had one pint.
Asked about the police getting involved following the allegation, she said: "It absolutely broke me."
Since retiring from the game in 2021 Priim has appeared on BBC, Channel 4 and Sky Sports as a pundit, reporter and commentator.
Jurors were sent out to consider their verdict on Wednesday.

items.title: Heating bills, chocolate and cat food: What the inflation figures mean for you
paragraphs: Nobody will be celebrating the fact that prices in the UK are rising at the fastest pace for a year.
Add to that an expectation of higher household energy bills and sharpening price increases and things look grim for everyone.
But there are some signs of hope that may take the edge off the rising cost of living. Here's how.
That headline is not missing a decimal point. The latest prediction for the increase in domestic energy prices in the new year is, indeed, 26%.

Millions of homes in England, Scotland and Wales are on tariffs affected by regulator Ofgem's price cap, which is set every three months. The next change for January will be officially announced next Wednesday, 25 November.

Energy consultancy Cornwall Insight, which has a good track record with its predictions, suggests that a household using a typical amount of gas and electricity will pay £2,166 a year - that's an increase of £443 from current levels.
Not all energy use for the year is between January and March, but a big chunk is owing to the cold, dark days and nights.
How much you pay depends on your use, with heavy users of gas likely to be the hardest hit.
The government has promised a £100 payment for people living in homes in council tax bands A to D in England to help cover winter energy costs. Other nations are planning similar support.
The latest inflation data shows that government assistance can have an impact on the general rate of inflation, external, as recorded by the Office for National Statistics (ONS).
Domestic energy prices rose by nearly 4% in October, but this was offset in inflationary terms by a cut in VAT on electricity bills.
While the rate of inflation in general was 3.6% in the year to October, food prices only went up by 0.9%.
It is partly the result of intense competition between the supermarkets. Like many retailers, they are facing higher costs but are not passing that onto their customers in full.
There may be some scars from the recent cost-of-living spike here. Shoppers suffered a period during the big rise in inflation in 2022-23 when food prices rocketed.
Those higher prices are embedded. While food prices overall aren't coming down now, they aren't rising anywhere near as fast as back then.
The detail here is very interesting. Take chocolate: world cocoa prices are down since 2024, and now chocolate prices are falling - down 2.9%, according to the latest data.
But the ONS has also pointed to cat food as one, albeit small, driver of the faster rate of rising prices.

Should high energy and fuel costs - which are driving the rising rate of inflation - persist, there are questions over whether the cost of producing and transporting food also goes up, and the chances of that higher cost being passed on to consumers are greater.

Economists have been closely studying whether there are any signs of those so-called second-round effects - where an initial price shock spreads to wages, services and broader consumer prices. So far, there are relatively few.

If prices rise then it takes a bigger chunk of people's income and so has a deeper impact on those whose finances are already stretched, so the latest data on food prices is good news for many people.

One set of economists who will consider whether there is evidence of second-round effects are the nine people who set interest rates, which heavily influences the cost of borrowing money - such as mortgages - as well as the returns people get on savings.
The Bank of England's Monetary Policy Committee meets again in December and, after that, in February.
Having just raised interest rates - for the first time in more than three years - to 4%, there's a widespread expectation among analysts that another hike is to come.
To be clear, we don't know if and when that will happen for sure.
The case for an increase would be if prices continue to accelerate. The Bank will want to slow that down.
The case against would be price rises remaining relatively confined to energy-related costs. Any easing of Middle East tensions could limit price rises without Bank of England intervention.
As far as wages are concerned, the latest official data suggests that rising prices are largely covered by rising pay.
That is an average - so is not true for everyone - but how long it remains the case may be key to how deep upcoming price rises cut into our personal finances.
How is the rising cost of living affecting your quality of life?

items.title: The off-and-on switch for U.S. aid leads to a cliffhanger for Zambia and Zimbabwe
paragraphs: This is a story that starts with a remarkable success story. However, the ending has become a cliff hanger — with potentially grave consequences.

The success is clearcut and remarkable: Both Zambia and Zimbabwe are beating back devastating HIV/AIDS epidemics. These neighboring countries in southern Africa are on the cusp of controlling the virus.

Between 2000 and 2025, new infections dropped by 76% in Zambia and 80% in Zimbabwe. In both countries, more than 95% of infected individuals are identified and 95% of them are on treatment, according to data from the Joint United Nations Programme on HIV/AIDS.
This progress is thanks, in large part, to billions of dollars in U.S. aid over the past two decades.

However, President Trump's new global health strategy is scrambling the landscape. After dismantling without warning the U.S. Agency for International Development in 2025, the administration is now hammering out government-to-government aid agreements as a new framework for how aid is provided.
That process leaves these two countries on very different paths and heading toward uncharted territory.

Just last month Zambian and U.S. officials signed an agreement — albeit for far less annual U.S. health aid than the country received in the past. Zimbabwe, in contrast, lost all U.S. health aid this fall after negotiations collapsed. To get an on-the-ground assessment of what has happened and what the future may hold, NPR interviewed a health worker in each country with experience in the HIV/AIDS world.

When the aid agreement was announced on ZNBC — Zambia National Broadcasting Corporation on October 8 — it was branded as "a new chapter" in which the U.S. aid dollars flow primarily through the government and aims to build up the national health system.

The negotiations behind the aid agreement were secretive and became contentious, explains Asia Russell, executive director of the HIV/AIDS advocacy organization Health GAP "There was a massive scandal because activists were able to show that the agreement was planning to condition access to [U.S. global health] funding on access to [Zambia's] copper and rare earth minerals," Russell told NPR. Her organization helped expose this situation. Ultimately, the discussion about mineral rights was decoupled from the health agreement.
"I felt a bit relieved," says the Zambian health worker. But, with the aid agreement finally signed, she says, "the work now begins."

The health worker asked NPR not to use her name because she helped make public that mineral rights were in play and fears government retribution. She worries the Zambian government is ill equipped to face down the obstacles of the HIV/AIDS epidemic.

For example, homosexuality is illegal in Zambia. "Because [people are] scared of being arrested when they go to the public health facility, they would rather just stay home and face the consequences of their illness," she says, adding that such a decision not only leaves them without treatment it also lets the virus spread further via unprotected sexual relations, drug activity and other routes.

Under the previous system, huge amounts of U.S. aid went through international and local non-governmental groups who have staff specially trained to reach those vulnerable populations. This new agreement sidelines those groups and instead aims to build up the government's health systems rather than a parallel system, according to the U.S. strategy.

The Zambian health worker is also concerned the country could trumpet success in addressing HIV/AIDS but that thorough outreach and treatment records won't be kept and the right infrastructure may not be in place. For instance, she says, the government may say: " 'We've employed 5,000 community health workers!' "
But, she asks: "What is the quality? What capacity do they have? Who will they be serving? Which district? "
This health worker says many in the medical field have not received answers about what the future health systems will look like.
"It feels like a big mess, honestly. It's scary," she says, "It feels like doing it right is not the priority, but people's lives are at risk."

The Zambian Ministry of Health did not respond to requests for comment. But in the press conference announcing the agreement, Health minister Roma Chilengi said the department plans to recruit up to 40,000 health care workers, including 15,000 front line workers such as doctors, nurses, midwives, scientists, pharmacists, as well as community health workers.
However apprehensive this health worker is, she says that what's happening in Zambia is still better than the situation in neighboring Zimbabwe.
In February, negotiations over the future of health aid between U.S. and Zimbabwean officials fell apart.

There was plenty of fingerpointing. Zimbabwean officials said the proposed agreement was lopsided. For example, Zimbabwe would have been obligated to provide data and biological samples of pathogens for research but would not have been guaranteed access to any treatments that result from that information. The U.S. Embassy in Zimbabwe said in a press release that the breakdown was regrettable. Whatever the reason, the result was clear. The country went from receiving well over $100 million in U.S. health aid each year to having none.

The health worker in Zimbabwe is baffled by this: "The U.S. put [in] 20 years of support — 20 years of support! — that's a huge investment which I think you cannot just throw away?" But he says that's what he's seeing.

This health worker also asked NPR not to use his name because he fears government retribution for speaking out. Without aid, he says, in his community, people's HIV medications are dwindling. "Within a period of six months or so, you will start to see a very huge impact," he predicts.

But he's concerned the world may never know the real impact. The U.S has had the best data collection and monitoring system for tracking and understanding the HIV epidemic and the response. Going forward the data coming out of Zimbabwe will be hard to verify or trust, he says. "We may not even know…if it's true or not."

The Ministry of Health and Child Care in Zimbabwe did not respond to NPR's requests for comment but this past summer, Zimbabwe's health minister, Dr. Douglas Mombeshora, pledged to expand the health workforce and infrastructure.

In a statement to NPR about the status of aid to the two countries, the U.S. State Department did not address the specific concerns of the health workers but said it's committed to working "with partner governments to define and advance shared global health priorities."
As for public reaction in the two countries? It's been muted, the health workers say.

Both say that in their communities people are mad but that a public outcry has been muted because they fear reprisal from their governments. Russell, of Health GAP, echoed this experience saying many people who she works with are afraid to speak publicly: "The problem is retaliation" because they lived under authoritarian regimes.
"People are trying to not lose more than they've already lost," the health worker in Zambia says. "So even the anger is there, the frustrations are there, but you do not see this very publicly."
Similarly, the health worker in Zimbabwe says, "you can be mad, you can be angry, you can be whatever. But if you talk, you know the consequences of what will happen to you."
Public outcry or not, the global health world will be carefully observing how the next stage unfolds for these two countries.

Jennifer Kates, senior vice president and director of global and public health policy at the research organization KFF, says her team is scrutinizing all the information it can get about the agreement and implementation of the aid agreement in Zambia. And Zimbabwe "is an important one to watch," she says. "It's made a lot of progress, heavily relying on the U.S." — and now the future is uncertain.
For stories about life in our changing world, subscribe to NPR's Global Health newsletter.
