In other words, if your phone, laptop or TV is on its figurative last legs, Black Friday is a sensible time to seek a replacement. But if you’re hoping to limit your ecological impact, it’s definitely worth considering refurbished options.

“As a consumer, you save directly 30-40% versus new, and you also have this feeling of doing the right thing,” says Peter Windischhofer, co-founder and CEO of Refurbed. “Because you buy a product that already exists, you don’t have to produce a new one.”
James Rigg, CEO of Trojan Electronics, agrees: “Very often, it’s the better choice: reliable performance, lower prices and a fraction of the environmental cost.

“Buy from someone reputable, look for transparency, and prioritise warranty and repairability over a too-good-to-be-true discount, and you can come out of Black Friday with great devices and a lighter footprint.”
Read the description Refurbished can mean different things. See what condition is promised, paying special attention to battery health.
Check the warranty and returns policy You want to know that you’re in good hands should anything go wrong.
Research the seller’s reputation Look at customer reviews and internet feedback. If on eBay, look for sellers in the company’s Refurbished programme.

Research your chosen device The older the device, the bigger the discount – but this is a false economy if you have to replace it sooner. With phones and laptops, especially, make sure they’re getting updates and will be able to cope with years of use.
Don’t cheap out A low price is only a bargain if it actually delivers. Prioritise customer service and a transparent refurbishment process over saving a few pounds.
It’s important at this point to define terms. People sometimes use the phrases “preowned”, “secondhand” and “refurbished” interchangeably, which may have given the latter a bad rap.

“They really are quite, quite different,” says Katy Medlock, Back Market’s UK general manager. “Secondhand could be peer to peer: you’re not buying it with a warranty, it hasn’t been through a quality check, you’re not buying it with all the mod cons.”

That separates refurbished marketplaces such as Back Market, MusicMagpie, Refurbed and others from sites where you buy directly from a member of the public, such as Facebook Marketplace or Craigslist. “Our mission is all about trying to make the process of buying refurbished electronics as good as buying something new,” Medlock says, highlighting the ability Back Market offers to split payments, its 30-day money-back promise, 12-month warranty and next-day delivery as ways of seeking parity with retailers shipping new stock.
By contrast, buying preowned or secondhand on the private market is a gamble, even if you sidestep the risk of being scammed.

“I’ve heard so many horror stories from peer-to-peer when it comes to electronics,” says Windischhofer. “I love using those platforms for low-value products; I use a lot of Vinted for clothing, and it’s great. But for electronics, my advice would be to go through a professional where you get a warranty and an invoice, and where, in case this product breaks after five days, they have great customer service to really help you out.”

Items sold privately may also have unseen defects or botched repairs using cheap, third-party parts. “There’s a very different performance between the cheapest phone screen that can be put on a phone and the correct screen,” says James Murdock, co-founder of Alchemy, a company that refurbishes old technology for resale. “Products get traded in at times with a $20 screen on an iPhone or Samsung [device] that really should have a wholesale cost of $150. They’re almost illegible.”

In other words, peer-to-peer buys are a gamble. If you insist on taking that risk, it’s best to buy in person and to take the opportunity to check both the screen and camera alongside signs of cosmetic wear and tear. If buying an iPhone or Android device, check the battery’s health in the phone’s settings and make sure it’s at least 80%.

If buying peer-to-peer on eBay, rather than through a certified refurbished seller, Eve Williams, general manager at eBay UK, encourages shoppers to look through the feedback and study photos and the product description. “Is this a reliable seller? Have they sold a lot of things in the past? What’s their feedback score? These are all things that are helpful to know that they’ve had good transactions with buyers in the past.”
What does that ecological improvement look like in real terms? Let’s take smartphones – the bestselling refurbished category.

According to research from Back Market, buying a refurbished model rather than a new one will save 178g of e-waste and 77,000 litres of water, while preventing 77kg of carbon emissions and 244kg of raw materials from being mined.

Trojan Electronics, meanwhile, estimates that a refurbished smartphone uses 91.3% fewer raw materials and 86.4% less water while putting 91.6% less carbon into the atmosphere compared with buying a new device.

Plenty of variables make the exact figures impossible to pin down. But while there’s still an impact from refurbished buys – especially if a new battery or screen is installed as part of the refurbishing process – there’s no denying that the harm is lessened.

“Every time you buy a smartphone, it’s about a 58kg CO2 offset if you don’t buy a new one [and instead] buy one that’s been refurbished,” says Murdock. “That includes the operation to actually refurbish it, and the existence of our business. It’s even more if you’re buying a laptop.”

It’s not just phones, either. “Now, people are turning to all different types of electronics, everything from refurbished air fryers through to hair accessories, TVs, coffee machines, ice-cream makers and games consoles,” says Williams. Unlike its traditional peer-to-peer sales business, eBay has a method by which it certifies refurbished-reselling businesses.

“There’s nothing to lose [from buying refurbished],” she says, pointing out that if you get the same 12-month guarantee as you would if buying new, you’re getting the same product at a lower price. “You’re getting something that otherwise would have ended up in landfill. We have this amazing seller called Preloved Tech. Matt and Andrea, who run it, started their business by working in schools, going in and seeing the times that schools were throwing out laptops and iPads because they didn’t know what to do with them. There are no rules around what some businesses should do to get rid of or recycle technology.
“They’re taking a lot of that tech and are able to give money and funding back to the schools, while also then being able to refurbish these items to sell on, and extend the life of them.”

“The best advice I can give for buying refurbished is to go via established retailers such as Back Market, Giffgaff and Vodafone, and if you’re buying through eBay then try to get a device that’s listed as ‘certified refurbished’,” says technology journalist Thomas Deehan. “You can also find different perks available depending on where you buy. For instance, Giffgaff provides a two-year warranty on ‘like new’ phones, while Back Market often gives you the option to have an entirely new battery fitted into your device of choice.”

In general, the more information a retailer provides about their refurbishing process, the better. “A proper refurbisher will tell you exactly what’s been checked, what’s been replaced, and how the product is graded,” says Rigg. “If you see vague descriptions like ‘used’ or ‘open box’ with no explanation, that’s your cue to walk away.”

Jon Miller, managing director at MusicMagpie, agrees. “As a rule of thumb, it’s far wiser to be careful when buying refurbished tech. Try to check the warranty length and what exactly that covers. Similarly, check the fine print and ensure ‘refurbished’ means the tech has been properly restored and tested, not just used.”

Is there any preowned technology you should avoid? “If you had asked me that question 10 years ago, I would have said: ‘Yes, because technology is so fast and, you know, the new iPhone is so much better than the last one,’” says Windischhofer. “But now? I don’t think there’s any product that I would buy new. I would always buy the generation before that.”

Alchemy, similarly, practices what it preaches. “We’ve got hundreds of MacBooks, iPhones and other products in the company. We have about 350 employees, and no one, including me, has ever had a new one,” says Murdock.

There are limits, however, to how old a device you should get, and it varies by category. A PlayStation 4 will continue to play all disc-based games made for it indefinitely, but something internet-reliant may end up losing functionality with time. Older OLED TVs, too, are considered more prone to burn-in than their modern counterparts.

Equally, buying a five-year-old refurbished phone will be cheaper than buying last year’s model, but if you end up needing to replace it sooner – for example, if it’s an Android that’s stopped receiving security updates – then it’s a false economy.

“It might be tempting to get an old MacBook Air from 2015, but it won’t receive regular updates like M-series MacBooks will,” says Deehan. “I think there’s a good balance to strike where you sometimes buy things new and other times go down the refurbished route. It’s about saving money where it makes sense so that you have the freedom to spend a bit more on a device that you’ll make the most of.”

Should you be worried about security exploits in refurbished technology? Eset’s global cybersecurity advisor, Jake Moore, isn’t especially concerned. “This is one of those threats that is more theoretical, I think,” he says. “I don’t think I’ve heard of [any cases] where they’ve pinpointed a refurbished device as the attack vector.”
Nonetheless, even as a theoretical threat, his advice mirrors what the other experts are saying: “It depends on who’s refurbed it; that would be my worry.”

As well as sticking to reputable names with a transparent refurbishment process, or the manufacturer itself, Moore suggests avoiding imports altogether, given the prevalence of malware originating from overseas. “If it’s going to take three weeks to arrive, that implies it is coming from another country, and I would consider something else,” he says.

He also has some guidance about assessing online retailers and making sure their warranties are worth the paper they’re written on. “If you find a review page that opens continually – as in you just keep scrolling, and you can keep seeing those reviews – point that site to ChatGPT and say, ‘Give me an analysis of the reviews that you can read’. It’ll read it much quicker than you, and it’ll give you a much better threat risk score.”
Finally, don’t forget the age-old adage of “buy cheap, buy twice”. Or, as Rigg puts it: “A gadget that fails quickly and can’t be repaired is only cheap for about five minutes.”

“Don’t be tempted by the cheapest offshore, interesting-looking eBay seller that looks like it’s been there for five minutes,” says Murdock. “Buy from a legitimate-looking local partner that’s offering a warranty, as they would with any other kind of new product, and is willing to stand behind that.”
For more, read our guide on what to look for in a refurbished phone
So you’ve bought a refurbished phone, laptop or tablet and now have one that’s surplus to requirements. What should you do?

Recycling is an option, but one that should be considered a last resort, according to Medlock, especially as there are limits on capacity. “With the amount of new electronics that are produced every year … there’s no way that … the amount sold in the UK could ever be recycled.”
Many sites will offer a trade-in when you buy the replacement, which will increase the likelihood of a device getting a second lease of life in the refurbished ecosystem.

Alternatively, you could take it to CeX or try your luck on the peer-to-peer market through Gumtree, Facebook Marketplace, Craigslist or eBay. If you go down this route, do be sure to wipe all your personal data first and give it a good spruce-up.

“This should go without saying, but prior to being listed or sold, your tech should be given a good clean to make it look the best that it can,” says Deehan. “Some retailers will dock the value of your device based on its cosmetic appearance, so make sure to do your part in keeping it all lint- and fingerprint-free.”

Donating is also an option. I recently donated an old laptop to Screen Share, which repurposes computers and phones for refugees to help tackle digital exclusion, and a quick search online will uncover many other worthwhile places to donate.

Whatever you choose, Medlock suggests putting some thought into the end of life for today’s Black Friday tech buys. “If people are upgrading, the pathway is obviously to buy refurbished … and encouraging people at that point to buy better.
“There is a cost saving there, so people can use that saving to buy devices that last longer, are built to last and built to be repaired.”
If you are in the market for a new phone, read our tried-and-tested roundup of the best budget phones

items.title: How new US chip restrictions on South East Asia will hit China
paragraphs: Xi and Trump when they met in Beijing in May
As US President Donald Trump heads to China, his administration has renewed efforts to curb Beijing's access to advanced semiconductors.
On Monday, Washington announced new interim rules that will increase scrutiny of data centre operators in Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand, Indonesia and Brazil.
The move not only restricts the export of advanced chips, but also access to their computing power, which Chinese firms currently rent abroad to train artificial intelligence (AI) models.
South East Asian countries in particular have invested heavily in data centres to power their AI ambitions - and Chinese firms seeking computing power overseas have been a key market.

But now these firms will need a US government licence to buy advanced chips from Nvidia or other American chipmakers. This allows Washington to monitor if those chips are being used to serve Chinese companies, or being smuggled to China.

This poses a fresh challenge for Beijing, which has become deeply dependent on compute from abroad in the wake of US export restrictions. At least 30% of China's advanced AI computing power is projected to come from renting overseas or smuggling in 2027, according to research by the Institute for Progress, external, a US-based think-tank.
China's foreign ministry called the new rules "economic coercion" and said Beijing "will take necessary measures to firmly safeguard its own legitimate rights and interests".

This is also a problem for South East Asian economies where large numbers of data centres have sprung up recently. Some of the firms behind them are accused of helping China evade US export controls on advanced chips.

One of those is Singaporean data centre firm Megaspeed, whose former director Alice Huang is suspected of being a Chinese spy. Calls for tighter export controls have grown after Nvidia's Jensen Huang admited to an affair with her and resigned as CEO.

Megaspeed, the biggest buyer of Nvidia's chips in South East Asia, is accused of illegally smuggling chips to Chinese companies after purchasing them for use in data centres in Malaysia, Indonesia and Thailand.

The company has denied these allegations, defended its business as "legitimate and lawful", and said it has "retained external legal counsel to conduct a thorough internal investigation". It also said Alice Huang stepped down from her role as director in late 2023 and left the firm last year.

The US Commerce Department's Bureau of Industry and Security, however, has said Brazil and the four South East Asian nations "present a higher-than-normal risk of diversion" of the chips that Washington wants to keep out of China's hands.

The new measures are aimed at ensuring sensitive US technology "cannot be circumvented through remote computing arrangements involving data centers in third countries," the bureau added. Licences will be issued on a "case-by-case basis", it said.
Batam in Indonesia is emerging as a major regional data centre hub

Countries like Malaysia and Thailand whose data centre roll out has been heavily driven by Chinese buyers could be hit hardest, says international trade expert Naoise McDonagh from Australia's Edith Cowan University.

But the new rules are unlikely to derail the data centre boom as a whole, says Reema Bhattacharya from advisory firm Verisk Maplecroft, adding that investment backed by major tech firms and clearly identifiable customers should "remain relatively resilient".

Singapore was an early adopter of data centres but when it began limiting new construction, investment flowed to neighbours Malaysia and Thailand. Johor in Malaysia and Batam in Indonesia have also approved billions of dollars worth of data centres to catch the spillover demand.
These countries have been offering incentives such as cheaper land to attract foreign investment, including from Chinese tech giants Alibaba and Tencent.
But now, the region could find it harder to get hold of advanced chips.
The BBC has contacted Singapore, Brazil, Indonesia, Malaysia and Thailand for comment.

Singapore said it is "engaging relevant US authorities" to understand the new rules better, and is "exploring how to facilitate trusted access" for local firms. Malaysia previously said it welcomes data centre investment but "will not allow itself to be used to get around export controls".
The new rules also come just ahead of Trump's meeting with Chinese leader Xi Jinping in Shenzhen this week.
Beijing has made self-sufficiency in tech a national priority and needs the best chips to build powerful AI models.

Chinese firms DeepSeek and MoonShot have come close to US rivals like Anthropic and OpenAI. So much so that The Institute for Progress estimates top US AI models lead the best Chinese platforms by only about six and half months.
"This is despite US AI companies having significantly better compute access and financing," it said.
Still, China needs advanced US chips to ensure its best AI models are competitive, experts tell the BBC.
The new restrictions on South East Asia and Brazil have taken away "one of the more practical routes Chinese AI developers had to accessing frontier computing power," Bhattacharya said.
But tighter restrictions could also push Chinese firms towards domestic semiconductors and further drive advancement at home.

That has been a longstanding dilemma for Washington, McDonagh said: whether to keep selling chips to China to retain its reliance on the US, or restrict access and risk further spurring Chinese innovation.

items.title: Do school cellphone bans work? New study says yes – but it's complicated
paragraphs: Ameriana Walker, a student in the Wyoming Area School District in northeast Pennsylvania, demonstrates how a Yondr pouch works in September 2025. Jason Ardan/Citizens’ Voice via Getty Images hide caption
Jason Ardan/Citizens’ Voice via Getty Images
Catch up on what you missed with our Education newsletter, sent weekly.

The rise of smartphones in the U.S. coincided with a dramatic slide in K-12 students' reading and math achievement. Now, new research suggests putting students' phones in locked pouches during the school day may help restore some of those historic losses.

"Around 2013, U.S. students started losing 2-3 weeks of learning each year," says Harvard University's Tom Kane, one of the new study's co-authors. "It's been a slow leak that, over time, has put U.S. 8th graders almost a year behind. Strict cellphone bans seem to plug about half of that leak."
Or the equivalent of 1-2 weeks of learning a year, according to the study released Tuesday. That's a small but, according to Kane, statistically significant improvement.
"That could add up over time, just as the initial declines did," adds Dartmouth College's Douglas Staiger, another co-author.

The study's authors say it is the first nationwide analysis of student-level test scores in math and reading both before and after schools enforced locked-pouch cellphone bans. It was a joint effort between Harvard's Center for Education Policy Research, Dartmouth and NWEA, a K-12 testing and research organization.

Kane, Staiger and their teams analyzed a nationwide sample of more than 3 million elementary-, middle- and high-school students over the past five school years, comparing the test scores in schools that adopted phone pouches to the scores at similar schools that did not.

Not only did strict cellphone bans appear to trigger small learning gains, the researchers say, those gains didn't seem to fade out after the first year of implementation. Instead, Kane says, the gains appeared to continue, year after year – at least up to three years after adoption.
Tuesday's headline finding, that locking phones during the school day led to small but statistically significant improvements in math and reading scores, comes with an important caveat:
A separate study, from April, found that these pouches had "close to zero" impact on student test scores – and if there was a benefit, it was not statistically significant.
"Overall, we didn't find evidence of meaningful achievement gains," says Brian Jacob, a co-author of that April study and a professor of education policy at the University of Michigan.
What should we make of these seemingly contradictory results?
Both are large-scale studies by well-respected teams of researchers. The April study has been peer-reviewed; the more recent study has not.

Both studies similarly focused on schools' adoption of lockable pouches made by the for-profit company Yondr. According to Tuesday's paper, more than 3,300 schools nationwide began using the pouches between the '19-'20 and '25-'26 school years. Typically, schools that use the pouches require that students put their phones in them at the beginning of the day and don't get them back until the end of the school day, when the pouches are unlocked by a school administrator with a special magnetic device.

But the two studies also differ in key ways. The April study pooled school-level mean test scores at several thousand Yondr-adopting schools, while Tuesday's study used student-level scores at the 844 schools that use both Yondr pouches and tests administered by NWEA.
Simply put, the study released Tuesday had more fine-grain, student-level data, but the study released in April was able to examine a much larger sample of schools.

But the two studies' findings also aren't as different as they may seem. Jacob and his co-authors did find statistically significant gains with Yondr pouches in high school math. It's just that those gains were offset by ban-related learning losses in middle school.

Overall, Jacob says, the new study "is encouraging. And if [the benefit] really persists and accumulates over time, it really could be a meaningful benefit. I think we'll just have to wait and see if that happens."

Another co-author of that April study, Tom Dee, a professor at Stanford University's Graduate School of Education, says of Tuesday's findings, "I hope they are right that these very small test score gains will aggregate and add up over time. However, I'm not comfortable making that extrapolation from estimates that are small, sensitive and based on just a few years of phone bans."
Taken together, Dee says, he considers the results from these early studies into cellphone bans "largely disappointing," and insists "we need continued study on this topic."

Kane sees the results differently. Even if the benefit is small, he argues, relative to the cost – roughly $25 per student – these pouches still make financial sense for schools. "That's still a lot less than having to pay teachers for an extra week or two of instruction."
For nearly a quarter-century, from 1990 to 2013, math achievement among fourth- and eighth-graders rose steadily. Reading scores also improved.

Then around 2013, student test scores began a sustained tumble that continued through the COVID-19 pandemic and has only recently begun to slow. For years, politicians and pundits blamed pandemic-era school closures for the losses, but the data tells a different story.

"Particularly in reading, test scores were going down for four to six years before the pandemic," Stanford University researcher Sean Reardon told NPR earlier this year. "In fact, you wouldn't really know there was a pandemic effect if you just looked at the last 10 or 12 years of test scores. There's been just a steady kind of decline regardless of the pandemic."
Which raises the question: What happened around 2013?
Possible explanations abound. The federal government began stepping back from holding schools accountable for low test scores. Many schools also saw funding cuts in the wake of the Great Recession.
This new study is the latest to make the case that the mass adoption of cell phones by children and teens also helped fuel those test score declines.

The researchers note that, in 2011, fewer than a quarter of teen students had access to smartphones. By 2018, 95% did. And similar rates in other industrialized countries coincided with similar student achievement declines.
Now, Kane says, he wants to study students' smartphone and social media use outside of school.

items.title: More than £160m needed to clean up one of Europe's largest illegal dumps
paragraphs: The contaminated Mobuoy dump is thought to cover more than 100 acres of land
ByMike McBride and Davy WilsonBBC News NI
More than £160m is needed to clean up and maintain one of Europe's largest illegal landfill sites, government officials have said.
The contaminated Mobuoy dump at Campsie in County Londonderry, discovered and shut down in 2013, was used to bury thousands of tonnes of rubbish at a site spanning more than 100 acres.
Last year, two businessmen were jailed for their part in the operation.
Northern Ireland's Environment Minister Andrew Muir said his department had now received an updated cost estimate of £161m for the clean-up over a 30-year period.
Muir described what happened at Mobuoy as "an absolute scandal" and said "the community rightly expects and deserves remediation of the site".
He is now seeking a meeting with the Finance Minister John O'Dowd to discuss how the work will be paid for - with funding from Westminster a possibility.
Once the finances are agreed, they will work towards appointing a contractor.
Andrew Muir says it could take a generation to clean up the Mobuoy dump in County Londonderry
Investigations indicate an estimated 1.6m tonnes of waste was present at the site and 627,000 tonnes of that was believed to have been dumped illegally.
The Mobuoy site is beside the River Faughan, which supplies a significant proportion of Derry's drinking water but officials have not found any contamination to it.
The area of polluted ground stretches to about 100 acres, or the equivalent of about 65-70 football pitches.
"This is a complicated project, as you'll understand, given the complexity of the site," Muir told BBC Radio Foyle's North West Today programme on Tuesday, .
The minister said he took environmental protection very seriously and would continue to push for the establishment of an independent environmental protection agency.
"One of the massive lessons that needs to be learned from the Mobuoy site is the need for stronger environmental protections, so people have confidence that our environment is being looked after."
The site, located on the outskirts of the city, is a former recycling plant
Muir said the next assembly election was fast approaching in May, so he understood there might be some concerns about the potential costs involved.
"I want to finish this mandate with a degree of certainty for the local community, so we have a road map here for remediation," he said.
"I am pushing ahead with real enthusiasm with this."
Muir said the drinking water was tested regularly to ensure it was safe and that he would continue to work with all agencies to provide the local community with greater assurances about the site.
Muir said the Mobuoy site remained in private ownership, but they were "actively" considering ways of transferring it.
One option is vesting, which allows government departments to obtain compulsory and legal ownership of land through a court order.

items.title: Dazzling Leonid meteor shower to peak on Tuesday night
paragraphs: Experts advise finding a safe, dark location away from sources of light pollution such as street lights.
The meteors will be visible with the naked eye, with no binoculars or telescope required.
However, giving your eyes some time to adapt to the dark, perhaps 20 or 30 minutes, will give you the best chance of spotting them.
A wide open space is the best place to be, giving a full view of the night sky.

Meteors could be visible anywhere but the Leonids' radiant, the point from which they seem to appear, will, as the name suggests, be around the head of the constellation Leo, meaning this is the best part of the sky to focus your gaze. Leo does not rise until around midnight, so the best time to look is after midnight and in the hours before dawn.
As with all celestial spectacles, clear skies will be a must.

items.title: Actors in UK to get more rights over their ‘digital replicas’ in deal on AI protections
paragraphs: Actors in the UK are to be given more rights over their “digital replicas” as part of a new agreement on AI protections with TV and film producers, secured after a growing on-set backlash.

Under a wide-ranging new deal secured by Equity, the actors’ union, performers will have the rights to be paid when their digital replicas are used and to consent to whether their digital replica is used or not.
Approval must be secured from an actor if a digital double or digital alteration is used to make “substantive changes” to scenes involving agreed levels of nudity or simulated sexual activity.
The agreement also makes clear that producers may not use a digital replica during a strike “in any circumstance where consent is required for such use”.
Contracts will now make clear that producers only obtain permission for a specific project, rather than obtaining “blanket consent” to an actor’s digital replica.

The deal, signed after years of talks with the production body Producers Alliance for Cinema and Television (Pact), marks an attempt to create some ground rules for the use of an actor’s image, with AI developing rapidly.

The three-year deal will be put to a vote among 8,000 Equity members, with the union’s leadership recommending they approve it. It also includes a 24% increase in pay rates for major films and a 9% increase for TV projects.
It comes after Equity members voted 99% in favour of taking industrial action and refusing to be scanned on set without further AI protections, in an indicative ballot last December.
However, Equity said there were areas that a new agreement simply could not cover, such as digital scanning traditionally undertaken in production for digital effects added later.

There have been mounting concerns on set about the use of AI, which has made many actors more wary of undergoing body scans. Many fear the data could be used to train AI models on their likenesses or poses, paving the way for the technology to take away work.
Last year, the actor Olivia Williams told the Guardian that actors should have as much control over the data harvested from scans of their body as they do over nudity scenes.

The star of Dune: Prophecy and The Crown said she and other actors were regularly pressed to have their bodies scanned by banks of cameras while on set, with few guarantees about how the data would be used or where it would end up.
Equity said that “despite our efforts”, the new agreement did not establish explicit contract protections regarding the use of actors’ performances for training AI systems.
In a note to its members, Equity explained that digital replicas could be made using the same photography captured for the production itself, without the need to scan artists.

However, producers must limit access to digital replicas to people with a legitimate business need and “use commercially reasonable efforts” to protect digital replicas from unauthorised access, use or copying.

The new deal also includes a commitment to safe casting and audition spaces, as well as training and reporting on sexual harassment. Producers also have a new obligation to provide artists of all ethnicities and cultures with adequate hair and makeup provision.
Paul W Fleming, Equity’s general secretary, said: “We set about to radically improve and modernise the terms and conditions for performers across UK TV and film. The result is groundbreaking.
“We’ve achieved the best AI provisions in the business – protecting performers and ensuring that human performance is valued and prioritised across the industry.”

items.title: Black timber elements traverse concrete fragrance store in Tokyo
paragraphs: Mexican design firms Esrawe Studio and Cadena Concepts divided the interior of this concrete building in Tokyo, designed for perfume brand Xinú, with angular black-timber displays.

Esrawe Studio and Cadena Concepts designed the timber elements as sculptural interventions that also organise the interior of the three-storey shop, which is located in the city’s Aoyama neighbourhood.
The black-laminated wooden planks span the interior walls at jaunty angles, as if puncturing the building, which was originally designed by Japanese studio Satoshi Hirano.
“We approached the project as an intervention within an existing building, rather than simply designing an interior,” said Esrawe Studio founder Héctor Esrawe, who also co-founded Xinú.

“By introducing a continuous architectural structure that traverses its different levels, appearing and disappearing throughout the volume, we intended to generate a new perception of the original architecture,” he told Dezeen.
“Both structures coexist, establishing a dialogue between what was already there and what has been introduced, creating an unexpected spatial experience.”
Long, overlapping shelves with mirrored accents display products on the ground floor, which is dedicated to body perfume.
Xinú’s room scents are located on the first floor, where hand-painted brass panels on the walls and ceilings add a touch of warmth to the concrete and black-timber surfaces.
Aiming to reveal the processes behind the perfume products, the top floor displays botanical specimens, raw materials, found objects and collages in drawers.

Esrawe Studio also designed cabinet drawers to reference the storage and organisation typically found in natural history museums, intending to give visitors a feeling of discovery when interacting with the furniture.
“For Xinú, architecture has never been conceived simply as a backdrop for products, but as an essential part of how they are experienced,” said Esrawe.
“Our intention is to create spaces that encourage curiosity, discovery and a more intimate relationship with objects, materials and scent,” he continued.
“In Tokyo, the inserted architectural structures move beyond conventional retail display, becoming sculptural elements that enhance the presence of the objects.”

Xinú Tokyo is the latest branch Esrawe Studio and Cadena Concepts have designed for the perfume brand. Other shops include a radial wooden pavilion in Mexico City and a showroom in Oaxaca informed by basalt rock formations.

items.title: Disney’s radical new animation technique will make Hexed the end of an era
paragraphs: It's clear that some people are getting tired of the contemporary Disney style. That can be seen in the allegations of Disney same-face syndrome, the disappointment that Hexed doesn't look like its concept art and the perennial controversy over the hybrid live-action remakes, with Moana being the latest flop.

The fatigue was evident at D23 this year. The announcements that generated the most excitement were a return of 2D animation, if only in combination with live action for the nostalgia-heavy TV series in Oswald, and the news that Disney's Clay will look like claymation even if uses CG.

A lot of fans will be happy then to learn that Clay won't be a one off but rather the start of a whole new Disney era after Hexed. The studio's developed a new animation pipeline that will allow it to apply different art styles to 3D models, potentially replacing the realism popularised by Pixar with a unique look for each new movie – and it's all starting with Lilo & Scratch.

Set to show in cinemas alongside Hexed, Lilo & Scratch is the first theatrical short from Walt Disney Animation Studios in five years. Written and directed by Fawn Veerasunthorn and Malcon Pierce, it will see the much-loved blue alien Stitch having to contend with the introduction of a mischievous cat called Scratch. Maia Kealoha voices Lilo, reprising her role from the 2025 live-action film Lilo & Stitch, and Chris Sanders with voice Stitch again.

Like all of the studios' feature animations in the last 15 years, the short was made using computer-generated animation with 3D models, but these are blended with hand-drawn elements to create a hybrid style that looks surprisingly faithful to Lilo & Stitch from 2002.

Disney's VFX supervisor Jeremy Sikorski has said that the new pipeline was developed through experimentation on the previous shorts Paperman and Once Upon a Studio. Pixar is also exploring the same direction, as we saw in the Gatto trailer: environments, characters and sets are modeled and animated in 3D to retain spatial depth, lighting and camera movement, but certain characters and other details are hand drawn.

Disney says about 25% of the backgrounds in Lilo & Scratch are watercolour paintings reused from the original Lilo & Stitch, while more than a dozen new background paintings were created by artists including Tia Kratter and Larry Wu. Some of these were digitally painted in Photoshop to look like watercolour, while others were hand-painted on paper.
Combined with digital backgrounds and set extension, this blend of old and new hand-painted watercolours helped the filmmakers remain faithful to the look of the 2002 feature, Disney says.

In an interview at the Governors Awards in LA on Sunday (see the post by Deadline below), Disney Animation Chief Creative Officer Jared Bush confirmed that all original Disney movies from Clay onwards will use this approach. That doesn't mean that they'll all look like Renaissance-era 2D animation, but that each with have its own "wildly different" look.
Zootopia 3 and Frozen 3 will still look like we would expect, but Hexed may be "the last original in the Disney art style as people know it," he says.

Jared Bush shares updates on ‘Zootopia 3,’ ‘Frozen 3’ and ‘Hexed’ and reveals the new, upcoming animated films at Disney will have “wildly different art styles”: “We’re really going to be pushing into some new areas” | #GovernorsAwards https://t.co/nw16Ci8WoDNovember 16, 2026

The new approach looks like a win for Disney. Despite some success with the live-action The Jungle Book and last year's Lilo & Stitch, the poor reception of Moana, Snow White and Mulan suggests waning interest in the remake formula is waning. Meanwhile, the 3D animation style that once looked so modern is starting to feel dated and generic.

Nostalgic audiences miss 2D animation, while younger audiences want something fresh. It sounds like Disney's new animation pipeline could make both things possible without sacrificing the efficiency that comes with 3D-based CG animation, which makes it much quicker and easier to swap and adjust environments, characters and props compared to traditional hand-drawn 2D, where even a relatively small change might mean having to redraw from scratch.The Disney principles of animation will remain in tact, but in a vast realm new possibilities.
I do wonder though. In ten years time, will people start to feel nostalgic about the much-maligned 3D Disney style?
Hexed will be released on 25 November. Lilo & Scratch will screen before it.

items.title: Want to know the secret to Prince George's impressive art?
paragraphs: Prince George made the headlines recently by displaying his artistic flair. The second in line to the throne impressed readers of Country Life magazine last week, when his colour pencil drawing of a kingfisher appeared in a special issue guest edited by his father, the Prince of Wales.

Shortly afterwards, the drawing went viral and amazed audiences on social media as well. It’s not hard to see why. The bird, which is playfully perched on a little branch and looking away from the viewer, demonstrates a level of craft you might not expect to come from the hands of a 12-year-old.

If you wish you could draw this well, and you’ve exhausted all of our how to draw tutorials, you might be in luck. Because shrewd online detectives may have figured out the secret behind the Prince’s handiwork.

Upon being shared on the likes of X and Instagram, people couldn’t believe how good the drawing was. Some commenters pointed out that he may have inherited his artistic talent from his family. After all, Prince George’s grandfather, King Charles, is an avid watercolour painter, and his parents both studied art at A-level. Catherine even studied history of art while at university.

The internet being what it is though, it wasn’t long until jealous users credited the drawing’s success to the amount of time and extra tuition the Prince surely enjoyed. However it seems he may have simply followed an easily accessible online course.

In amongst the comments, it soon became apparent that Prince George’s drawing bears more than a passing resemblance to the kingfisher featured in Matt Fussell’s course titled 3 Little Birds. And while no official confirmation has been made at the time of writing, everything from the pose to the positioning on the branch appears to be very similar.

This isn’t to take away from the Prince’s drawing. His picture still showcases a great level of skill and a keen understanding of the materials. In this case, if he followed the tutorial to the letter, Prince George used wax-based Prismacolor Premier Pencils on smooth Bristol paper. Both of which can be easily picked up from most local art supply shops.

If anything, it should be an encouragement to aspiring artists. With the help of one course, which can be enjoyed as either videos or step-by-step written instructions, you too can start layering your colours and creating your own beautiful bird illustrations (see our how to draw a bird tutorial, for example).

According to the course outline on his website, Matt’s instructions make the drawing process easy by breaking everything down into simple lessons. These cover everything from the proportions to colour transitions, as well as texture and highlights. Follow the course through to the end, and you’ll also learn how to draw a blue jay with oil-based polychroma pencils by Faber Castell, and a hummingbird with wax-based luminance coloured-pencils from Caran D’Ache.

On top of helping you draw like Prince George, these are also useful skills that can be carried over into future studies. And if you’re not happy with your results, Matt even offers a 30 day money back guarantee on his $57 course.

Dom Carter is a freelance writer who specialises in art and design. Formerly a staff writer for Creative Bloq, his work has also appeared on Creative Boom and in the pages of ImagineFX, Computer Arts, 3D World, and .net. He has been a D&AD New Blood judge, and has a particular interest in picture books.

items.title: Millionaire factory: Anthropic IPO set to fuel AI gold rush in London’s high-end property market
paragraphs: Sporting hoodies and white trainers rather than the gilets of London’s banker and lawyer class, tech bros can struggle to be taken seriously by the capital’s luxury property agents. “We worked with a young tech entrepreneur with a substantial budget, who agents assumed was looking to rent a one-bedroom flat,” says Jo Eccles, a buying agent who sources off-market properties for ultra-wealthy clients.

But this week’s float by Anthropic, the AI developer behind the chatbot Claude, promises to bring even more credibility for the growing cohort of tech millionaires, which could breathe life into London’s ailing high-end property market. Its IPO on Thursday, expected to value the company at $1.4tn (£1.1tn), is likely to turn more than 4,000 of its staff into millionaires as their stock options vest. SaaStr, a California research firm, has estimated that the minimum value generated for staff at the AI lab will be $20m each.

Anthropic’s millionaire factory promises to expand the group of tech buyers, who range from senior staff at major AI labs to founders who have sold their startups, with budgets that range from £2m to £40m, Eccles says.

Tech’s wave of wealth has already reshaped Silicon Valley – notably in San Francisco – driving up demand for already scarce housing as young entrepreneurs and engineers became millionaires overnight. Now, that money is washing up on British shores too.

Anthropic, which employs about 5,000 people worldwide, has more than 200 employees in the UK. The company, founded in San Francisco in 2021, has announced plans to expand its presence in London, with a new office that is capable of accommodating up to 800 people.

The company’s UK filings show that it spent £24.1m employing an average of 43 staff in 2024 alone – a mean average of £560,000 per person. Job listings this year have advertised base salaries of up to £630,000 before stock options for research engineers.

Salaries across Britain’s AI sector are flying: OpenAI’s staff in London each received £2.3m on average last year – about 58 times the median UK full-time employee earnings. That puts them on par with partners at top law firms such as Linklaters and Clifford Chance, and ahead of some bankers in the City.

UK-based investors in these companies are also watching the value of their stakes grow at breakneck speed. Alex Gerko, the billionaire founder of the trading firm XTX and an early investor in Anthropic via the venture arms of the business, is expected to make hundreds of millions of pounds in paper gains when the company joins the stock market this week.

The flush of technology cash is already evident in London’s commercial property market. First, a wave of startups led to Shoreditch being nicknamed Silicon Roundabout, before tech firms began expanding across the capital. Now, US AI firms are expanding at pace in the UK, clustering tightly inside the King’s Cross “knowledge quarter” where Anthropic, OpenAI and Meta all work a stone’s throw from each other.

They have followed in the footsteps of Demis Hassabis, a totemic figure in AI’s breakthrough era who co-founded DeepMind in 2010 and sold it to Google for £400m four years later. He was one of the first to set up in the north London enclave. Isomorphic Labs, his AI drug discovery startup that is also now owned by the Google parent Alphabet, is in the area.

The AI gold rush is already being felt at the highest end of London’s housing market. Although tech bosses may be younger than the sector’s traditional client base, agents report that interest – while spread across London – includes plenty of familiar wealthy haunts.

In February, the Times reported that Igor Babuschkin, the billionaire co-founder of Elon Musk’s AI venture xAI, had bought a £57m penthouse overlooking Hyde Park, in one of the biggest deals in the city this year.

Meanwhile, Providence House, the Reform UK treasurer Nick Candy’s former mansion on the grounds of the Royal Hospital Chelsea in London, was reportedly sold for £270m to the founder of the quantitative investment firm Quadrature Capital, Suneil Setiya. Aidan Devane, the chief executive of the firm, attributed its success partly to its proximity to AI labs in the city, telling the Financial Times: “We are probably in the golden age of London quant.”

Tech wealth, increasingly generated by gains in the AI sector, “has become a force at the very top of the prime central London market”, according to the super-prime estate agent Beauchamp Estates, which has a portfolio including a £42m sub-penthouse overlooking Hyde Park.

Jeremy Gee, a managing director at Beauchamp, says inquiries from tech and AI buyers have risen noticeably over the past year. “Some are international buyers, principally from the US, but a growing number are based here in London,” he says, adding that many have amassed their fortunes with remarkable speed.

“They tend to be younger, they move quickly and they are very clear about what they want. Location and quality matter most and they will pay a premium for something genuinely special,” he says. “London offers culture, history, world-class schools and a growing AI community of its own.”

Even the traditional bastions of old British money are adapting. According to Shona Baijal, the managing director of wealth at Coutts, the private bank long associated with the British aristocracy, the tech and AI sectors are increasingly a source of new clients. One of the key challenges, she says, is helping young entrepreneurs who are coming into vast amounts of wealth very quickly.

“A lot of people feel overwhelmed,” she says. “We have to discuss the emotional aspects of what it means to come into wealth. We might say: you’ve come into the money, but do not rush to do anything.”
Coutts found last month that eight out of 10 properties in London’s most exclusive neighbourhoods – such as Mayfair, Belgravia and Knightsbridge – now sell below asking price.
But sellers and property agents hoping the AI industry may ride to London’s rescue face a glaring problem: much of these new AI fortunes remains on paper.
At founder level, many are “paper rich, cash poor”, Baijal says – meaning until they sell their businesses or their shares vest, their wealth is largely theoretical.

At the same time, Britain’s wider economy is growing more reliant on the sector’s momentum. Last week, official figures showed that the UK economy grew by 0.7% in the third quarter, its fastest expansion in two and a half years, almost entirely due to strong and widespread growth in services, led by the IT sector. Separate analysis by Bloomberg found that roughly a quarter of UK economic growth this year had been powered by AI.

That dependence makes the prospect of an AI bubble bursting all the more dangerous. There have been months of warnings over the valuations of AI companies, and there has been a groundswell of public opposition to datacentre construction and worries around AI safety.

Investors were reminded again of the fragility of the AI trade last week after a scandal involving extramarital affairs and an alleged Chinese spy sent shares in one of the most valuable AI companies in the US, the chip designer Nvidia, tumbling.

Other market indicators have been flashing warning lights. This year one popular measure used by investors to assess whether a market is overvalued – the CAPE, or cyclically adjusted price-to-earnings, ratio – rose to its highest level since 2000, showing that the US stock market was unusually highly valued compared with its profits. That was before the Anthropic’s blockbuster debut.

For now, the AI boom’s physical footprint is unmistakable. In San Francisco, the average one-bedroom property now rents for $4,400 a month, up more than 25% from last year and nearly three times the US average. Landlords have been trying to capitalise on the boom, particularly in areas closest to the offices of the biggest AI companies including OpenAI and Anthropic.

Meanwhile in London, the transformation of King’s Cross from a railway goods yard once notorious for criminal activity into an international hub for tech and AI is well under way. Whether this new class of wealth is permanent, or a temporary flash in a historic tech bubble, is yet to be seen.

items.title: The Creality Falcon T1C engraver could be a game changer for personalisation businesses
paragraphs: There's already a lot of competition among the best laser cutters and engravers for crafters, and Creality makes the best budget pick in our guide with its Falcon A1. Today, it's thrown a new contender into the mix, and it looks like it could be a game changer for small personalisation businesses and crafters who want to work remotely.

The next-gen Creality Falcon T1C promises high-performance customisation capabilities, but it's also impressively compact, making it versatile and convenient for things like making custom gifts or adding names, photos, custom text or unique designs to everyday products on location at craft markets and other events (also see our guide to the best 3D printers).

The Falcon T1C is built has a dual-laser configuration that makes it compatible with a wide range of materials. A 15W blue diode laser can process wood, bamboo, leather and dark acrylic, while a 5.5W infrared laser is designed for precision metal marking, dark acrylics and a range of synthetic materials.

Creality says the machine's galvanometer setup (the system that uses motorised mirrors to steer a laser beam) is capable of very fast scan speeds of up to 6,500 mm/s in specified image engraving modes. Using the company's PixelFlow control technology, the system coordinates galvo movement and laser power to preserve fine grayscale details while boosting image-processing efficiency by up to 8x compared to conventional processing under laboratory conditions.

Ultra-fine laser spot sizes (as small as 0.06 x 0.05 mm for the blue diode and 0.03 x 0.03 mm for the infrared laser) promise accurate reproduction for delicate lines, including intricate textures and tiny text, making it possible to personalise very small items.

Aside from the focus on precision, In think what really makes the Falcon T1C a potential game changer is its compact footprint. This makes it an appealing choice for small home studios and workshops but also for anyone who wants to take their customisation business on the move to pop-up event markets. This compactness doesn't necessarily mean sacrificing on potential project size either. The standard 120 x 120 mm working area can be expanded to 120 x 480mm with an optional extension bed for larger items.

One-touch autofocus and camera-assisted positioning should be helpful for speeding up workflows, while the Falcon Design Space software's preset layers eliminate the need to physically swap laser modules or re-align positions, again increasing efficiency for working remotely. It also provides AI Outline Tracing, AI Background Removal, Smart Fill, and AI Filters—to quickly transform design concepts into production-ready physical goods.

An expanded engraving cloud includes MakerMuse and CraftSeek, which provide users with access to an extensive digital design library, cloud storage and collaborative tools to streamline design preparation and manage projects.

But what about price? Pre-orders for the Creality Falcon T1C opened today ahead of a commercial release in mid-December 2026. In the US, the Standalone Edition has an MSRP of $1,699, but if you reserve today with a $50 deposit, you can save $500 reducing the pre-order price to $1,199.
A Combo Edition including the AP1S Air Purifier has an MSRP of $1,859. Preorder with a $60 reservation to receive $600 in savings, bringing the price down to $1,259.
To pre-order, visit the Creality US store.

items.title: Microsoft stops on Friday the 13th – level 1
paragraphs: A big computer problem at Microsoft stops many services around the world on Friday. People cannot use Outlook email, Teams, or other work apps for hours.
Microsoft says that its main computers have too much work. They stop working. But it is not an attack by hackers. The company starts slowly fixing the problem.

Technology experts say that companies should not use only one big tech company for everything. If one system breaks, people cannot do their jobs. Businesses need good backup plans so they can keep working when a problem comes.
Difficult words: main (the biggest or most important thing), fix (to repair), backup (an extra copy of data or a plan for a situation when something stops working).

items.title: Isern Serra designs bold colour-blocked interiors for Barcelona pilates studio
paragraphs: Spanish design practice Isern Serra combined organic architectural forms with a vibrant colour palette for Circl, a fitness studio and matcha cafe located in Barcelona’s historic Eixample district.

Set just below street level, the 180-square-metre space was designed to offer an escape from the busy city centre and contains an entrance cafe, reception area, changing rooms, bathrooms and a pilates studio.
“The project began with the idea of bringing together two worlds: pilates and matcha,” Isern Serra told Dezeen.
“Although different in nature, both share a common philosophy centred on wellbeing, balance and the connection between body and mind,” he continued.
“Architecture plays an essential role in this experience, accompanying visitors on a gradual transition from the energy of the city towards a more intimate and introspective environment.”

His studio introduced a series of colour-blocked spaces to guide customers through different phases of the interior, with colours that were specifically chosen to correspond to the function and tone of each area.

“This vision of wellbeing takes shape through a carefully choreographed sequence of spaces, where each change in level, colour and atmosphere guides users away from the bustle of the city and towards an increasingly introspective environment,” said Serra.

Serra combined cream banquette seating with dark wooden tables and alabaster sconces to create a calm, meditative environment for the cafe part of the space. A sculptural, mirrored service counter was also incorporated to reflect natural light around the space.
To signal the transition into the pilates studio, the designers introduced a deep-green reception hallway with tiered seating blocks and a spherical light installation.
The bright green circulation area is connected by an open archway and features curved architectural volumes that house the changing rooms, bathrooms and a water fountain.
Another rounded archway then leads to the main studio.
The main pilates studio was designed as a white space to reflect the coloured light from a sculptural LED light installation attached to the vaulted ceiling.
The aim was to create diverse exercise environments and enable the lighting to control the mood and energy of the space.
“The white surfaces act as a neutral canvas for coloured light, allowing different hues to transform the atmosphere,” Serra said.
“This system also offers flexibility for brand collaborations, as the lighting can be adapted to reflect different identities and experiences,” he added.
In the studio, the designers used mirrored walls to create the illusion of a circular room and added full-length perimeter curtains to soften the space’s texture.
Other interior projects recently featured on Dezeen include Matteo Thun designs for Milan’s Torre Velasca skyscraper and SABO’s design of an apartment on Manhattan’s Lower East Side.

items.title: New Zealand tricks and annual leave - the lengths fans are going to for GTA 6
paragraphs: Gamers have long been known to book time off work for major releases.

When Red Dead Redemption 2 launched in October 2018, social media users were sharing plans to take the day off, with one analytics firm reportedly finding, external more people talking about calling in sick for it than any other game that year.
Similar conversations took place ahead of Cyberpunk 2077's release in December 2020, with fans discussing , externaltaking several days off to play.
GTA 6 is no exception, but it appears to characteristically be taking things to a whole new level.
For the game's launch day, HR software company BrightHR, external looked at absence data from more than 1.2 million employees from 70,000 businesses across the UK.
It found GTA was mentioned in 4.6% of time-off requests by employees. Throughout November and December, it said an estimated 83,000 days had been booked off for the game.

According to the HR firm, one person put "new GTA is coming out! I will be spending a week on the sofa in my pants!" as the reason for their leave request, while another said: "play the new GTA - I've waited a billion years".
A third said in their request: "GTA Release - I'll put my notice in if this is denied."
The company added it had no way of tracking if the requests had actually been approved by employers.
Aside from taking time off, some gamers have also been discussing a technical loophole which could give them valuable extra hours of play before it officially unlocks in their country.

Because GTA 6 will release at midnight local time in all regions, New Zealand will become one of the first places where it is available, due to it reaching midnight earliest because of its position near the international date line.
This has led to some investigating ways to "trick" their consoles into thinking they're based in the island country when they are in fact thousands of miles away.
According to Google Trends, searches for the "GTA 6 New Zealand trick" have surged by more than 5,000% in the UK over the past month.
Games journalist Vic Hood said many gamers would be looking to play earlier to "get in on the action as soon as possible", as well as to prevent spoilers.
"As New Zealand is 13 hours ahead of the UK, that's 13 hours of gameplay that has time to spread across the internet and potentially spoil some key story beats and in-game surprises," she said.
"Took an extra day of paid time off when I found this out," one fan posted on Reddit on the trick.
It also means gamers would be playing the game at the much nicer time of 11:00 GMT, rather than having to stay up all night.

But another Xbox user shared caution on Reddit, noting that while the loophole had been exploited for many years for other game releases, GTA 6 "might be the game where Microsoft finally does something about this 'exploit'" - which could include banning players.
GTA 6's developers Rockstar and publishers Take Two Interactive have not commented on the loophole, and neither has Sony nor Microsoft.

Louise Wooldridge from analyst firm Ampere Analysis said both Microsoft and Sony had "rules governing regional accounts and purchases" for the Xbox and PlayStation, adding that Sony's were "slightly more restrictive".
Players who choose to use the workaround could therefore risk breaching those terms and conditions and potentially face restrictions on their accounts or lose access to their digital games.
Some gamers will have to wait even longer than their console-playing counterparts to get their hands on GTA 6, as the game will not be available on PC at launch, similar to previous GTA releases.
"Spare a thought for the PC users who will have to live vicariously through others' YouTube videos and Twitch streams," gamer Stephen Finn told the BBC.
A PS5 now costs from £520, while the more powerful PS5 Pro is nearly £790.
Despite the hefty price tag, for some the temptation to join the community in playing what many have called the biggest game launch of the year, if not decade, has been too great.
Reddit posts and videos, such as one by US YouTuber isoish, external, show fans buying consoles specifically to play the game.
"So, the only game I'm going to have on here is GTA," the content creator said in the video.
After more than a decade of waiting, it seems some fans are determined not to waste a single minute of GTA 6's release - no matter what the cost or extra effort.

items.title: Iranian Kurdish opposition groups reject amnesty-for-surrender deal
paragraphs: Editor's note: this story was translated from the original VOA Kurdish article.

Iranian Kurdish opposition leaders based in Iraq’s Kurdistan Region have ruled out turning themselves in to Tehran as part of potential amnesty deal, citing lack of trust in Iran to guarantee their safety.

Their comments come after Iraqi officials reported progress in negotiations involving Baghdad, the Kurdistan Regional Government (KRG) and Iran over the future of Iranian Kurdish opposition groups that have a maintained presence in northern Iraq for decades.

Iraq's Foreign Minister Fuad Hussein confirmed last week that one of the options discussed during the trilateral talks included potential amnesty for the Iranian Kurdish armed group members who wished to return, if they felt safe.

Amanj Zibaee, a member of the central committee of the Kurdistan Democratic Party of Iran (KDPI), an armed opposition group seeking greater autonomy for Kurds in Iran, and the party’s representative in Erbil, told VOA that his group categorically rejects the prospect of surrendering to Iranian authorities.
“The Islamic Republic of Iran makes many promises but offers nothing in practice. Surrendering to it is something we completely reject, and it is not even an option we have discussed,” he said.
Zibaee said his party would wait for an official announcement over the proposal discussed between Baghdad, Tehran and Erbil before determining its response.
“Once the Iraqi government and the Kurdistan Regional Government officially announce their positions, the KDPI leader will make an appropriate decision,” he said.
He said his organization has acted responsibly and has not used Iraqi territory to attack Iran, a key demand by Baghdad.
“We have never used the Kurdistan Region of Iraq as a base to launch attacks against a neighboring country. We have acted responsibly, and we will continue to do so,” Zibaee said.
Khalil Nadri, spokesperson for the Kurdistan Freedom Party, also dismissed the possibility of accepting an Iranian amnesty.

“We have an agreement with the Kurdistan Region that we will not conduct military operations against Iran from its territory. Our struggle against Iran takes place inside Iran, in Eastern Kurdistan,” Nadri told VOA, referring to predominantly Kurdish areas of western Iran.
He said his party had respected Iraqi sovereignty and helped defend the region against the Islamic State and Iran-backed armed groups, including the Popular Mobilization Forces.
“Iran is not in a position to grant us amnesty,” Nadri said. “Our homeland has been occupied. We will return when our homeland is liberated and the enemy has withdrawn.”

Iran has repeatedly over many years launched missile, and drone strikes targeting Iranian Kurdish opposition groups based in northern Iraq that have been fighting for Kurdish regional autonomy or independence in Iran. The attacks surged following the outbreak of the conflict in the Middle East as Iran launched retaliatory attacks against neighboring countries.
The Iranian Kurdish armed opposition Komala party said Monday that two missiles struck the entrance to one of its bases in the Balisan Valley in Iraq's Kurdistan Region.
Idris Kolahdozi, a member of the party's Central Committee and its head of relations in Sulaimaniyah, told VOA that the attack caused no casualties or property damage.
There was no immediate independent confirmation of who carried out the attack.

Iraqi Foreign Minister Hussein said the latest round of negotiations between Iraq, Iran and the Kurdistan Regional Government that started in October in Baghdad are continuing and that several options were under consideration.
In an interview with France 24, Hussein said the parties had reached a degree of understanding about how to address the opposition groups’ presence in Iraq.
He raised a possible amnesty deal that could allow Iranian Kurdish opposition members to return to Iran, provided they received credible guarantees for their personal safety.

Earlier this month, Iraqi government spokesperson Haider Aboudi told VOA that discussions had reached an “advanced stage” and that Baghdad hoped to resolve the issue soon, though no final deal has been publicly disclosed.
Aboudi emphasized that Iraq was determined to prevent its territory from being used to attack neighboring countries.
KRG spokesperson Peshawa Hawramani similarly told VOA that the regional government would not allow its territory to be used to harm neighboring states.

The negotiations come amid continued Iranian pressure on Baghdad and Erbil to remove Iranian Kurdish opposition groups from Iraqi territory. Tehran has repeatedly accused the groups of threatening its security, allegations the opposition parties deny.
Last month, KDPI spokesperson Khalid Azizi told VOA that his party had largely complied with Iraqi requests to withdraw from areas near the Iranian border.
He said the party had engaged in discussions with Iraqi and Kurdish authorities, with United Nations involvement, over the region's security for several years.

items.title: Met Office yellow warning in place as snow could disrupt Tuesday morning travel
paragraphs: A weather front is pushing north and east across the UK bringing a spell of rain to many areas. As this rain reaches northern England it will encounter a reservoir of colder and drier air.

Some of the rain will evaporate in this drier air, which will cool the atmosphere further by a process known as evaporative cooling - the same process involved in cooling your body down when you sweat.

Eventually rain will start to turn to snow, initially over higher hills in the Pennines, moving to lower hills with time. As the precipitation moves northwards and eastwards, the snow will spread to the Cumbrian hills and into Scotland's Southern Uplands.
The snow will come down in big, wet, chunky flakes which could stick to powerlines and tree branches.
The extra weight of the snow combined with wind gusts of 40-50mph over high ground could bring down tree branches and powerlines, bringing an additional risk of some localised power cuts.

items.title: Discover this year's Dezeen Awards Designers of the Year
paragraphs: Dezeen has announced the six winners of Dezeen Awards 2026 Designers of the Year at this evening’s ceremony in London, which include Lina Ghotmeh, Keiji Ashizawa and Yinka Ilori.
Our Designers of the Year awards recognise the best emerging and established talent whose innovative work has made a notable impact on the industry across architecture, interiors and design.
This year, Ghotmeh took home the architect of the year award, while studio duo Shohei Kuma and Elsa Escobedo were named emerging architect of the year.
Interior designer of the year was awarded to Tokyo-based Ashizawa, and Australian designer Yasmine Ghoniem was named emerging interior designer of the year.
London-based Ilori won designer of the year with Stockholm-based Simon Skinner named emerging designer of the year.

Ghotmeh, who is the founder of architecture practice Lina Ghotmeh Architecture, is one of the world’s most sought-after architects. Among her high-profile projects was the 2023 Serpentine Pavilion and she was recently appointed to renovate the British Museum’s Western Range galleries.
“From Beirut to Paris and beyond, Lina Ghotmeh creates architecture that feels both rooted in history and entirely of the future,” said the judges.

“Her poetic approach to materials, memory and landscape brings buildings to life with a rare sensitivity to people, place and planet. We anticipate her studio continuing to go from strength to strength.”

Ghotmeh is known for her sustainable and historically rooted designs, including the Stone Garden apartment block in Beruit, which was named architecture project of the year at Dezeen Awards 2021. She has received multiple accolades, including being named on the Time100 Next list in 2025 and winning the 2023 Great Arab Minds Award.
Emerging architect of the year: Shohei Kuma and Elsa Escobedo
Founded by Japanese architect Shohei Kuma and French‑Spanish architect and urban designer Elsa Escobedo, Kuma&Elsa is an emerging architecture studio with offices in France, Spain and Japan.

“Shohei Kuma and Elsa Escobedo’s emerging practice brings a fresh sense of curiosity to architecture, balancing bold forms and material experimentation with tactility and unexpected gestures,” said the judges.
“Working between Japan and Europe, Kuma and Elsa are creating an architectural vocabulary that feels both regionally distinctive and deeply connected to its surroundings.”
Among the studio’s varied and intriguing work is Nakano House in Japan’s Fukuoka prefecture – an apartment block informed by the design of a traditional Japanese engawa.
Interior designer of the year: Keiji Ashizawa

Interior designer Ashizawa runs his interdisciplinary, craft-oriented studio based on the ideal of “honest design”. Along with interior spaces, his Tokyo-based studio designs everything from lighting to furniture and products.

“Prolific designer Keiji Ashizawa brings a quiet confidence to interior design, where natural materials, considered details, refined craftsmanship and a sense of calm take centre stage,” said the judges.
“His distinct spaces reveal the beauty in restraint, proving that the most powerful interiors are often those that will quietly stand the test of time.”
Recent work from the studio includes a tea shop in central Shanghai, a holiday home clad in charred cedar in central Japan and a showroom for Japanese furniture brand Karimoku.
Emerging interior designer of the year: Yasmine Ghoniem
Australian designer Ghoniem has found great success since founding her interior studio YSG in 2020 with the aim of creating bold, holistic design experiences.
“Yasmine Ghoniem takes a bold, instinctive approach to interior design, bringing together rich textures, unexpected colour and cultural references,” said the judges.
“Often challenging convention, her interiors are expressive and distinctive, and full of character, warmth and individuality that defy easy categorisation.”

Among her recent – and varied – designs are a wellness hotel in Bali, the revamp of a Sydney apartment, a warehouse conversion in Sydney designed to evoke the Mojave desert and a bar for gin brand Four Pillars.
Ilori designs pavilions, installations, pop-ups, products and furniture, all united by a bold use of colour informed by his Nigerian heritage.
“Yinka Ilori injects design with an irresistible dose of colour, humour and optimism, turning everyday objects and spaces into lively celebrations of culture and community,” said the judges.

“Rooted in his British-Nigerian heritage, his exuberant work reminds us that design can be as joyful as it is meaningful, bringing people together through shared experiences and bold creative expression.”

Ilori has designed numerous pavilions, including the Colour Palace in London and an events space for the Estrel Berlin hotel in Germany. On a smaller scale, he has designed products including a watch for Swiss brand MB&F and his own range of branded homeware.
He also recently created an extensive collection of furniture, fabrics and homeware for Dunelm.
Emerging designer of the year: Simon Skinner
Swedish designer Skinner is well-known for his furniture, sculpture and installations that explore how materials can be rethought or reused.

“Simon Skinner is a burgeoning talent who brings a fresh perspective to contemporary Scandinavian design, pairing a thoughtful approach to materials with a refined, understated visual language. His work subverts the familiar, creating distinct new objects that hint at an exciting new direction for design.”
Recent examples of his varied, multidisciplinary work include a range of sculptural lights made from second-hand bowls, ashtrays and cat figurines.
