items.title: James Bond: What we know so far about the next 007 film
paragraphs: When a bartender asked James Bond in 2006's Casino Royale whether he'd like his vodka martini shaken or stirred, the irritated spy replied: "Do I look like I give a damn?"
Such throwaway lines were a clever way of signalling to the audience that this was a new era for 007 - and that the film series launched in 1962 was being overhauled with the arrival of Daniel Craig.

Over the next few films, producers struck a balance between nodding to the past while also moving away from some of the cheesier elements of the series, no longer sticking rigidly to all of the tradition and tropes of Bond.
"Were you expecting an exploding pen?" Ben Whishaw's Q later asked the secret service agent in Skyfall. "We don't really go in for that anymore."

Two decades on from Craig's debut, the series is about to be rebooted once again, with a new actor and new creative team. It's an exciting time for Bond fans as they wait to see what shape the next era will take. Here's what we know so far.
Pattinson is known for films including Twilight, The Batman and Tenet
British actor Robert Pattinson has been confirmed as the next actor to play James Bond.
He shot to fame as Cedric Diggory in 2005's Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire, and went on to star in Twilight.
Pattinson appeared opposite Kristen Stewart in the series of five films based on Stephenie Meyers' vampire novels.
He has gone on to star in other major films and franchises including The Batman and Christopher Nolan's recent adaptation of The Odyssey.
But Pattinson is also respected within the industry for his unusual choice of roles, often appearing in independent, arthouse and experimental films.
His other credits include The Lighthouse, Mickey 17, Life, The Drama, Good Time, Primetime, The Rover, Bel Ami, Tenet and The Lost City of Z.
L-R: Callum Turner, Jack Lowden and Jack Barton are all thought to have auditioned for the role
A handful of actors were thought to have made it to the final screen tests before Pattinson scored Britain's biggest film role. They included:
Jack Lowden, 36 - whose credits include Slow Horses and Pride and Prejudice
Josh O'Connor, 36 - The Crown, Wake Up Dead Man: A Knives Out Mystery
Callum Turner, 36 - Masters of the Air, The Capture
Jack Barton, 31 - Heartstopper, SAS: Rogue Heroes
Nicholas Hoult, 36 - About A Boy, Superman
Paul Mescal, 30 - Normal People, Gladiator II
But while many of the names are seen as hot, up-and-coming actors, Pattinson was arguably the most bankable movie star.
The film is expected to go into production in 2027, before its release in 2028. No exact dates have been announced.
Film schedules can be notoriously fluid, but it's clear that development is well under way, with the director and writer already in place.
It will be the 26th film in the official film series, but the title has not yet been confirmed.
Steven Knight (left) will write the script, while Denis Villeneuve will direct the film
The movie will be directed by Denis Villeneuve, known for Prisoners, Sicario, Arrival, Blade Runner 2049 and the recent Dune trilogy starring Timothée Chalamet.

"Some of my earliest movie-going memories are connected to 007," the French-Canadian director said last year. "I grew up watching James Bond films with my father, ever since Dr. No with Sean Connery. I'm a die-hard Bond fan. To me, he's sacred territory."
He added: "I intend to honour the tradition and open the path for many new missions to come. This is a massive responsibility, but also, incredibly exciting for me and a huge honour."
Bond 26 will be written by Steven Knight, known for TV series such as Peaky Blinders and House of Guinness, and films including Burnt, Spencer, Locke and The Girl in the Spider's Web.
Knight has said it had always been on his "bucket list" to write a Bond film, adding that he felt he was "doing my duty for King and country" by joining the franchise.
He told the BBC he planned to "write the character, not the actor", adding: "The thing with Bond is it's its own universe and franchise. So there are certain rules.
"Obviously you have to move it along, but I love where it sits. I love that it's British. I love that it's not DC or Marvel... So I feel a responsibility to the text."
Irish actor Pierce Brosnan starred in four Bond films, including 1999's The World Is Not Enough
Sean Connery starred in six official Bond films between 1962 and 1971
George Lazenby starred in just one Bond film, in 1969
Roger Moore starred in seven Bond films between 1973 and 1985
Timothy Dalton starred in two Bond films, in 1987 and 1989
Pierce Brosnan starred in four Bond films, between 1995 and 2002
Daniel Craig starred in five Bond films between 2006 and 2021
You might have noticed some overlap in the above dates.
That's because Connery returned to the lead role for 1971's Diamonds Are Forever, after Lazenby took his place for 1969's On Her Majesty's Secret Service.
Connery also later appeared in 1983's Never Say Never Again, a Bond film produced by a different studio and not part of the official film series.
Roger Moore pictured filming 1985's A View To A Kill
If you discount the films not in the official series, there have been 25 Bond films in total. In order, they are:
Daniel Craig (pictured with co-star Léa Seydoux) stepped down as Bond with 2021's No Time To Die
With the change in ownership and a new creative team now in place, the new Bond film is likely to make a fresh start.
It would be difficult to continue the story chronologically given the ending of 2021's No Time To Die, but that still leaves producers with plenty of options.

A different version of James Bond, who exists in a different universe, would be easily pulled off in an era where audiences are used to major film franchises restarting in a different world or timeline.

Bond 26 could even be set in a significantly earlier era - an idea that gained more popularity after Tony Gilroy revealed he and fellow director Steven Soderbergh previously pitched a 1960s version, external of Bond.

Separately, actor Ralph Fiennes recently said, external he had once been in talks to play Bond, and had suggested producers make a "black and white and very sort of film noir-y" version set in the 1950s.
Neither idea materialised, but the suggestion went down well with some Bond fans, who noted a period piece would help make the film truer to Ian Fleming's original character and books.
Exactly what shape the next film takes will become clear at a later stage. For now, Christmas has come early for fans who have been waiting for years to find out who the next 007 will be.
In Robert Pattinson, producers have finally found their spy.

items.title: From Batman to Bond - how Robert Pattinson landed the role of 007
paragraphs: Robert Pattinson has starred in films including the Twilight franchise and The Batman

Robert Pattinson's career is already flying high with roles in films including the Twilight series, The Batman and The Odyssey, so signing up to play James Bond will propel his profile into the stratosphere.
He's already established himself as a leading man, action star and character actor, which is clearly why he is about to play the suave, British secret agent 007.

At 40, he is slightly older than some of the other men reportedly lined up for the role, but he's also the most famous - something the new Bond studio Amazon-MGM may have favoured, with an eye on the box office.
His recent work has garnered both critical and box office success, including Christopher Nolan's summer blockbuster The Odyssey, in which he played the villainous Antinous.
Pattinson was also called "Oscar-worthy" by the Independent and "superb" by The Times, for his performance in November's Primetime, as the real-life host of US TV show To Catch a Predator.

He also helped lead 2022's The Batman to the second-biggest North American opening of the Covid-19 pandemic behind Spider-Man: No Way Home. The Guardian said he played the "brooding" role with "appealing vulnerability, external".

Meanwhile in dark romantic comedy The Drama, he and his co-star gave a "career-highlight performance", external. It's one of three films he appeared in with Zendaya this year, along with The Odyssey and Dune: Part Three.
Robert Pattinson starred in 2022's The Batman, which was described by critics as a grim, gritty, and gripping super-noir
Born in Barnes, south-west London, Pattinson grew up with his father, a classic car trader and mother, who worked at a modelling agency, and two elder sisters.
His interest in acting started while he was still at school, when he joined the Barnes Theatre Club.
"I wouldn't be acting if it wasn't for that little club," he told Your Local Guardian in 2008, external.
"I went originally because a lot of pretty girls went there," he said. "I worked backstage and I started acting when all the good people left and I was the only one tall enough to play the lead.
"In a weird sort of way, that stuff was probably the best I've done and the stuff I am most proud of."
He landed his first big film role more than two decades ago, playing Cedric Diggory in 2005's Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire. A relatively minor character, but it was enough to get him noticed.
Robert Pattinson and Kristen Stewart starred in five Twilight films from 2005 to 2012

Three years later, he had a starring role in the first of five Twilight films, along with Kristen Stewart, in which they played star-crossed lovers - vampire Edward Cullen and mortal-turned vampire Kristen Stewart.
Based on Stephanie Meyer's hugely popular young adult books, the films globally grossed more than $3bn (£2.2bn) by 2012, and established Pattinson as a heartthrob.
He spoke in his early career of finding his often adoring, screaming fans hard to deal with.
"Although is part of the job, it feels like they have been paid to turn up and scream at me at 7.30pm," he said.
"Nothing I don't think can prepare you for the fans. I don't know why I'm not getting used to it but I'm completely overwhelmed every time."
Pattinson and Zendaya have appeared in three films together this year - The Drama, The Odyssey and Dune: Part Three

The following year though, he was back in big-studio territory, with Odyssey director Christopher Nolan, in sci-fi thriller Tenet, and again in 2022 with The Batman, directed by Matt Reeves and co-starring Zoe Kravitz and Paul Dano.
Pattinson told Screen Daily why he returned to big-budget films, explaining: "I guess I was trying to do the opposite of what I've been doing. I started thinking, 'I really want to do a big thing.'
"I hadn't done something with a massive budget for ages. But you approach it exactly the same way."
The Batman got generally positive reviews, re-establishing Pattinson with a broader range of fans.
By 2025, when he was on the red carpet for Parasite director Bong Joon Ho's sci-fi black comedy, Mickey 17, he said it was "quite strange" to have a fanbase that was now dominated by men, external.
"There's like a bunch of guys, which is a new one for me!" he told the Associated Press.
Pattinson's private life has often created interest in the press, not least his previous relationships with Stewart, and then the singer FKA Twigs.
Since 2018, he has been in a relationship with model Suki Waterhouse. They got engaged in December 2023 and had their first child, a daughter, in March.
Robert Pattinson and Suki Waterhouse have been a couple since 2018
With his latest role as James Bond, Pattinson will be extremely busy, not least because the forthcoming Batman sequel is reportedly due out in 2028.
But the actor will have a head start as 007, having already worked with Bond 26 director Denis Villeneuve, who also helmed Dune: Part Three.
Pattinson was full of praise for him on their most recent film, despite the strain of working in the furnace-like heat of the desert.

"The scale of this stuff is just unbelievable, you're having your own Dune theme park, where the gimbal is going upside down and flying, and this is not like work at all," he told the New York Times, external.
"There are no negatives. Apart from having your sweat drained out of the top of your head, and getting like bulbous sweat bubbles. But even then, I didn't even really notice them.
"He's so easy to work with, Denis, it's never really a stress."
Sounds like Pattinson will have the cool head needed to juggle his forthcoming roles - including James Bond. You could even say he may end up being shaken, but not stirred.

items.title: The first scene from the new Harry Potter series just dropped – and it's sparked a fierce filmmaking debate
paragraphs: It seems fair to say that HBO's new Harry Potter series has a lot to live up to. Will it do justice to the books? Can it recapture the (ahem) magic of the movies? Will it step outside of the shadow of the controversies surrounding its author? But most importantly, won't somebody think of the blocking?

Yes, blocking—the staging and positioning of actors on screen—has become a buzzword after HBO dropped the very first piece of footage from the show, depicting a feast in the grand hall of Hogwarts. Fans are naturally comparing the scene to its 2001 movie counterpart, and not favourably.
Harry Potter and the Philosopher’s Stone | The Start-of-Term Banquet Clip | HBO Max - YouTube

Viewers have been lamenting for years the move towards dark and washed out colour grading in modern movies and TV shows, and it seems not even Hogwarts is immune to the gloom. Compare this grand hall scene to the same one from the movie version of Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone and difference is night and day. HBO's offering looks like somebody at Hogwarts forgot to top up the electricity meter.
But it's the staging that's raising the most eyebrows.

Remove the color and focus on the composition and blocking. Even in black and white, the remake looks flat. The 2001 clip contained so much more exposition: house ghosts, Snape, student backstories. Every square inch of the frame is used. The new Dumbledore and McGonagall look botoxed and appear in vanity makeup, everything is center frame so that it can be shared on social media in vertical videos.November 15, 2026
A Great feast banquet hall scene Harry potter HBO (2026)/Harry potter and Philosopher's stone (2001) https://t.co/86bQoRP5IRNovember 15, 2026

Indeed, many individual shots from the 2001 original tell a story through the simple fact of their composition. When Harry spots Snape through the crowd, the framing of the two characters creates instant intrigue and drama. But here, the individual shots look much duller and less vibrant.

Overall, the whole looks rather like a recession indictor. From the darker palette to what looks like a vastly reduced food offering at the so-called 'feast', the whole thing looks, to quite Ryanair, "cheaper than a Ryanair flight". And given the recent response to the new posters for the series, the whole thing has a long way to go to win round fans.

Daniel John is Design Editor at Creative Bloq. He reports on the worlds of design, branding and lifestyle tech, and has covered several industry events including Milan Design Week, OFFF Barcelona and Adobe Max in Los Angeles. He has interviewed leaders and designers at brands including Apple, Microsoft and Adobe. Daniel's debut book of short stories and poems was published in 2018, and his comedy newsletter is a Substack Bestseller.

items.title: Nike Tuned Air "a huge stride forward" in air-filled trainer design says innovation lead
paragraphs: Sportswear brand Nike has unveiled the 3D-printed air bags that will be used for its next generation of air-filled trainers. In this interview, the brand’s chief innovation, design & product officer Phil McCartney explains why it is a technological and performance advance.
“I see it personally as a revolution, not an evolution,” McCartney told Dezeen from the LeBron James Innovation Center in Oregon. “It’s a huge stride forward.”

Tuned Air was designed to give Nike much greater control of how air is used within the midsole to provide cushioning and support. Using a combination of proprietary 3D printing and “selective lamination” allows Nike to create midsoles that perform in different ways under different parts of the foot.
Informed by the raised vibrant colours on magazine covers, the airbag is built up from layers of ink.
“We can engineer the structure and tune the structure in the heel differently to the forefoot,” said McCartney.
“We can also tune the height, so you can have a variety of different heights, and we can tune the structure inside.”
Nike unveiled the technology and concept images for a running shoe today, and is planning for the first Nike Tuned Air trainer to be launched next year.

The trainers will be the first in what Nike sees as a third major generation of its air-filled shoes, since Nike CEO Phil Knight worked with inventor Frank Rudy to use a cushioning system filled with gas in the late 1970s.
Following the Nike Air Tailwind in 1978, Nike developed Air Max in the 1980s and Air Zoom in the 1990s.

“At its core, Air, for 50 years, has been this magical combination of lightweight, cushioned and resilient – it doesn’t break down over time,” said McCartney. “That’s why from day one when Phil [Knight] struck the deal with Frank Rudy, we’ve been so committed to it – it just delivers a really unique benefit.”

“If Max Air is about maximal cushioning and impact protection, Zoom Air is more about responsiveness and snappiness,” he continued. “Tuned Air, because of this proprietary ink and selective lamination process, allows us to literally tune the sensation within the airbag, which enables us to sort of move free from the constraints of typical geometry and shape.”
According to McCartney, this change in how the airbags are manufactured opens up possibilities, especially in customisation.

“It is the first step in exploring all the different places that this will go,” said McCartney. “The capability and what we’re able to do with this proprietary ink and the selective lamination allows us to really unlock the real potential of air.”
“It also creates this canvas for all the design explorations that we’ve always wanted to do, but the limitations of the manufacturing process didn’t allow,” he continued.

“So now the handcuffs are off in terms of it being a canvas – what expressions do we want to explore? What different visuals, geometries, and different ways to articulate the benefit can we explore? We’re looking at all of that. “
While the air-filled midsole has been manufactured, the trainer is still in development. However, McCartney expects the shoe to look close to the concept render that was revealed today.

“There’ll be a few modifications,” he said. “Knowing where the design is going to go. It’s pretty representative as an illustration, but it isn’t the final design.” He noted that the final air bag design will be close to the prototype.
“What we’re exploring now is how do we take the idea of lightweight cushioning and this idea of tuned [and find] what that looks like in an expression and an experience on the upper.”

One key design element that will feature in the commercial release next year will be the full-length, visible air bag, which McCartney said is an “important part of the design and important part of this platform”.

The midsoles are the latest innovation in Nike’s exploration of using air within footwear and apparel. While it has made millions of shoes containing air, it has also recently unveiled the inflating Air Milano Jacket at 2026 Winter Olympics and its Radical AirFlow t-shirts that counterintuitively use more material to make a wearer cooler.
In all the areas of innovation that McCartney oversees at Nike, air is where he sees the most potential.

“There’s a number of areas, but if I had to pick one, I think that [air] is the platform that intrigues us most, that drives our creativity the most, that also translates into the biggest athlete benefit. And I mean athlete in the broadest sense of the term – if you’ve got a body, you’re an athlete.”

“We’re really intrigued and fascinated by the notion of being able to harness what’s all around us to further performance,” said McCartney. “That started in footwear, obviously. This is the next revolution.”

items.title: US basketball player arrested with 75lb of marijuana at Nigerian airport, say authorities
paragraphs: An American basketball player has been arrested in Nigeria for allegedly attempting to smuggle 33.95kg (75lb) of marijuana into the country.

Nigeria’s National Drug Law Enforcement Agency (NDLEA) said a 28-year-old player named as Greene Da’monte Khiree from the state of Georgia was arrested at Lagos’s main airport last Wednesday after he arrived on a flight from Thailand via the United Arab Emirates.

The NDLEA said the player told them he had come to Nigeria to “build networks” for his basketball career. The agency said evidence on his phone suggested he had “knowledge of and involvement in the drug trafficking activity”. The NDLEA said it detained the player when he attempted to leave the airport with his hand luggage after abandoning two checked-in bags. The agency said those two bags were found to contain 32 parcels of marijuana, and a tracking device.
Nigeria has strict drug laws, and trafficking carries a sentence of life in prison.

A basketball player by the name of Damonte Greene is listed on the roster of the Pattani Raptors in the Thai Premier Men’s League. Greene, a Georgia native, played college basketball for Reinhardt University and South Georgia Technical College. He played semi-professional basketball in the US before representing a number of teams in Thailand.

WNBA star Brittney Griner and former Utah State player Jarred Shaw were imprisoned in Russia and Indonesia respectively for marijuana offenses. Griner was released in December 2022, while Shaw remains in prison.

items.title: The Scouse actor reaching new heights in Liverpool drama This City Is Ours
paragraphs: With millions of viewers and a major role in a Bafta-nominated series, you might not expect Adam Abbou to know much about feeling self-conscious.
"When we were kids it wasn't so cool to be from Liverpool," the This City Is Ours actor says.
"I'd be in these rooms with people who were really posh and I always felt out of place."
The Liverpool-based BBC series has become a hit, with Abbou, who plays Freddie, stepping into a prominent role for its second season.
But it's not just the storylines on drugs, gangs and murders hooking audiences - it's the setting too, and the Scouse actors bringing it to life.
Created by Liverpudlian writer Stephen Butchard, This City Is Ours recruited heavily from Merseyside.
Lead actors James Nelson-Joyce, Jack McMullen and Mike Noble were all born in Liverpool, as was Abbou, who grew up in Anfield.
But like many young and aspiring actors, for a long time he thought where he came from could hold him back.
"I didn't see a lot of [Liverpudlian accents] on TV when I was a kid," the 23-year-old says.
As a result, acting "always felt really out of reach".
Abbou played the title role in a touring production of Billy Elliot the Musical in 2015, and has since appeared in dramas like Casualty, Time and Waterloo Road.
He says he wasn't expecting his latest gig, where he plays Freddie, gangster Banksey's son, to become so significant.
"If you would have asked me 10 years ago, I would have said you probably need to move to London," he says.
"So for me to be able to do a show like this in Liverpool, it just further proves that you can do it from anywhere."
From the reaction he's had locally, Abbou thinks the series has been a boost for Liverpool overall.

The reaction has been "quite crazy" in the city, he says, "but of course it would be because people love to see themselves and their accent reflected on TV and when it is, you almost feel like you know the person".
"It has truly been incredible to see the rise of the Scouse accent," he adds, crediting the Netflix series Adolescence, starring and co-created by Stephen Graham, with accelerating the change.
"Stephen Graham really was the one who started the wave for Scouse actors," he says.
"And then the likes of Jodie Comer and now you've got your Mike Nobles, your James Nelson-Joyces... and now your Adam Abbous.
"We're making waves for young Scouse talent."
As for what's next, Abbou says the series has helped push his career forward and he has some "exciting projects lined up" which he can't speak about just yet.
"I just want to do things that make me feel creatively fulfilled and mean something and have a voice."
- The last episode of The City Is Ours season two airs on BBC One at 21:00 GMT.

items.title: Shisuo Design Office creates "surreal" rural house in China using salvaged steel
paragraphs: Jiang Deng Lu is a house in rural Anhui designed by Chinese studio Shisuo Design Office using stainless-steel offcuts salvaged from the client’s own factory.
Described by Shisuo Design Office as a “surreal rural house”, the compact building is raised partially on stilts to look as though it is floating above its sloped riverside site.
It sits beside the client’s ancestral home and serves as both a memorial for his late father and a separate dwelling where his elderly mother can host visiting relatives.

“The client wanted to build a house beside the old family home, providing a comfortable place for his mother and relatives to gather and share meals during holidays,” Shisuo Design Office told Dezeen.

“But beyond this practical need, there was a deeper emotional connection. The old house was left by his father, while the new one represented his own way of creating new memories for the family,” it continued.
“We hoped the house would bring the family together more often, beyond just festive occasions.”
Jiang Deng Lu’s proportions were determined by the recycled stainless steel offcuts and unused windows salvaged for the project by the client, who is the owner of a stainless steel factory.
“The building’s geometry was strictly reverse-engineered from these salvaged materials,” said Shisuo Design Office.

“Instead of imposing a predetermined architectural form, we meticulously measured and mapped these specific surplus components. The building’s precise dimensions, roof pitches, and structural envelope were entirely reverse-engineered from this salvaged inventory,” added the studio.

“The resulting structure starkly contrasts the client’s modern, lightweight metal industry with the heavy, rooted legacy of his father’s masonry, translating familial love into a rigorous tectonic language,” the studio said.

Externally, the house is wrapped in a full stainless-steel facade, which the studio said deliberately contrasts with “traditional rural vernacular”. This is punctured by the salvaged windows, positioned to frame views of the river.
It has a rectangular plan, with a balcony that is suspended over the river on one side.
Inside is a living space, which sits raised above a dining area accessed directly from the foyer. A bathroom and shower room sit off this dining space.

Interior finishes are pared-back, with stone flooring and white walls complementing the cool-toned exterior of the home. Wooden furnishings and greenery seen through the windows add warmth to the space.
According to Shisuo Design Office, the highlight of the interior is a nine-metre-long window that cantilevers 2.2 metres outward, providing shelter for the terrace below.
“The most distinctive feature is a nine-metre-long horizontal window facing east, overlooking a grove of trees planted by the client’s late father,” said the studio.
“For the client, these trees are more than a landscape; they hold personal memories of his father. We wanted to bring the grove into everyday life, rather than simply frame it as a view.”
Jiang Deng Lu is shortlisted in the rural house category of the 2026 Dezeen Awards, alongside projects including Casa Plaj by Extrastudio and Hata-Mazanka Guesthouses by YOD Group.
Another house featured on Dezeen with a distinctive metal facade is Bondi House, a two-storey, two-bedroom dwelling by Nick Kent Design in Sydney.

items.title: Casa Mouda opens Lagos gallery to promote design in Nigeria
paragraphs: Papa Omotayo, Gemma Sfeir and Nifemi Marcus-Bello have helped design two spaces in Lagos for the local creative studio Casa Mouda to host exhibitions that promote design in West Africa.
Casa Mouda’s initiative includes the launch of an exhibition to mark the opening of two spaces in Lagos – aiMe Gallery at Eko Hotel and aiMe Concept on Eko Atlantic.

AiMe Gallery was redesigned by Lagos-based architect Omotayo at the entrance to the hotel’s conference centre, while aiMe Concept was designed with interior designer Sfeir and designer Marcus-Bello in a storefront in the larger Eko Atlantic development.
Both spaces feature exposed concrete walls and columns with touches of warmth, including an earthen bar and screen in aiMe Gallery.
Casa Mouda founder Caline Chagoury Moudaber said that the spaces, together, were designed to highlight the work done by designers in Lagos.
“As we began to conceive our first chapter of Casa Mouda, we knew we needed to start by recognizing some of the people who had already built so much of its foundation,” said Chagoury Moudaber.
“There are incredible designers producing on the continent that have done extraordinary work, often taking on alone what usually takes an entire industry elsewhere.”
The inaugural exhibitions include designers from Lagos, but also those who have chosen to work in the city from abroad.

Among the latter group is American designer Germane Barnes, who showcased his wooden Corona Chair, which features inverted pyramidal legs, and his take on a peacock chair, both produced in Lagos in collaboration with Casa Mouda.

Beyond his contribution to the interior layout, which includes permanent seating for the hospitality at aiMe Concept, Marcus-Bello showcased his LM stools and M2 shelves. The works showcase the production possible in Lagos, but also a more modern, minimalist angle for Marcus-Bello, who is known for his massive metal collectible design pieces.
“Nifemi Marcus-Bello has been quietly doing the legwork to set up real pathways for production for years,” said Chagoury Moudaber.
On the more craft-oriented side, the collection showcased works in bronze and wood by craftsman Jean Servais Somian, also produced in collaboration with Casa Mouda.

Servais Somian’s work includes an armoire with gridded screen wooden doors, a console with stacked oval shelves, stools in wood with painted recesses that have a graphic appearance and textural cast bronze stools and side tables. It is an impressive array showcasing the craftsman’s range.
French studio Hall Haus showcased its metal basketball hoops and chairs, a blend of African aesthetics with Parisian urban ephemera, reflecting the cross-cultural background of the studio’s members.
Meanwhile, Moroccan designer Hajar Daide showcased a mix of delicate Nigerian woven wood techniques with lush blue Moroccan fabrics for her Friction Bench.

Atmosphere was top of mind for the designers, and Casa Mouda worked with US musician Malloy James to create custom speakers at the entryway for aiMe Gallery, while aiMe Concept features a listening station.
The spaces have also been set up to further promote craft in the region through display and retail, such as textiles, bags and other smaller items such as jewellery.

“The designers who have forged the way are sharing information on what they have learned; the ones new to this area of production are bringing new techniques and perspectives,” said Chagoury Moudaber.
“It has been an incredibly collaborative, generous, and inspiring process – and we are only just beginning.”
Other recent design showcases include the inaugural Walker Design Triennial in Minnesota and Danish design initiative The Mindcraft Project, curated by Christian + Jade.

items.title: Relocation of Cape Town baboons to sanctuary ignites heated protests
paragraphs: The relocation of a troop of baboons in Cape Town to a wildlife sanctuary has triggered furious protests by local people opposed to their capture, which officials argue is necessary to stop human-wildlife conflict in the city.

The 44-member Waterfall troop (named after the area they mainly inhabit) was captured in the southern seaside suburb of Simon’s Town on Friday and Saturday. A second, smaller Seaforth troop is also due to be moved.

The growth in both baboon and human populations in Cape Town in recent years has led to increased conflict and more baboons dying as a result. Meanwhile, a heated debate has raged between people who believe that baboons and humans can coexist and those who argue that baboons in urban areas are in danger and in some cases need to be relocated. Some animal rights activists have compared authorities’ baboon management to apartheid.
During Friday’s relocation, outraged protesters tried to stop vehicles taking the baboons away. One person sprayed a fire extinguisher, according to the Daily Maverick, a local news outlet.

After the confrontation, the local Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals branch urged those opposed to the baboons’ capture not to try to stop the vehicles. “Capture and transport are already stressful for the baboons,” it said in a statement. “Delaying their arrival prolongs their time in crates and risks adding to that stress – this is not fair on the baboons.”
It said it remained opposed to the baboon’s relocation, adding: “Our presence did not imply support … our inspectors are present because the animals need someone looking out for them.”

On Sunday, dozens of people sat outside the wildlife centre in a silent protest, some tying flowers to the fence. Baboons from a different troop also gathered at the boundary, calling to the newly captive animals, the Daily Maverick reported.

“We stand together for the Seaforth and Waterfall troops, for their freedom, their dignity and their right to live as wild animals,” Mandy Neal, the administrator of the Save Kogelfontein Baboons Facebook group, posted on Monday, calling for weekly Sunday silent protests. “ Our message is simple: CAPTIVITY IS NOT CONSERVATION.”

The City of Cape Town said in a statement on Sunday that the relocation had been successful, with the baboons being monitored 24/7 after being checked by vets and the females receiving contraceptive implants.

It said: “The Waterfall troop has been relocated due to the severity and persistence of human-baboon conflict in the Simon’s Town urban environment, the limited available natural low-lying habitat, the increasing risk to the baboons’ welfare, and public safety concerns … [and] as a very last resort after other interventions were evaluated and deemed ineffective, and as an alternative to culling.”

Prof Justin O’Riain, a behavioural ecologist at the University of Cape Town, said the baboon management plan had undergone two years of public consultations. “It has thus been disappointing watching members of the public and select NGOs, many which did not engage in the stakeholder process, now compromising the safety and welfare of the baboons and people through violent actions directed at staff and baboons in transit.”

items.title: Apple MacBook Pro M6 review: probably the last of its generation
paragraphs: Apple’s base-model MacBook Pro gets a solid speed bump, offering most of the features from its top-level siblings but in a design that has just been superseded and may soon be phased out.

It is the starting model in Apple’s popular MacBook Pro line, but that doesn’t make it cheap. Costing from £1,999 (€2,299/$1,999/A$3,199) it is £300 or equivalent more than its predecessor as RAMageddon continues to jack up prices. It is, at least, £500 cheaper than the other new MacBook Pros.

The laptop’s solid aluminium body, look and feel are identical to its predecessors, using the design first introduced in 2021. With five generations of the machine having been and gone, it is a bit of a known quantity, but the 120Hz miniLED screen is still brilliant, as are the first-class keyboard and trackpad. The port selection is also solid and the MagSafe charging cable remains a delight.

The M6 model only comes with the smaller 14.2in screen, which is still the sweet spot for portability and productivity. It reaches a sustained 1,000nits brightness for standard content and working – double that of the MacBook Air – and hits 1,600nits to make HDR content pop. It is only really beaten by the OLED screen on the new MacBook Pro design, which costs considerably more.
Screen: 14.2in mini LED (3024x1964; 254 ppi) ProMotion (120Hz)
Connectivity: wifi 7, Bluetooth 6, Thread, 3x Thunderbolt 4/USB 4, HDMI 2.1, SDXC, headphones

The M6 is Apple’s latest generation chip and was first used in the Mac mini to great effect. Compared with the M5 generation of chips, including the current MacBook Air, the M6 MacBook Pro is about 11% faster for day-to-day usage and 24% for more intensive multi-core tasks. The extra performance wasn’t that noticeable in day-to-day tasks, but just like the M5 version, it absolutely flies during use.

However, it also has up to 57% faster graphics performance, beating many of Apple’s older M-Pro chips. That makes the M6 quite a leap from older machines with more than enough power for many creative work tasks.

The MacBook Pro also has fantastic battery life, lasting about three days of light work between charges using the browser, messaging, notes and word processing apps. That makes it one of the longest-lasting laptops for general use, but even for more intensive work, developing and editing photos, the battery still lasted about two days.

The MacBook Pro is made of 45% recycled materials, which Apple breaks down in its environmental impact report. The battery should last in excess of 1,000 full-charge cycles and can be replaced for £225 by Apple. Apple makes repair manuals available. The company offers trade-in and free recycling schemes.
The MacBook Pro M6 costs from £1,999 (€2,299/$1,999/A$3,199).

For comparison, the 14in M5 Pro MacBook Pro costs £2,499, the 14in OLED MacBook Pro costs from £2,899, the 13in MacBook Air costs £1,299, the Dell XPS 14 costs from £2,038.45 and the Microsoft Surface Laptop Ultra costs £2,599.
The M6 MacBook Pro is a potent machine for general use that is let down by its high price, mostly thanks to the scourge of RAMageddon.
But it is also likely one of the last iterations of its design, having been superseded by the new thinner, lighter and OLED-equipped MacBook Pro.
The M6 is a great laptop with fantastically long battery life and a quality screen, keyboard and trackpad, built on the foundations of the many great MacBook Pros over the last five years.

But at £1,999 or equivalent it is also a difficult pill to swallow, primarily aimed at Apple buyers who want a nicer screen or more ports than a MacBook Air and are prepared to pay £700 more for it. For everyone else, there are better models available with more grunt or a cheaper price.

Pros: great performance from M6 chip, minimum of 16GB memory and 1TB storage, super-long battery life, great ProMotion screen, great Centre Stage camera, plenty of ports and an SD card slot, great speakers, Touch ID, top-class keyboard and trackpad, wifi 7, Bluetooth 6 and Thread support.
Cons: no Face ID, no USB-A, RAM or SSD cannot be upgraded after purchase, very expensive, not a big upgrade on M5 version, no OLED screen, heavier than newer design.

items.title: Art psychotherapists are already regulated | Letters
paragraphs: We welcome the discussion about public protection, professional accountability and the importance of appropriate regulation within counselling and psychotherapy (Letters, 5 November). However, we feel it is important to highlight a distinction that may be helpful to readers.

Art psychotherapists are already a statutorily regulated profession in the UK, regulated by the Health and Care Professions Council (HCPC). The HCPC regulates 15 health and care professions, including arts therapists (art psychotherapists, art therapists, drama therapists, music therapists) and the titles art therapist and art psychotherapist are legally protected. Practitioners must meet HCPC registration requirements, standards of proficiency, conduct and ethics, and continuing professional development requirements.
This means that art therapists occupy a different regulatory position from counsellors and psychotherapists, whose professional registration is currently voluntary.

We do recognise the importance of extending statutory protection across professions where it is currently absent, but would appreciate recognition that we, along with drama therapists and music therapists, are a statutory regulated profession. Elizabeth Donnelly Chief executive officer, British Association of Art Therapists

items.title: Holly Humberstone: People can't connect to a pop star who's 'too polished'
paragraphs: Holly Humberstone says she was having an identity crisis on a weekly basis
You might know her as a pop star, endorsed by everyone from Taylor Swift to Sam Fender, but Holly Humberstone has a secret double life.
In her spare time, the singer-songwriter is literally a cat burglar.
"We've stolen one of our neighbours' cats by accident," she laughs, in a Zoom call from her fixer-upper in New Cross, south-east London.
"He's a tiny little black cat who's come into our garden and simply chosen us."
Under the slightest scrutiny, however, her story crumbles like a biscuit in a hot cup of tea.
"OK, we've been coercing him into the house with treats," she admits. "He's just so cute.
"But we're not trying to keep him. We literally push him out every night."
Humberstone's excuse for this feline felony is that, last year, her parents sold her childhood home in Lincolnshire, external and moved to Wales – taking her pets with them.
One, a cat called Tsuki, had even been immortalised in the song Lucy as a confidante who listens to her problems but "never judges".
"Oh, she knows some secrets!" laughs the singer. "I'm so glad she can't talk."
"We actually tried to bring her to London with us, but she's a countryside cat and she hated it so much. We had to send her to Wales where she can be free and frolic."
Her parents' relocation was disruptive for the human Humberstones, too.
Their house, a "freezing cold, falling down" property 20 minutes outside of Grantham, played a huge part in the singer's success.

Her early EPs were all written there, inspiring the "wonky sonics" of her indie-leaning pop sound. The 2021 single Haunted House is even dedicated to the "friendly" spirits who inhabited the property.
"It's a place I always felt I could go back to, to remind myself of who I am," she says.
Instead, she spent 2025 "packing up 23 years of stuff my family and I had accumulated", from her old ballet shoes and poetry books to forgotten bits of jewellery.
The singer shared photos of her old bedroom, and the artefacts she'd rediscovered, while clearing out her parents' "haunted house" in Grantham (pictured, left).
The process was unsettling. Already grappling with the idea of leaving childhood behind, Humberstone found herself literally throwing away her past.
"I felt uprooted. I was having some sort of identity crisis almost weekly," she says.
So she did what she's always done, and poured those feelings into her second album, Cruel World, which entered the UK charts at number four earlier this year.
"Writing these songs felt like building myself a little shield and a kind of safety bubble," she says. "There's an escapist, fantasy element to so much of the album."
Maybe that's true, but Humberstone has always had the ability to locate a song's emotional core, and the lyrics on Cruel World don't disappoint.
"To lose somebody is to know you're only human, honey," she sings on To Love Somebody, external, soothing her elder sister as she endures an agonising break-up.
Undeterred by that heartbreak, she throws herself headfirst into a new affair on Die Happy, external, declaring: "Hit the gas, I want it fast, want it reckless."
But the most revealing song is the closing track, Beauty Pageant, external.

Fragile and raw, it's the sound of Humberstone in her dressing room, addressing the woman in the mirror who'd "die for the applause" but who struggles with the impossible beauty standards imposed on female artists.
Humberstone's biggest songs include Falling Asleep At The Wheel, The Walls Are Way Too Thin, Die Happy and Scarlett
"That's a song that I wasn't really setting out to write," she confesses.
"Writing about other people often feels easier than turning the magnifying glass on yourself."
The lyrics, she says, draw on a "very specific" mindset she acquired at her all-girls school in Grantham.
"It was drilled into me: You're all in competition. You're only rewarded if you're the best. And if you're not, you're worthless."
The experience "really warped the way I view other girls", she says.
Musical success made it worse. After winning the Brits Rising Star award in 2022, Humberstone found herself competing with megastars, even though her music leaned towards the alternative side of pop.
"I'm a very small fish and I recognise that, but suddenly I was in meetings being compared to all these people on my label's roster, who are on a completely different scale," she says.
"It's something I really, really struggled with in the early days and it's something I've really had to unlearn."
Nowadays, Humberstone has stopped benchmarking herself against her peers, recognising that the need for validation never fades.
"I don't think that there's a point I could get to, or an award that I could win, where these feelings would disappear," she says.

"Everybody feels like they've still got something to prove, so I'm done with setting myself goals - because then I lose sight of the real reason that I'm doing this, which is to write music that represents me, and have other people feel understood through that music."
"I pray that one day I'll turn and face the mirror with a smile," sings Humberstone
That mindset comes to fruition in the new, expanded edition of Cruel World, whose five new songs were largely written after the original album was handed in.
"I was super proud of Cruel World and, when you've got that in your back pocket, there's room to experiment and break some of your usual parameters."
The new tracks find Humberstone embracing a new persona – more confident, more flirtatious, a little salty – with music inspired by a playlist featuring Abba, Madonna and Robyn.
The single Too Cute To Be Lonely, external is a will-they/won't-they story set at a house party.
"Don't leave a girl upset, in such a pretty dress," she teases the object of her affections.
Terminally Yours takes place a couple of weeks later, when Humberstone realises she's fallen head-over-heels in love.
"Your stupid face is my sorry fate," she harrumphs, cross at herself. "For [expletive]'s sake, I'm in love."
Silver Sky, a gorgeous acoustic ballad, tells another side of the story, as she settles into her lover's arms and drifts into blissful reverie.
"I wrote that on a kind of Hail Mary trip, seeing what fell out of the air in Nashville," she reveals.
"We went over to [co-writer Maddie Diaz's] house, took a guitar into the garden and wrote Silver Sky outside, while all of these gorgeous red cardinals were singing around us.
"I usually write a lot about my mental health struggles, but I was just in the mood to write something that made me feel good."
Humberstone won the Brits Rising Star award in 2022, joining the ranks of former winners such as Sam Fender, Florence + The Machine and Adele
Not that her mental health issues are in the rear view mirror. Humberstone admits her stage nerves have only intensified since the release of Cruel World.

"It's the proudest I've been of any of my work and, for that reason, I struggled with shows because I felt a lot of pressure to go out and deliver it to the standard that I think people are expecting.
"But on the other hand, it's totally fine if you mess up or sing a wrong note. People can't connect to a pop star that feels too robotic and polished.
"So maybe my strength is that vulnerability, and I need to recognise that more."
That vulnerability has won Humberstone millions of fans, even if a hit single has (so far) eluded her.

And her audience keeps growing. In May this year, her breakout single Falling Asleep At The Wheel was awarded a silver disc... five years after its release, indicating that her songs have staying power in an era of disposable hits.
Astonishingly, this is news to Humberstone, who learns about the accolade during our interview. But it helps to clarify a thought that's been knocking around her head.
"If I'm going to be doing this for years to come, I've just got to keep making music that feels right, trusting my gut and realising there's no end point," she says.
"Reaching an end point would mean I've 'made it', but I think, maybe, that's a myth that doesn't really exist."

items.title: 'Can you believe it?': SpaceX catches part of its Starship rocket on return to Earth
paragraphs: SpaceX has successfully caught the top part of its huge Starship rocket on its return to Earth for the first time.
"Can you believe it?," a commentator said as large crowds cheered at the launch site in Texas.
The company had hoped to catch both the bottom and upper stages of the rocket using mechanical arms - nicknamed chopsticks - on its launch tower.
But the first catch of the rocket's booster was aborted a few minutes after the launch on Friday. The booster was diverted to the ocean, bursting into flames just above the sea.
The top part, known as the Ship, returned to Earth a few minutes behind schedule at around 15:20 local time (21:20 GMT) on Saturday, in the first-ever successful catch attempt.

items.title: ‘It’s an architect’s dream’: five beautiful eco buildings around the world
paragraphs: With construction accounting for more than a third of global emissions, sustainable architecture is central to the world meeting its climate targets. The following five creations from around the world exemplify how “green” buildings can also be beautiful.

In Tocantins, central Brazil, the Canuanã school is a boarding school whose pupils come from remote farming communities across the region. In 2017, architects gave the school’s 540 boarders two new “villages” of dormitories, one for girls and one for boys.

The buildings are made from locally sourced timber and earth bricks. A vast canopy shades the complex, and perforated brick walls let air pass through, so the bedrooms stay comfortable without air conditioning even when temperatures reach 45C. Under the roof, rooms open on to shady, landscaped courtyards and airy verandas.

David Mikhail, the co-founder of Mikhail Riches, a UK practice specialising in sustainable design, says: “It is absolutely fantastic. So beautiful. It does a lot with little resource, which is the essence of a sustainable approach.” He adds: “I love the economy of it, and the huge sense of place they managed to evoke through such elegant and limited means.”

The architects have said their biggest challenge was convincing pupils and teachers that earth, brick and timber could feel modern rather than old-fashioned. They managed to do so by listening to students through 10 days of workshops to understand what they wanted from the design.

The Green school in Bali is surrounded by jungle and promotes sustainability through learning in a natural environment. Since it opened in 2008, it has been built almost entirely in bamboo. Its gymnasium, the Arc, was completed in 2021.

Inspired by a mammal’s ribcage, the Arc’s bamboo arches span a 760 sq metre sports court without a single column interrupting the floor space. The arches support an undulating canopy, and natural ventilation comes from breezes that flow in at the base, while warm air escapes through vents at the top.

Bamboo is a highly sustainable building material because of how quickly it can regrow; large varieties reach building strength in just three to six years. “It is so fast-growing and sequesters a lot of carbon dioxide very quickly, so using it for building is a bit of a no-brainer if you can make it work,” says Mikhail. “And not only have they made it work, they’ve done it absolutely beautifully.”

Skellefteå, a small city just south of the Arctic Circle, is surrounded by 480,000 hectares (1.2m acres) of forest, and features wooden schools, a wooden road bridge, even a wooden multistorey car park. In 2021 it added Sara Kulturhus, a 20-storey cultural centre and hotel that is one of the tallest timber buildings in the world. It houses two theatres, a museum, an art gallery, the city library and a hotel.

The building is made of glulam – layers of timber glued together – and cross-laminated timber, a kind of super-sized plywood. The hotel rooms arrived as prefabricated wooden pods and were stacked into place. Building in wood saved a year in construction time compared with steel and concrete, while the timber came from trees harvested within 40 miles of the site, and replacement trees have since been planted.

“It promotes a love affair with wood and timber, and the localism of that in an area like Sweden is fabulous,” Mikhail says. “The lovely thing about cross-laminated timber is that the trees you use to make the panels don’t have to be elderly specimen trees. They can be relatively fast-grown and sustainably farmed.”

When the University of Tasmania was planning the redevelopment of its main campus in central Hobart, the architects chose to adapt what was already there rather than demolish it and start again. Two early 20th-century brick warehouses and a heritage-listed glass dome were stitched together into a single campus of classrooms and study spaces, which opened in February 2026.

At its heart is the glass dome, built in 1997. It is filled with about 3,200 native plants, including various species of ferns, and has an integrated watering, misting and fogging system that recreates rainforest-like growing conditions.

“You could argue the most sustainable building is actually no building, and the second most sustainable building is a refurbished old building,” says Mikhail. “That’s what this is: they’re taking existing structures and breathing new life into them, reimagining what they could be.”

On the site of a former brickworks in the Wiltshire countryside, this house has been built from the ground beneath it. Rammed earth, which has been used since the Neolithic period, is a building material made of soil that has been compacted layer by layer into thick walls. Here, clay-rich soil was dug up and mixed with rubble from demolished outbuildings and local limestone.

The earth is “unstabilised”, meaning no cement has been added, which makes this one of only a few UK buildings made that way. Unstabilised earth could, in principle, simply go back into the ground if the house were ever demolished.

Rammed earth’s thermal mass also evens out temperature and moisture indoors, which the architects say will matter more as the climate warms. “As a piece of architecture, I think it’s phenomenal,” says Mikhail. “It’s an architect’s dream, and I’m slightly envious of it, I’ll be honest.”
“It’s like a beautiful piece of jewellery, and it riffs on lots of really lovely sustainable ideas.”

items.title: Why so much love between Ireland and Garth Brooks?
paragraphs: Country music superstar Garth Brooks will perform a multi-city tour of Ireland in 2027
Fans of Garth Brooks will be brushing off their Stetsons and polishing their cowboy boots after the country music superstar announced he will be performing in multiple cities across Ireland in 2027.
The tour includes Belfast, Galway, Kilkenny, Limerick and Cork and will be the first time he has played in Northern Ireland since his King's Hall gig in November 1998.

The singer has said in the past that Ireland is his favourite place in the world to sing, and the love appears to be mutual as his first two Belfast concerts sold out, with an extra date already added.
So why has an American country music star remained so popular with Irish fans for so many years?
Cathy O'Reilly previously saw Garth Brooks live at two of his Dublin concerts in 2022
Cathy O'Reilly, who is originally from County Monaghan but lives in Belfast, managed to get her tickets for the very first show of Garth Brooks' tour on 21 May 2027 at Boucher Road Playing Fields.
She has already seen Brooks perform live before - twice during his run of concerts in Dublin in 2022 and her love of his music was passed on from her parents and uncles.
"It's growing up listening to him it brings me back to my childhood. My uncle gave me his cd, he didn't even buy me one - just gave me his because I loved him so much."
She believes the Irish link to the US and the fact that fans on the island give the best welcome to performers, are the reasons for Garth Brooks' popularity in Ireland.
"He [Garth Brooks] gives us energy and we're giving it back ten-fold nearly, and we're just so welcoming so he really enjoys coming here."
Garth Brooks last performed in Ireland in 2022
Peter Aiken, from Aiken Promotions, told Irish broadcaster RTÉ that the new Belfast gig is "red hot".
"There could be a fourth show in Belfast," he said.
Brooks is the biggest selling artist in US history and is the only artist to pass 200 million albums sold.
In 2014 about 400,000 fans booked tickets to five concerts he had planned for Dublin's Croke Park but Dublin City Council only granted permission for three of them.
Brooks said he would only perform all five concerts or none at all and so the shows were cancelled.
Stephen Butler performs as a Garth Brooks tribute act with the band Thunder Rolls and described his job as "easy" due to the love of Garth Brooks' fans
Stephen Butler from Newtownabbey performs as a Garth Brooks' tribute act with the band Thunder Rolls.
His love for the musician also goes back to his childhood.
"My mother was a fan when I was younger, she was always playing his music and buying his albums so I loved the songs.
"I knew, with me loving Garth and there being such a following in Ireland, I knew it was the right thing to do."
He went to the Dublin concert in 2022 and while he hasn't yet got tickets for the Ireland dates next year, he hopes to get tickets to at least one of them closer to the time.
Butler said in order to embody the stage persona of Garth Brooks, you "have to be passionate about his music"
"I was able to get four or five tickets about a week or two before the Croke Park shows, I'll definitely go - I have to go.
"His band is amazing, he's amazing, and his songs - he's got an endless amount of anthems."
Butler said in order to embody the stage persona of Garth Brooks, you "have to be passionate about his music".
"I'm not saying I'm as good as Garth Brooks, but I definitely have his enthusiasm.
"I talk about him and how much I love him throughout the songs and I just identify with them as much as I can.
"My job is easy, I just have to go on there and get everybody singing along with me."
Garth Brooks performing at the King's Hall in 1998
Butler says he thinks the reason Garth Brooks remains so enduringly popular in Ireland is because the people here identify so strongly with his songs.
"Everybody loves Friends In Low Places, people of Ireland love it, they love Callin' Baton Rouge.

"I speak to a lot of people after I play the shows and a lot of people identify with some of the words in the songs, they tell me about a relative that's passed and they seem to have some kind of identification with the songs Tomorrow Never Comes or Unanswered Prayers - it talks about love and about how Garth feels.
"And in amongst Thunder Rolls and the big hits that Garth has, he sings big rocky country rock and ballads, so it's exciting and it's sad - it's an emotional roller coaster," he said.
"And he's such a down-to-earth, genuine, caring person, he seems to be a good soul and I think people people identify with his personality.
"It's a big working-class country and they love someone that's genuine and that talks from the heart."

items.title: Even Grand Theft Auto's original creators haven't been able to play GTA 6
paragraphs: GTA 6 will feature brand new protagonists Jason and Lucia - the first playable female character in any of the 3D games
After a 13-year wait, two delays, and several high-profile leaks, the launch of Grand Theft Auto 6 is fast approaching.
The next chapter in the nearly 30-year-old series, where players explore open worlds and break the law, has created an extraordinary level of anticipation.
And with developer Rockstar Games keeping their biggest release yet, tightly under wraps, even the people who helped bring the original to life aren't getting special treatment.
"We're all waiting to see what they've done," Dave Jones, GTA's co-creator, tells me, sitting alongside the original game's writer and publicist, Brian Baglow.
Have either of them been able to play the new game ahead of launch?
Baglow shakes his head. He's not complaining, though. "I've got the pre-order," he says.
Brian Baglow (left) and Dave Jones, worked on the original Grand Theft Auto
The original Grand Theft Auto was released in 1997 in Dundee, Scotland by DMA Design, a relatively small team, at least judging by later games' standards.
Following its success with puzzle game Lemmings, the studio was toying around with the idea of making a racing game, initially called Race'n'Chase.
Sitting in the state-of-the-art computer lab at Dundee's Abertay University decades on, Jones tells me the developers still felt they had to bring something new to the table.
"At DMA, we always wanted to do something different," he says. "What was the unique spin we could put on it?"
Part of the answer, he said, came in what feels like a premise gamers take for granted now - "just getting out of the car".
He says the idea of being able to not only drive but switch and steal cars, running about on foot as you did so, meant "all of a sudden you had this interesting mix of gaming coming together".
The original Grand Theft Auto came out in 1997 and featured a top-down view in 2D
The team envisioned a game, Jones says, where you could play as both a criminal and a police officer.
But he quickly reconsidered the second option, as it would require players to behave "by the book".
"At some point we just said, you know what, it's way more fun playing the bad guy, so that's what the game was about," he adds.
Despite some of these novel approaches to the game's design, Jones says it was a "slow burn" in sales compared with Lemmings - partly because you had to "play it to get it".
"For the whole of the year that GTA came out, it just kept going and selling and selling," says Baglow.
"And we reckoned it was the word of mouth. The people who had played it going, oh my God, have you played this game?"

Its themes of criminality and violence sparked controversy - leading to debates in the UK Parliament and calls to ban the game. Yet it later transpired much of that was generated by the game's own publisher, BMG Interactive, as a viral marketing stunt.
"We just did things that we felt were fun," says Jones. "We never at any point kind of thought, should we do that? Is it controversial? We never thought that way."

Although relatively basic in appearance, with its top-down 2D view and more arcade-like graphics, the original game forged the blueprint for the series' signature satire still seen in much later, more advanced GTAs today.
Despite being set in an exaggerated version of American cities, its Scottishness could still be found in its humour and its outsider perspective, says Guardian video games editor Keza MacDonald.
"It's a deeply satirical game," she says. "It really takes aim at the hyper-individualist, hyper-capitalist nature of the US."

Partly out of necessity due to their comparatively low budget and the cost of real-world licenses, the team came up with cheeky brand names and fake radio stations players could listen to while driving around and causing mayhem.

Though some of these choices were made out of limitations, Baglow says the world-building is the element he's most proud of from the original, which is still a big part of what makes a title feel like GTA.
"It's the business names, it's the radio stations, it's the lyrics, it's the DJs," he says.
"Every part of that is making you believe that this environment you're in is a big cohesive whole."
The new game's location - the fictional state of Leonida - is expected to be double the size of GTA V's map
When GTA V launched in 2013, it made $1bn (£760m) in just three days - faster than any entertainment product had achieved at the time.
The series evolved into a cultural reference point itself - something people recognised, understood and even referenced outside gaming.
"I've seen movies where someone says 'don't go all GTA on me'... it was just surreal," says Jones.

MacDonald, joining me in Glasgow's gaming cafe, RCade, tells me there's an argument now that while earlier GTAs "took a lot" from the big screen, films are now "probably more influenced by GTA" than the other way round.
She says later titles in the series have a cinematic feel, but also reflect the distinct identity it has forged for itself.
As for why Jones believes the game has become such a cultural phenomenon, he says it's the simple fact that it's "based on real life".
"It's not like a lot of games like sci-fi or adventure or fantasy," he says. "There's nothing you have to learn about it, as long as you know a city and driving."
"It means so much to so many people," says Baglow, left
GTA 6 is expected to surpass its predecessor on every level, not only in scale and scope, but also in revenue.
Already, both PlayStation and Xbox, the two platforms the game is initially releasing on, have said the game has become the most pre-ordered title in their digital stores' history.
This may be partly down to its huge size (212GB), meaning many are pre-ordering to "pre-load" the game, ready to play it immediately at launch rather than waiting to download it.

The hype has spilt into the real world, with London's Selfridges transformed into a Vice City-themed pop-up attraction and fictional GTA brands appearing on billboards across Miami, the city that inspired the game.
"Everyone is extremely excited for this," says MacDonald.
"It's hoping to be a shot in the arm for the general games industry, but also every player is looking to see what Rockstar's been doing for all this time.
"It's very rare that we have this one massive game that everybody's going to be, if not playing, then certainly interested in."
Do Jones and Baglow ever wish they were still working on the game now, given the huge amount of global attention focused on it?
"I think everybody loves having their time on it, for one, two, three versions," Jones says.
"But eventually you want to go off and do other things as well."
Baglow adds that watching "the rest of the world fall in love with the game over the last 29 years has just been joyful".
"It means so much to so many people - it's been fantastic."

items.title: Brand, Walliams and MAFS: Is this a reckoning for the entertainment industry?
paragraphs: This week, the dark side of television has come crashing into the open.
On Monday, disgraced entertainer Russell Brand was jailed for rape and sexual assault.
Twenty-four hours later, author and comedian David Walliams was unmasked and accused of preying on young women.
By Friday the Metropolitan Police had launched an investigation into further allegations about him.
Also in the last week, Married at First Sight UK has been cancelled following allegations of rape on the hit TV show.
These are all very different stories, but each can be seen as a major reckoning with abuse of power and culture in the industry.
In reality, the glut of recent days is something of a coincidence.
All these revelations began with journalistic investigations that started years ago.

From my own experience - including in my Panorama on Married at First Sight UK - I know investigations typically take a very long time to reach a conclusion, from initial tip-off, to evidence-gathering, corroboration, getting responses, and eventually reporting.
"The truth is, these stories have a long build up. It can be incredibly difficult to get [them] in the papers," Sunday Times columnist Hadley Freeman told me.
In the case of Brand, there was then a police investigation too, before an outcome was reached in court.
Together these stories represent the consequences of changes that began years ago, rather than a sudden cultural shift in the entertainment industry.
It should also be said that Walliams denies the allegations against him. The men accused of rape and sexual misconduct on MAFS UK have also denied all the allegations.

What has changed is that women (because it almost always is women) have seen others speaking up - which, according to broadcaster Kirsty Wark, has given them "courage to do the same". She describes those who have come forward as "beyond brave".
When looking at what’s driving more women to speak up, much can be traced back to the revelations about Harvey Weinstein and the #MeToo movement.
It changed the perception of whether victims would be believed.
In the past, women alleging this sort of behaviour faced barriers - being seen as opportunistic, fearing retaliation, believing they might be the only one.
Now, there can be a snowball effect. Once one, two or three come forward, that prompts others to revisit their experiences - which they may have dismissed or subdued.
"There is more of a sense that you will now be listened to," said Freeman.
It's also clear that when women see action taken, it can encourage others to speak up as well - as it helps counter the widely-held assumption that reporting abuse results in nothing.

When another high-profile man, MasterChef presenter Gregg Wallace, faced accusations of a very different and much lesser order, relating mostly to inappropriate sexual language and humour, the reaction was similar.

Last summer, an independent inquiry upheld dozens of claims against him, and he was sacked. Wallace said "none of the serious allegations" against him had been upheld but that he was "deeply sorry for any distress caused".
One young woman I spoke to in my investigation into Wallace texted me at the time, to give her reaction to his sacking.
"I really believe this will encourage young girls going into the TV industry to have the courage to speak up, if they feel something is wrong," she told me.
But unions say it is still difficult for junior freelance workers, who often find their income unstable and unpredictable, to speak up.
Vulnerable workers "continue to fear raising concerns", said head of broadcast union Bectu, Philippa Childs.
She's echoed by Freeman, who said an "attitude of protecting the talent" remained.

"There will always be wealthy famous predators," she said. But, she added: "Hopefully more and more people at TV stations and movie studios are willing to hear these young people and will take them seriously”.
For more senior people in TV, raising the alarm can also be difficult.

Earlier this week, comedian Lucy Beaumont told Sky News: "The reason high-profile people are not saying anything is because they lose work, because you're seen that you might be a trouble causer. It does need to be said that there needs to be some intervention."
Social media has also played a role in encouraging people to speak up.
And policing investigations have had to keep pace - and adapt - with media scrutiny often prompting authorities to investigate.
Attitudes towards women who speak up are also starting to change – although not always.
Some of what unfolded in court during the Russell Brand case felt like a throwback to how rape cases used to be conducted.
Many have commented on Brand's lawyer's defence tactics against the accusers on the stand - behaviour Freeman said would have been "standard" in the past.
But Freeman noted it was heartening to hear the judge’s remarks in summing up the case - which have also been widely shared by women online and praised for dispelling rape myths.
When Mr Justice Bennathan sentenced Brand to ten-and-a-half years, he told him: "Whatever women wear, wherever they go, indeed whatever they drink, they retain the right to say no."
"I think attitudes have changed,” said Freeman. “It doesn't mean those assaults don't happen any more but attitudes around them have changed.”
Events of the past few weeks highlight how figures who rose to prominence in the nineties and noughties did so in an era with different standards.
Lad culture and celebrity status shielded Brand and others from scrutiny.
Now, behaviour once dismissed as eccentricity or womanising is increasingly being reassessed and called out. Times are catching up with some men of that era.
However, it would be an error to assume this sort of behaviour is confined to the past.
"This is not just about nineties/noughties culture," Wark told me. "It can't be dismissed as a hangover of the past, this is about right now and the industry changes that must happen.
"There will be more cases to come, sexual abuse, coercive control, verbal and physical abuse. It is not OK, and it never was OK."
This week, comedian Deborah Frances-White told BBC Radio 4's The World at One that young women were "definitely" still being exploited in the comedy industry.
And in the past few days, I've had tip-offs about other celebrities allegedly abusing their power. No doubt other journalists have too.
None of those is reportable, yet. As Freeman said: "There are other names out there, but you and I couldn't name them as we'd be sued".

But one "cheering thing", she said, was that the sort of jokes and innuendos from the nineties and noughties, or even the optics of seeing a much older man with a younger girl would no longer be "glossed over".
"It wouldn't be laughed at, and it wouldn't be 'nudge nudge'," Freeman said. "That kind of open, in your face, weirdness won't happen any more".
"On the downside, that may make it harder to identify predators, if it means these things are kept more in the shadows."
Then there’s the use of gagging orders and other legal routes often used by celebrities and media organisations to stop women speaking out.
Last week, a High Court judge rejected an injunction request by Walliams, clearing the way for him to be named.

"There are lots of barriers to speaking out, and those that have access to wealth or fame will often use legal measures to deter alleged victims from doing so," Harriet Wistrich, from the Centre for Women's Justice, told me.
This week, multiple government ministers have spoken against non-disclosure agreements and called for further restrictions on their use.
Next week, Culture Secretary Lisa Nandy will convene industry leaders to urge them to improve safeguarding practices - while Channel 4 bosses are due to appear in front an MPs on Tuesday.
When MAFS UK was cancelled, Channel 4 said the programme had "run its course" and apologised to the women involved in the investigation.
It said the review found that in Channel 4 and production company CPL's handling of the issues raised at the time, there was no breach of Ofcom's broadcasting code.
There is growing recognition that those at the top of media organisations have a responsibility to root out abuse. It can't just be down to the victims.
"People in positions of power have a duty to speak up too," said Wark.

"Broadcasters, production companies and those financing productions all have a responsibility to ensure protections are upheld," added Josephine Brassey, from Women in Film and TV, while Philippa Childs urged the creative industries to accept that their current internal reporting mechanisms were "inadequate".
What everyone seems to agree on is that this can't be another empty tipping point with no real, lasting change.
Maybe this time it could really be a watershed moment.
If you have more information about this story, you can reach Noor by email at noor.nanji@bbc.co.uk

items.title: Street photography through an Australian lens – in pictures
paragraphs: From a sleepy restaurant to a climbing leopard, the Australian Street Photography awards celebrate the best contemporary street photos taken by Australians. Twenty-five finalists have been selected by an independent jury through Aussie Street, a platform for photographers. The pictures celebrate ordinary public life through images of observation, chance, humour, tension, ambiguity and human connection.
